Abdul Quayum with Ali Reza Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Monzoorul Karim Kazal, Advocate ------ For the Opposite-Parties.
parties:
Komola Kanta Mokhupaddaya ------ Petitioner
VS
Salam Jomadder and others ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-17 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 15-3-2003 passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 80 of 2002 reversing those dated 17-3-2002 passed by the Assistant Judge, Bakergonj in Title Suit No. 246 of 1985 dismissing the suit should not be set-aside.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the rule are that the opposite parties as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 246 of 1986 for declaration that the `kha' schedule decree regarding the Ka schedule land is false, fraudulent, collusive, concocted and not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. It is stated in the plaint that the suit property was auction sold in Title Suit No. 251 of 1902 and Decree Execution Case No; 79 of 1903 and the possession was delivered on 19-9-1904 by Modhusudon chattapaddya and subsequently one Samcharan Chattapaddya took lease of the said property in 1333 BS in favour of the plaintiffs. Thereafter, the suit land .was recorded in the name of Asmot Ali Jomadder whose name was recorded in RS Khatian being No. 3279.

4. It is further stated in the plaint that they came to know from one Muzaffar Howlader on 11-3-1385 BS that the `kha' scheduled land was fraudulently decreed ex-parte on 19-3-1958 in Title Suit No. 333 of 1957 in the Court of Munsif 3rd Court, Barisal suppressing the summons upon the defendants of the aforesaid suit and hence the suit.

5. The defendant .appeared in the suit by filing written statements stating that his father auction purchased the suit land in the benami of Madhu Sudan who made kolekarsa pattan to one Jagat Chandra Das, his son Bisha Nath Das inherited the land and died without any issue. The wife of Sree Sushila Bala Dasi for paying rents and taxes of the Estate and for other charges including of favored charge of her late husband transferred the suit land on 21-4-1942 to the defendant No. 1 on the basis of which he filed the suit being No. 333 of 1957 against the. wrong record of right in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor Asmot Ali Jomadder who being the employee and collusively recorded his name and after knowing about the aforesaid record suit No. 333 of 1957 was filed and subsequently after duly serving the summons upon the defendant suit was decreed on 19-3-1958 with the full knowledge of the present plaintiffs and thus the suit is liable to be dismissed.

6. The trial court after, hearing the parties by its judgment and decree dated 17-3-2002 dismissed the suit of the plaintiff against which the defendants as appellants preferred Title Appeal No. 80 of 2002 before the District Judge, Barisal and on transfer it was heard by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Barisal who by his judgment and decree dated 15-3-2003 allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and decreed the suit of the plaintiff.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the appellate court defendant-respondent-petitioner preferred revisional application before this court and obtained the present rule.

8. At the time of hearing Mr Abdul Quayum with Mr Md Ali Reza, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the petitioner. On the other hand, Mr Monzoorul Karim Kazal, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

9. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner submits that the plaintiffs-opposite parties could not prove their case by adducing oral and documentary evidence and on considering the evidence. on record and the exhibits produced by the parties trial court rightly dismissed the suit of the plaintiff but the appellate court on misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record and without proper perusal of the exhibits improperly decreed the suit of the plaintiff by setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court by which committed an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

10. Learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that the trial court after framing proper issues discussed all the issues and decided the same based upon the evidence and the exhibits on record but the appellate court without proper reversal of those findings of the trial court allowed the appeal without deciding those issues not based upon the correct appreciation of the law and facts of the case. Thus, the appellate court committed an error of law which occasioned a failure of justice.

11. He also submits that the decree challenged by the plaintiff was passed on 19-3-1958 and the present suit was filed on 3-1-1979 i.e. after 20 years of the alleged decree. Thus, the suit is barred by limitation and the appellate court without considering the aforesaid fact and without giving proper reasoning on this point arrived at a wrong decision that the suit is not barred by limitation.

12. He further submits that the plaintiff opposite parties claimed in the `ka' schedule land through Asmot Ali Jomadder who attested the defendant's kabla deed dated 21-4-1942 and his signature was identified by his own son Abdul Ali Jamadder DW 2 and in his deposition Abdul Ali Jamadder stated that his father never possessed `ka' schedule land but the appellate court without considering the aforesaid important evidence on record improperly reversed the judgment of the trial court by which committed an error of law in the decision' occasioning failure of justice.

13. He next submits that the appellate court as the last court of fact without proper appreciation of the evidence of the parties and without applying judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the 'case improperly passed the impugned judgment and decree by ignoring the evidence of the DWs both oral and documentary though the plaintiffs opposite parties by adducing oral and documentary evidence could not prove their case.

14. He also submits that the trial court after proper discussion of the evidence found that the defendants have possession in the suit land long before and the appellate court without proper appreciation of the evidence of the D.Ws. wrongly held that the defendants have no title and possession of the suit land.

15. Finally the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court is not a proper judgment in the eye of law which should be set-aside for the ends of justice.

16. On the other hand, Mr Monzoorul Karim Kazal, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties contended that the appellate court as the last court of fact after proper discussion of the evidence on record and the exhibits rightly and properly reversed the judgment passed by the trial court by which the trial court wrongly held that the plaintiff could not prove their case by adducing oral and documentary evidence on record.

17. He further submits that the appellate court after independent discussion of the evidence on record found that the plaintiffs have title and possession over the suit land and their name was recorded in RS and SA Khatian and they are paying rent to the Government and on considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances the appellate court arrived at a correct decision that the plaintiffs have title and possession over the suit land.

18. He also submits that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 333 of 1957 on 19-3-1958 was obtained fraudulently by suppressing the summons and on considering the aforesaid fact appellate court properly found that the plaintiffs opposite parties have no knowledge about the aforesaid ex-parte decree and thus the suit is not barred by limitation.

19. It is further contended by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties that the appellate court properly arrived at a decision that the decree obtained on 19-3-1958 is not acted upon and the defendants have no possession in the suit land.

20. He finally argued that the appellate court as the last court of fact arrived at a proper decision on considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances and there is no error of law in the decision which occasioned any failure of justice. Thus, the rule is liable to be discharged.

21. I have heard the learned Advocate for both the parties and perused the revisional application along with the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court as well as the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and examined the papers annexed with the revisional application and also the exhibits. I have also perused the lower court records.

22. Since, the impugned judgment is a judgment of reversal, let us examine the judgment passed by the courts below.

23. The trial court framed as many as 6 issues in the suit. Wherefrom issue No.3- Whether the suit is barred by limitation? Issue No. 4- Whether the plaintiffs have title and possession in the 'ka' schedule land? Issue No. 5- Whether the `kha' schedule decree is liable to be set-aside? These are the main issues framed by the trial court.

24. While discussing the issue No.4 trial court found that admittedly Modhu Sudan Chattapaddya purchased the suit land in auction and the claim of the plaintiff is that Modhu Sudan Chattapaddya himself purchased the auction. On the other hand, the defendants claim is that his father Shama charan Mukhapaddya purchased the auction in Benami of Modhu Sudan Chattapaddya.

25. The trial court discussed the plaintiff's claim that the predecessor of the plaintiff Asmat Ali Zomadder was the owner of the suit land. After auction, Samacharan Mukhapaddaya obtaining kabuliyat from Asmat Ali Zomadder possessing the suit land. Thereafter, Samacharan Mukhapaddaya again leased out the suit land to Asmat Ali Zomadder and RS record was in the name of Asmat Ali Zomadder.

26. The trial court discussed the case of the defendant that Samacharan purchased the auction in Benami of Madhu Sudan Chattapaddaya and Jagot Chandra took pattan from Shama Charan Mukhapaddaya who died leaving behind his son Bishanath; Bishanath died leaving his wife Sushila Bala without any issue; Sushila Bala transferred the suit land to the defendant on 21-4-1942 by a registered deed. The predecessor of the plaintiff Asmat Ali Zomadder was employee of the defendant and he collusively recorded his name in RS operation.

27. The trial court also discussed that in the original plaint, the plaintiff's claim is that Jagot Chandra Das was the owner of the suit land. Later on it was amended by the plaintiff on 3-1-1979. But PW1 Mozahar Ali Zomadder in his cross-examination admitted that earlier Jagot Chandra Das was the owner and before that Shama Charan was the owner. Trial court found that from the above admission of the PW 1 it appears that Jagot Chandra Das was in possession and he had title in the suit land.

28. The trial court also found that Asmat Ali Zomaddar was an employee of the father of the defendant. Thus, the claim of the plaintiff is that Shamaya Charan took pattan from Asmat is not believable in the then social condition.

29. Trial court further found that in his cross-examination PW 1 admitted that Sushila Bala is the wife of Bishanath, son of Jagot Chandra. From the recital of the deed dated 21-4-1942 (exhibit-'Ica') it appears that Sushila Bala transferred the suit land for legal necessity to the defendant No.1 and in the aforesaid deed the father of the plaintiffs Asmat Ali was an attesting witness and it was identified by his son Abdul Ali son of Asmat Ali Zomadder DW 2. Trial court also found that in his cross-examination PW 1 admitted that Asmat Ali Zomaddar was an employee of his father Shama Charan and, as such, he was experienced about the land purpose. Thus, the argument made by the plaintiff that Asmat Ali had no knowledge about the recital and contents of the aforesaid deed, is not at all believable.

30. It is further found by the trial court that from the exhibit-ka the RS Khatian No. 3279, it appears that Shama Charan was the original owner of the suit land and his name was recorded in RS operation which was admitted by the plaintiff.

31. Trial court also found that in his evidence DW 2 stated that the suit land is owning and possessing by the defendant and the record in the name of the plaintiff is wrong.

32. On considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances and the evidence on record trial court found that the claim of the plaintiff that Asmat Ali took pattan from Shama Charan has not been proved, rather the claim of the defendant that the ownership of Jagot Chandra by way of kolkarsha and the subsequent transfer to the defendant No.1 has been proved. Thus, the plaintiffs have no title in the suit land.

33. Trial court while deciding the possession of the suit land discussed the evidence of the P.Ws. and the DWs. Trial court discussed the evidence of PWs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and also discussed the evidence of DWs 1, 2, 3 and relying upon the evidence of DW 2 Abdul Ali Zomadder, who is the son of Asmat Ali Zomadder, the predecessors of the plaintiffs and the evidence of the DW 3, found that the defendants are in possession of the suit land and the plaintiff witness could not prove that the plaintiffs are in possession in the suit land.

34. While discussing the issue No.3-Whether the suit is barred by limitation? Trial Court found that the plaintiff witness in their deposition claimed that they have no knowledge about the ex-parte decree and it was obtained fraudulently and at first they came to know about the decree on 11-8-1385 BS from Mozahar Howlader in presence of Nur Mohammad Talukder of village Bharpasha, though the plaintiffs adduced 6 witnesses, but they could not produce the aforesaid Nur Mohammad Talukder or Mozahar Howlader as witness in support of their first knowledge.

35. Trial court found that only PW 4 Sharif Mosharaf Hossain, in his deposition stated that on 11th Agrahayan, 1385 BS Mozaffar Howlader informed about the aforesaid decree in presence of him to the plaintiff No. 1 and Nur Mohammad was present at that time but the plaintiff, in the plaint, did not mention the name of aforesaid witness Sharif Mosharaf Hossain.

36. Trial court further found that on an application filed by the plaintiff the record of Title Suit No. 333 of 1957 was called for and it appears from the order sheet that the summons were duly served upon the defendants of the aforesaid suit.

37. On considering that the plaintiff could not prove the knowledge about the decree of 1958 by adducing witnesses mentioned in the plaint of the suit and on considering that in the order sheet it is found that the summons were duly served upon the defendants, the decree passed on 19-3-1958 was passed in accordance with law and is valid in the eye of law and the plaintiffs claim has not been proved that they had no knowledge about the aforesaid decree. Thus, the present suit which was filed on 3-1-1979 is barred by limitation. While deciding the issue No. 5 trial court found that the notice and summons were duly served upon the defendants i.e. the present plaintiff's in Title suit No. 333 of 1957.

38. Moreover, the plaintiff could not prove their title in the suit land and the decree dated 19-3-1958 is not liable to be set-aside and with the aforesaid findings trial court arrived at a decision that the plaintiff could not prove their case by adducing oral and documentary evidence and dismissed the suit of the plaintiff.

39. On its turn, the appellate court while disposing of the appeal heard the learned

Advocates for both the parties, perused the memo of appeal, evidence of the witnesses and the exhibits.

40. The appellate court discussed the claim of the plaintiff and the defendant. The appellate court found that Shamacharan was the original owner of the suit land and his name was recorded in R.S. operation and the name of Asmat Ali was recorded as tenant under Shamacharan. The plaintiff side produced two rent receipts-one is in 1360 BS and 2nd one is 1384 BS in the year of 1978 from which it appears that the rent was paid up to 1384 BS but no rent receipt was produced by the defendant side that they have paid any rent to the Government.

41. The appellate court further found that the defendant could not produce any documents that Jagot Chandra Das took pattan from the original owner thus, by the deed which was transferred to the defendant No. 1 by Sushila Bala, has no basis. There is no existence of title in the name of the defendant No. 1. The findings of the trial court on this regard that the plaintiff could not prove their title by way of inheritance in the suit land, is not correct.

42. The appellate court also found that P.W.4 Sharif Mosharaf Hossain in his deposition stated that at first the plaintiff came to know about the disputed decree on 21-4-1978 and the plaintiff within 1 (one) year filed the suit and the suit is not barred by limitation.

43. The appellate court on the aforesaid discussion found that the plaintiffs have title in the `ka' schedule land and the defendant's decree in Title Suit No. 333 of 1957 is liable to be set-aside which was obtained ex-parte. With the aforesaid findings, the appellate court allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court.

44. At the trial, trial court framed issues on whether the plaintiffs have any right, title, interest and possession in the suit property and also framed issues whether the kha' schedule decree is liable to be set-aside.

45. It is decided by the trial court that the suit is barred by limitation. The trial court took decision considering two points-1) The plaintiff could not prove their knowledge about the date of decree dated 19-3-1958. 2) The summons and notices were duly served upon the defendants of the Title Suit No. 333 of 1957. On the other hand, the appellate court reversed the findings of the trial court that PW 4 Mosharaf Hossain proved the date of knowledge and from that date within 1 (one) year the suit was filed. Thus, the suit is not barred by limitation. Now, let us see from the record and the evidence that which findings of the courts below is correct and based oh evidence on record.

46. In paragraph-4 of the plaint it is stated that the plaintiff came to know on 11th Agrahayan, 1385 from one Mozaffar Howlader of Vorpasha village in presence of Nur Mohammad Talukder, thereafter, obtaining certified copy of the aforesaid decree on 21-4-1978 plaintiff filed the suit on 3-1-1979.

47. It appears from the evidence on record that in support of the statement given in paragraph 4 the plaintiff could not produce Mozaffar Howlader and Nur Mohammad Talukder before the court to prove the date of knowledge according to the plaint.

48. From the order sheet of the Title Suit No. 333 of 1957 found that the notices and summons were duly served upon the defendants. So, the suit was filed after long laps of 21 years of the alleged decree. From the record of Title Suit No. 333 of 1957 and from the order sheet it is found that order No. 4 dated 21-1-1958 plaintiff filed Hazira, summons were served duly but the defendant was absent. Considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the suit issued registered card with A/D upon the defendants fixing next date on 11-2-1958 for appearance of the parties.

49. Order No. 5 dated 11-2-1958 plaintiff files hajira, Order No. 6 dated 20-2-1958 plaintiff files hajira along with postal receipts, Order No.7 dated 4-3-1957 plaintiff files hajira, and Order No.8 dated 19-3-1958 plaintiff files hajira. Defendants take no steps though registered cards have been issued and served and are found absent on repeated calls. The suit is taken up for ex-parte hearing. PW 1, Krishnakanta Mukhopadhya is examined. Documents marked exhibits-1, 2, 3-3(c). Case is CF on plaint is sufficient. The suit is decreed ex-parte.

50. The appellate court as the last court of fact when deciding the issue did not at all consider this documents and improperly found that P.W.4 Mosharaf Hossain proved the date of knowledge by adducing evidence so, the suit is not barred by limitation.

51. In the case of Ahmedur Rahman Chowdhury vs Braja Mohan Saha reported in 3 DLR 46 wherein it is held, "An application under Order IX, rule 13 CPC for setting aside an ex-parte decree. Returns of the service of summons having been destroyed, entries in the order-sheet were relied on for the finding that the summonses were duly served, presuming under illustration (E) of Sec. 114 of the Evidence Act that the official acts were duly performed."

52. The learned Advocate for the petitioner also referred to a decision in the case of Mrs Shamsun Nahar Begum vs Mr Salauddin Ahmed reported in 4 MLR (AD) 405 = 4 BLC (AD) 285 wherein it is held, "Code of Civil Procedure, 1908-Orer 9 rule 13-Exparte decree-Setting aside of-service of summons-proof of date of knowledge-Order 5 rule I 9B(2)-Legal position of service of summons by registered post with acknowledgment due slip-Even if the acknowledgment due slip is not received within 30 days of the date of sending the summons by registered post, the court shall declare that the summons upon the defendant has been duly served."

53. From the order No. 4 of Title Suit No. 333 of 1957 it appears that the learned Judge applying judicial mind to the fact passed an order for serving notices upon the defendant by postal A/D and from the order No.8 it appears that the learned Judge confirming the serving of the summons that it was duly served upon the defendants taken up the case for ex-parte hearing.

54. Now, in the present suit the plaintiffs claim is that they have no knowledge about the ex-parte decree and first came to know on 11th Agrahayan, 1385 BS which was stated in paragraph 4 of the plaint and it is stated in the plaint that the plaintiff obtained knowledge from one Mozahar Howlader and Nur Mohammad Talukder but none of them was produced as witness in support of the aforesaid claim. So, the plaintiff of the present suit could prove by adducing evidence about the date of knowledge and, as such, the suit is barred by limitation. Thus, the existence and validity of the decree dated 19- 3-1958 is not liable to be set-aside.

55. Learned Advocate for the opposite parties in this regard referred to a decision in the case of Md Wazed All Sardar vs Md Afsaruddin Sardar reported in 16 BLD (AD) 4 = 1 BLC (AD) 179 wherein it is held, "Once the defendant denies service of summons upon him the whole onus shifts to the plaintiff who has to prove satisfactorily that summons was in fact duly served."

56. It is mentioned above that in the present suit plaintiff has miserably failed to produce those two persons from whom the plaintiff got knowledge. Though, the plaintiff adduced 6 witnesses. Only PW 4 in his deposition stated that he was present but in the plaint his name was not mentioned that he was present at the time of alleged knowledge stated in paragraph-4 or any other paragraph in the plaint.

57. Thus, on perusal of the order sheet of the Title Suit No. 333 of 1957 and paragraph-4 of the present plaint and the evidence of the P.Ws. it may be concluded that the plaintiff in the present suit could not prove the alleged date of knowledge which was stated in paragraph-4 and on the other hand from the order sheet of the earlier suit it appears that the notices and summons were duly served and the decree was passed in accordance with law in the earlier Title Suit filed by the defendants. Thus, the appellate court wrongly found that the suit is not barred by limitation and the decision arrived at by the trial court is proper that the suit is barred by limitation.

58. Now, if the suit is barred by limitation then the other issues which were decided by the courts below has a little value to be decided, yet from the discussions it appears that the appellate court did not discuss the evidence on record independently while deciding the question of title and possession of the suit in question. As the last court of fact the appellate court without following the provision of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure passed the impugned judgment and decree in a slipshod manner and the judgment and decree of the appellate court has been passed as a non-speaking judgment, as all the issues framed by the trial court were not discussed and reversed by the appellate court.

59. In this regard learned Advocate for the opposite parties referred to a decision in the case of Abdul Motaleb vs Md Ershad Ali reported in 18 BLD (AD) 121 = 4 BLC (AD) 150 wherein it is held, "section 115 Non-speaking Order-Simply because the impugned order was not a speaking order, could not by itself be a valid ground for interference by the High Court Division Unless it can be shown that the subordinate Court has committed any error of law 'resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice'."

60. Referring this decision learned Advocate for the opposite parties argued that though the appellate court did not properly discussed the evidence on record and reversed the findings of the trial court but the decision arrived at by the appellate court resulted no failure of justice.

61. It is discussed above that while deciding the issues of limitation and as well as the main issue that the decree obtained ex-parte is liable to be set-aside. The learned Judge of the appellate court without any discussion and without perusing the documents of the earlier Title Suit No. 333 of 1957 setting-aside the judgment of the trial court and declared the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land.

62. The trial court discussed the question of title of the parties. The trial court believed the evidence of DW 2 Abdul Ali Zomadder who is the son of Asmat Ali Zomadder and attesting witness of the deed dated 21-4-1942 exhibit-Ka by which the suit land was transferred to the defendant No. 1 by Sushila Bala which is a registered deed.

63. The argument advanced by the plaintiff-opposite parties that Asmat Ali Zomaddar had no knowledge about the recital of the deed. Trial court disbelieved this proposition of the plaintiffs considering that Asmat Ali was an employee of the predecessor of the defendant Shama Charan Mukhapaddaya and it is admitted by the plaintiff side. If so, it is not believable that without knowing about the contents of the deed Asmat Ali Zomaddar signed as attesting witness.

64. In this regard, the learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to a decision in the case of Shrish Chandra Das vs Sri Sri Chatteswari Debj Bigraha represented by shebajts Chandra Sekhar Chakraborty reported in 6 BLD (AD) 291 = 38 DLR (AD) 283 wherein it is held, "Attesting of a document-When attestation makes one a consenting 'party-Where it is shown by other evidence that when becoming an attesting witness, a person must have fully understood what the transaction was, his attestation may support the inference that he was a consenting party. He cannot take advantage of his own wrong-He cannot both approbate and reprobate at the same time-Transfer of Property Act (IV of 1882)."

65. From the aforesaid decisions and the deposition of the PW 2 Abdul Ali Zomaddar the son of Asmat Ali Zomaddar who is an attesting witness of the deed dated 19-4-1942 and DW 2 identified the signature of his father, so, it is believable that Asmat Ali Zomaddar knowing fully well about the contents of the deed and signed over it and his son denied the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land.

66. Thus, this point decided by the appellate court that the plaintiffs have title and possession over the suit land is a wrong finding and not based upon the evidence and documents on records and the exhibits.

67. Learned Advocate for the petitioner also referred to a decision in the case of Md Ibrahim vs .Md Alauddin reported in 27 DLR 413 wherein it is held, "Matters not specifically raised in pleadings-Parties cannot be allowed to lead evidence on such matters."

68. And also in the case of Azmal Khan vs Md Afzal Khan reported in 64 DLR (AD) 17 wherein it is held, "Order VI, rule 17 & section 153 Partition Suit-Where a party has admitted certain facts, he cannot subsequently be allowed to disown those admissions by way of amendment and if such prayer is allowed, it will, instead of promoting ends of justice, defeat the ends of justice."

<u>69. From the evidence it appears that in the plaint, plaintiffs admitted the title of the predecessor of the defendant but after deposition of the PW 1 which was ended on 29-3-1987 and prayer of the plaint was amended on 25-7-2001 and PW 1 in his cross-examination admitted that Jagot Chandra was the earlier owner of the suit land. So, admitting the tile or ownership of any party in evidence, that cannot be denied by an amendment of the paint later on.</u>

70. The trial court on considering the deposition of the DWs properly found that Sushila Bala has title and interest in the suit land through Jagot Chandra and the plaintiff could not prove their title and possession on this point and the appellate court on wrong appreciation of the evidence and the documents on record decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff which is liable to be set-aside.

<u>71. From the discussions made above and on consideration of the evidence and the exhibits on record and the decisions referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioners, I am of the view that the appellate court as the last court of fact without proper discussion of the evidence on record independently and without applying judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and without following the provision of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure passed the impugned judgment and decree by setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court which was passed properly after framing proper issues and discussing those issues properly and independently. Thus, the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court cannot be sustained in law and is liable to be set aside.</u>

72. Accordingly, the rule succeeds.

73. In the result, the rule is made absolute.

74. The impugned judgment and decree dated 15-3-2003 passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 80 of 2002 is hereby set-aside. The judgment and decree dated 17-3-2002 passed by the Assistant Judge, Bakergonj in Title Suit No. 246 of 1985 is restored.

75. Accordingly, the suit is dismissed.

76. The order of status-quo granted earlier by this court is hereby vacated.

Send down the lower court records along with a copy of this judgment at once.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 13th of March, 2014 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2866 of 2010)
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 13.03.2014 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2866 of 2010 discharging the Rule.

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the appellant as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.4007 of 2008 in the Court of Assistant Judge, 8th Court, Dohar, Dhaka for declaration. She stated that her husband died on 16.12.1982 leaving behind four sons named Hazi Kamal Uddin, Hazi Hafez Sharif Uddin (defendant No.1), Hazi Md. Tauz Uddin and Hazi Md. Nasir Uddin and three daughters named Most. Kaniz Fatema, Most. Anisa Khatun and Most. Rahisa Khatun and herself and they became the owner of the suit property according to Shariah Law. The disputed house was bought in the name of the plaintiff from Hafiz Nuruddin on 18.01.1972 through registered saf-kabala No.314. Thereafter, defendant No.1 at the end of the year 1994 told the plaintiff to sign some written documents which were necessary for the sale of their business and the plaintiff without knowing the contents of the documents on bona fide belief signed the documents. Thereafter, defendant No.1 got the suit property mutated in his name through Namjari Jama Bhag Case No.3999 of 1994-1995 and the plaintiff having collected the documents relating to mutation and the photocopy of affidavit came to know that defendant No.1 claimed that the plaintiff orally gifted the suit property by an affidavit through notary public on 10.12.1994. The plaintiff claimed that she never gifted the suit property to defendant No.1 and the defendant falsely created and fabricated the deed since the witnesses of the said affidavit made declaration before a notary public that the plaintiff never gifted the suit land before them and the other witnesses died. The plaintiff then made affidavit No.1164/2003 on 30.09.2003 before the Magistrate, 1st class, denying the affidavit made on 10.12.1994. Thereafter, defendant No.1 in order to grab the property gifted the same to his sons named Hazi Md. Zakir Uddin and Hazi Md. Taher Uddin (defendant Nos.2 and 3 respectively). The plaintiff claimed that when the plaintiff went to pay the tax of the suit land on September, 2003, she came to know about Namjari Jama Bhag Case Nos.3999 of 1994-1995 and 15 of 2005 and after attempts for meditation, they failed to reach a decision and from that failure, the cause of action for the suit arose in May, 2008.

3. The defendants contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and the suit was barred by law of limitation. The defendants there-after stated that the disputed house was bought in the name of the successors of Hazi Faiz Uddin. After the death of Hazi Faiz Uddin, the successors amicably made a partition deed through notary public wherein the plaintiff got the disputed house along with other property. Thereafter the plaintiff having been charmed by the natural love and affection, gifted the suit property to her son, i.e. defendant No.1 in front of notary public through registered affidavit No.30 dated 10.12.1994. Defendant No.1 therefore got his name mutated through Namjari Case No.3999 of 1994-1995 and enjoyed the suit property by way of tenancy. When the defendant went to mutate his name in the City Corporation, the plaintiff was informed of the matter through notice and the plaintiff thereafter in front of Kamal Uddin Kabul, i.e. Ward Commissioner of Ward No.64 issued a no objection letter dated 09.09.1995. Thereafter, defendant No.1 mutated his name and paid rent, tax accordingly. Therefore, the name of defendant No.2 was recorded in Dhaka City Survey. The plaintiff informed the Deputy Taxes Commissioner, Circle-20 about the gift and paid income tax without the disputed house in the income tax statement. The TIN number of the plaintiff was 051-1000-5218/Sa-20. Thereafter the other sons and the daughter became aggrieved about the gift and put pressure on the plaintiff to file a Miscellaneous Case No.70/2003 against Namjari and Jama Bhag Case No.3999/1994-95. Thereafter the plaintiff understood the conspiracy of her issues and withdrew the miscellaneous case voluntarily and thus the Assistant Commissioner (Land) con-firmed Namjari Case No.3999 of 1994-95. Thereafter, defendant No.1 on 30.12.2004 gifted the suit land to defendant Nos.2 and 3 through registered Hiba Deed No.5315. Defendant Nos.2 and 3 then got their names mutated through Namjari and Jama Bhag Case No.15 of 2005 dated 31.07.2005 and paid rent accordingly. The plaintiff due to pressure from her other children had filed this suit. The defendants claimed that the plaintiff had no prima facie arguable case and thus they prayed for dismissal of the suit.

4. On conclusion of the trial, the learned Assistant Judge, Dohar Court, Dhaka by his judgment and decree dated 01.06.2009 decreed the suit. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendant preferred Title Appeal No.274 of 2009 before the District Judge, Dhaka. On transfer, the appeal was heard by the Additional District Judge, Court No.6, Dhaka, who after hearing the parties allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Then the plaintiff preferred Civil Revision No.2866 of 2010 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was discharged. Against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division, the plaintiff filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2037 of 2014 and leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner:

"I. Because the defendant-petitioner being owner of the suit property and being in possession of the same with her 4(four) sons including defendant No.1 and 3(three) daughters and children of the deceased daughter in ejmali and there being no evidence that the plaintiff ever handed over the possession of the suit property to defendant No.1 excluding her other sons and daughters and formal possession in support of the alleged oral gift having not been made in favour of defendant No.1, it cannot be said that the oral gift allegedly made by plaintiff petitioner was acted upon and the High Court Division committed an error in affirming the judgment of the appellate Court by not considering the aforesaid aspects of the matter.

II. Because the plaintiff as mother having stated on oath that she has not gifted the suit property in favour of her son defendant No.1 and that defendant No.1 obtained her signature on false plea of business purpose and innocently she had given signature in some papers in good faith and the alleged oral gift having been denied by the plaintiff mother, the Court of appeal below and the High Court Division committed an error in disbelieving the statement of the plaintiff in respect of the alleged oral gift.

III. Because defendant No.1 having executed a registered partition deed on 20.10.1998 and in the said partition deed the suit property having been allotted in the saham of the plaintiff, and said fact clearly proves the falsity of the alleged oral gift in favour of defendant No.1 by the plaintiff and the High Court Division has failed to consider the consequence of execution of the partition deed by defendant No.1 after the alleged oral gift and erred in affirming the decree of the appellate Court.

IV. Because the High Court Division as well as the Court of appeal below has failed to consider the statement of plaintiff who stated oath that there is no reason to gift the suit property in favour one of her sons to the exclusion of her other sons and daughters and children of her deceased daughter by way of oral gift.

V. Because the fact of transfer of the suit property by defendant No.1 in favour of his two sons immediately after the alleged oral gift clearly proves that defendant No.1, created the alleged affidavit illegally obtaining the signature of his mother on false plea in support of his alleged oral gift."

5. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Counsel, appearing on behalf of the appellant made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He further sub-mitted that the registered partition deed of 1998 giving the suit property to the saham of the plaintiff belies the defendants' claim that there was any gift by the plaintiff in favour of defendant No.1 in 1994.

6. Mr. M.A. Sobhan, learned Advocate, appearing for respondent Nos.1 and 3 and Mrs. Sufia Khatun, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for respondent No.2 made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. It was also submit-ted that the plaintiff was a party to the instrument and in view of the proposition of law, the suit was not maintainable without making a prayer for cancellation of the documents on payment of ad volarem Court fee. It was submitted that the averments of the plaint did not refer to any point of time on which date the plaintiff came to know about the affidavit dated 10.12.1994 and the suit, as it appeared, filed on 10.07.2008 was hopelessly barred by the law of limitation. It was submitted that the appellate Court being a final Court of facts arrived at a specific finding reversing those of the Court of first instance that the defendant had been maintaining and possessing the suit property on payment of required taxes to the Government and therefore the case of the defendant of transfer by Hiba stands proved. It was submitted that the evidence on record revealed that the defence witnesses in a voice deposed as to the genuineness and the validity of oral gift and even on close scrutiny, it also revealed that the witness of the plaintiff supported the case of the defendant and in such view of the matter, the case of the plaintiff was not sustainable in law. It was submitted that from the registered deed, it is revealed that there was a huge property left by the husband of the plaintiff and it was partitioned long back among the successors of deceased Faizuddin and the plaintiff herself gifted the property to defendant No.1 which was admitted by both the parties and the defendant has been possessing the suit property with right, title and interest. It was submitted that the evidence on record revealed that requirements of a valid gift which were (a) manifestation of the wish to give on the part of the donor (b) the acceptance by the donee, either impliedly or expressly and (c) the taking of subject matter of the gift by the donee, either actually or constructively are complied with for making the transaction. It was submitted that it was a settled principle of law that a Moslem lady made gift of her house to her son by means of oral gift and it would be apparent from the evidence that the possession of the house was transferred and the mother and son continued to live in the house after the deed and the son continued to pay the required taxes by mutating his name and it was rightly held that it was a valid gift.

7. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

<u>8. From the judgment and decree of the trial Court, it appears that the trial Court found that the plaintiff’s date of knowledge was September, 2003 and the suit was filed on 10.07.2008, and therefore the same was not barred by limitation. It was an admitted fact that the deed was signed by the plaintiff, but the defendant collusively obtained the signature. The trial Court noted that the plaintiff denied that she gifted the suit property to defendant No.1 and defendant Nos.2 and 3 deposed that the gift deed was not executed in their presence. The trial Court also found that the plaintiff lived in the suit property and that fact was admitted by the defendants. The trial Court concluded that the gift deed was not proved and it had no validity in the eye of law.</u>

9. The appellate Court found that defendant No.1 having his name mutated in the suit property was paying rents, taxes and was in possession. The appellate Court further found that the suit was barred by limitation. The appellate Court found that PWsl, 2 and 3 deposed that the defendants were in possession in the suit property by renting. The appellate Court found that defendant No.1 was in possession in the suit property before the gift dated 10.12.1994 and it was admitted. The appellate Court found that exhibits-'Ka', 'Kha', 'Ga', ‘Gha’, 'Uma', 'Cha' produced by defendant No.1 showed that defendant No.1 was in possession and he was paying all rents and taxes in the suit property.

<u>10. The High Court Division upheld the judgment and decree of the appellant Court relying on the fact that PW4, Md. Kamaluddin admitted putting his signature on 09.09.1995 on a no objection certificate. The plaintiff in the no objection certificate stated that she had no objection if the suit properties were recorded in the name of defendant No.1, her son, Hafez Md. Shard Uddin in place of her name. The High Court Division found that the oral gift made by PW 1 on 01.11.1994 (sic.) has been proved by PW3 in clear language in his deposition. This is not correct. We find the PW3 specifically denied that his mother-in-law gifted the property to defendant No. 1. The High Court Division found that an oral partition was made some time after the death of Faizuddin on 16.12.1982 and it was admitted by PW5. PW5, son of late Faizuddin, deposed that the property was partitioned after the death of his father. PW1 in her deposition admitted that her husband died on 16.12.1982 leaving behind four sons and three daughters and in 1993, an Advocate was called in her house and a partition was made regarding their business and the suit property. The High Court Division found that all the defence witnesses deposed that the suit property was gifted in 1994. This is clearly one sided since the evidence on record shows that all me PWs, including PW3 did not admit the oral gift made on 10.12.1994. In fact all the PWs, including PW3 denied the oral gift. We also note that all the PWs deposed that they signed papers in good faith and those were used by defendant No.1 to create the documents in favour of his claim.</u>

<u>11. The High Court Division took support of the gift having been made in 1994 after oral partition was made because it was later recorded in the registered deed of partition of 1998. The High Court Division was of the view that the registered partition deed of 1998 did not alter the earlier oral partition. Here lies the fallacy of the reasoning of the High Court Division. There is nothing on record to show that the registered partition deed of 1998 is merely the written memorandum of the oral partition within the family which took place in 1993. The High Court Division assumed that the deed of 1998 is no more than a reflection of the family arrangement of 1993, and, therefore, the suit property was in the plaintiff’s saham in 1994 and she lawfully gifted her property to her son in 1994. However, this begs the question that if the plaintiff gifted her property in 1994 and it was mutated in the name of defendant No.1 in 1994, then there would be no reason to include the property in the saham of the plaintiff in the partition deed of 1998. The fact that the property was given in the saham of the plaintiff in 1998 indicates that she retained title and possession of the same in 1998 and that it was not gifted to defendant No.1 in 1994.</u>

12. All said and done, the subsequent registered deed of partition dated 20.10.1998 must be given credence and value as documentary evidence. This deed clearly shows that the suit property has been given in the saham of the plaintiff. This deed must be taken to state the correct state of affairs vis-à-vis the property in dispute as on the date of its execution. Hence, it cannot be denied that the title of the suit property stands in favour of the plaintiff as on 20.10.1998. Whatever might have transpired prior to that date is superseded by this deed. The recital in the deed will be taken to speak the truth of the existing state of the property, whether it is a memorandum of the earlier family arrangement or otherwise. It is undoubtedly a document giving title of the property to the plaintiff. Defendant No.1 did not deny the validity of the deed of partition dated 20.10.1998. So far as the plaintiff is concerned nothing happened to change her title to the property since 1993 and her position has been solidified by the grant of saham comprising the suit property in her favour by the registered partition deed of 1998, the veracity of which has not been challenged.

13. We may add that from careful scrutiny of all the materials on record, we do not find any earthly reason why the plaintiff would gift a six-storey building, which appears to be their family home, to one of her children while depriving all her other children.

<u>14. The finding of the High Court Division that the suit was barred by limitation cannot also be sustained since the appellate Court did not reverse the finding of the trial Court which was based on the plaintiff’s claim of knowledge of the deed of gift in September 2003. The appellate Court did not make any reference to date of the plaintiff’s knowledge nor gave any reason why that date would not be relevant for computing limitation. The appellate Court simply mentioned that the gift was on 10.12.1994 and the suit was filed on 10.07.2008 and thus it was barred and, therefore, the High Court Division noted that the plaintiff did not mention the date of her knowledge and found that the suit was barred by limitation. But the High Court Division also ignored the trial Court's finding that the plaintiff had knowledge from September 2003 and thus trial Court found that the suit was not barred by limitation, and the appellate Court and the High Court Division did not reverse such finding.</u>

15. In the light of the facts and circumstances discussed above, we find that the impugned judgment suffers from misreading as well as non-consideration of relevant evidence and materials, which in our view calls for interference.

16. Accordingly, for the reasons stated above the appeal is allowed, without how-ever, any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and the judgment and decree of the trial Court is restored.

End.

Mr. T.H. Khan, Senior Advocate & Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate (with Mr. Qumrul Haque Siddique, Advocate) instructed by Mr. Md. Taufique Hossain, Advocate-on-Record, For the Appellant. 
Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate (with Mr. Subrata Saha, Advocate) instructed by Ms. Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record, For Respondent No.1 
Mr. Giasuddin Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record, For Respondent No.6 Respondent Nos.2-5 & 7-8: Not represented.
parties:
HAJI SHAMSUL ALAM ---------- APPELLANT
Vs.
DR. ASHIM SARKER AND OTHERS ------- RESPONDENTS
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 22.08.2006 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No.17 of 2004 affirming those dated 25.10.2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Chittagong in Partition Suit No.72 of 2003.

2. The relevant facts, for the disposal of this appeal, are that the respondent Dr. Ashim Sarker instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration of his title, confirmation of possession, for declaration that exchange deed No.786 dated 20.07.1996, sale deed No.787 dated 20.07.1996, sale deed No.804 dated 27.07.1996 of Fatebad S.R. Office and deed of exchange No.3628 dated 06.10.1999 of Hathazari S.R. office were not acted upon and those deeds are not binding upon the plaintiff and for partition together with the prayer for buying up of the land described in the schedule-3 to the plaint stating, inter alia, that the land appertaining to R.S. Khatian Nos.693, 131, 667, 945, 1817 and R.S. Plot Nos.6963, 6964, 6972, 6959, 6957 and 6958 of Mouza South Madrasha, P.S. Hathazari, District-Chittagong measuring an area of 1.53 acres described in schedule No.1 to the plaint originally belonged to Pran Krishna Dey and Ishan Chandra Dey. R.S. record of right was prepared and published in their names. They were the full brothers. Ishan Chandra Dey died leaving no issue and his interest was devolved to Pran Krishna Dey. Pran Krishna Dey had three sons namely, Umesh Chandra Sarker, Jugendra Lal Sarker and Surendra Lal Sarker. Jugendra Lal Sarker died before the death of Pran Krishna leaving wife Niroda Bala and two brothers Umesh Chandra Sarker and Surendra Lal Sarker. Pran Krishna Dey died leaving two sons Umesh Chandra Sarker and Surendra Lal Sarker. Thus, Umesh Chandra Sarker got 1/3rd share, Surendra Lal Sarker got 1/3rd share and Niroda Bala wife of Jugendra Lal Sarker acquired life interest in respect of 1/3rd share. She transferred some land to Sunil Kanti Sarker by kabala deed dated 16.04.1969. Umesh Chandra Sarker purchased .22 acre of land out of the suit land which was recorded in his name in R.S. Khatian No.131, 945 and R.S. Plot No. 6957/7527/6957   corresponding to B.S. 7527 Khatian Nos.767 and 1306 in B.S. Plot Nos.8095,7921 and 7922. Umesh Chandra Sarker died leaving four sons, Manik Lal Sarker, Sunil Kanti Sarker, Dilip Sarker and Amalandu Sarker by his two wives. Manik Lal Sarker is the son of first wife and rest of the sons are by his second wife. Surendra died leaving only son Babul Chandra Sarker, the defendant No.1. Sunil Kanti Sarker died leaving three sons Dr. Ashim Sarker, the plaintiff, Shambhu Sarker and Sanjib Sarker, the defendant No.2. Babul Sarker gifted .13 acre of land to plaintiff Dr. Ashim Sarker and Shanjib Sarker by two deeds of gift dated 09.03.1999 and 10.09.1999. The plaintiff Dr. Ashim and his brothers are in joint possession of the lands. He requested the defendants to effect partition of the suit land but the defendants did not pay any heed. Shamsul Alam, defendant No.5 (appellant) threatened the plaintiff to dispossess him and his family members on 02.06.2002 from the suit land stating that he has purchased some land from Sunil Kanti Sarker, the defendant No.3 and Dilip Sarker, the defendant No.4. He expressed his desire to construct structures in his purchased land. Getting such information, the plaintiff, obtaining certified copy of the deeds on 11.07.2002, confirmed about the transfers and, thus, filed the instant suit.

3. The defendant No.5-Shamsul Alam, the present appellant, contested the suit by filing a written statement contending that the suit land originally belonged to Pran Krishna Dey and Ishan Chandra Dey. Ishan Chandra Dey died leaving his full brother Pran Krishna as his heir. Pran Krishna Dey died leaving two sons Umesh Chandra Sarker and Surendra Lal Sarker and another son Jugesh Chandra Sarker, predeceased Pran Krishna, leaving his widow Niroda Bala. Niroda sold her share to plaintiff's father, the defendant No.3 by kabala deed dated 16.04.1959. Surendra Lal Sarker died leaving only son Babul Chandra Sarker, the defendant No.1. Babul Chandra Sarker transferred his share to Anima Sarker by a kabala deed dated 04.05.1978. Sunil Kanti (defendant No.3), father of the plaintiff, instituted Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1986 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Hathazari against Anima Sarker to get the said land by way of pre-emption which was allowed. Anima Sarker preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.37 of 1988 which ended on compromise and Sunil Kanti got the said land. Sunil Kanti and Umesh Chandra Sarker gifted their share to Charu Bala by deed of gift dated 11.03.1970. Charu Bala gifted the said land to Sunil Kanti Sarker, the defendant No.3, father of the plaintiff and Dilip Chandra Sarker, the defendant No.4 uncle of the plaintiff. Umesh Chandra Sarker executed a will on 26.03.1970 in favour of Sunil Kanti Sarker, Dilip Chandra Sarker and Amalendu Sarker who filed Probate Case No.70 of 1988 which was subsequently registered as civil suit No.04 of 1990. The said suit ended on compromise and Sunil Kanti Sarker, Dilip Chandra Sarker obtained order of probate. Sunil Kanti Sarker and Dilip Chandra Sarker purchased the share of Amalendu Sarker by kabala deed dated 28.12.1969. All the co-sharers effected an amicable partition of those land on 28.10.1995. Thereafter, the defendant No.3 Sunil Kanti Sarker, father of the plaintiff and defendant No.4 Dilip Chandra Sarker, uncle of the plaintiff, sold .66 acre of land to this defendant No.5 by kabala deed No.787 dated 20.07.1996. They also sold .23 acre of land to this defendant by another kabala deed No.804 dated 27.07.1996 and delivered possession. They also transferred some other lands by a deed of exchange. One Mabia Khanom filed Miscellaneous Case No.74 of 1996 in the 3"I Court of Joint District Judge, Chittagong for getting the said land by way of preemption which ended on compromise. In view of such circumstances, the suit should be dismissed.

4. The trial Court decreed the suit in preliminary form. It declared that the deeds No.786 dated .15.07.1996, 787 dated 15.07.1996, 804 dated 19.07.1996 and 3628 dated 06.10.1999, executed in favour of the defendant No.5, have not been acted upon in respect of the land described in schedule 2 to the plaint and those are not binding upon the plaintiff .

5. The trial Court allowed the prayer for buying up in respect of the land described in schedule-3 to the plaint, that is, measuring an area of 1.18½ acres and directed the plaintiff to deposit Tk.7,67,299/- within 30 days from date, in default, the prayer for buying up shall stand dismissed. The trial Court allotted saham to the extent of 1.261/2 acres (.08 as owner+.18½ by way of buying up) as described in schedule-2 to the plaint in favour of the plaintiff. It also allotted saham to the extent of .071/4 acre of land to the defendant No.4. It also directed the defendant No.5 appellant to remove the structures constructed in the suit land.

6. The defendant No.5-appellant preferred First Appeal No.17 of 2004 in the High Court Division and the High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and decree, dismissed the said appeal. Thus, he has preferred this appeal getting leave.

7. Mr. T.H. Khan, A.J. Mohammad Ali, and Mr. Qumrul Haque Siddique, learned Counsel appeared for the appellant. On the other hand, Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel appeared with Mr. Subrata Saha for respondent No.1 .

8. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that it is apparent from the plaint that the plaintiff was not a co-sharer in interest of the dwelling house of an undivided family when the appellant purchased his 1.18Y2 acre of land so the prayer for buying up was not maintainable. They submit that to avoid limitation, the plaintiff filed partition suit intending to buying up the appellant's land inasmuch as the plaintiff knowing fully well that some other co-sharers filed pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.31 of 2000 against the defendant-appellant, the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that the instant suit filed by the plaintiff was malafide and the prayer for buying up was not at all maintainable. They submit that the courts below committed an error of law in holding that the transfer deeds of the defendant No.5 appellant had not been acted upon inasmuch as he took over possession of the disputed land and the trial Court, finding his possession, directed him to remove the structures constructed by him and that he has been paying electric bills, rent etc. and also receiving house rent etc.

9. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent No.1 in his submission, contended that the instant suit for partition along with the prayers for buying up, declaration of title and confirmation of possession was maintainable., the courts below rightly decreed the suit.

10. It appears that the trial Court declared that the title deeds of the defendant No.5 appellant had not been acted upon inasmuch as the trial Court directed the defendant No.5 to remove the structures as admittedly constructed by this defendant No.5 appellant after purchasing the said land. It also appears that the defendant No.5, after purchase, mutated his name in the khatian (ext.Uma is the mutated khatian) and has been paying rent (ext.Ja series are rent receipts) and electricity bills regularly. The appellant, purchasing his 1.181/2 acres of land by the impugned deeds, took over possession of those lands, mutated his name and paid rent to the Government, that is, he did something pursuant to those deeds. In such view of the matter, the findings of the courts below that the transfer deeds executed in favour of the defendant No.5 appellant were not acted upon has got no basis.

11. Another important question for adjudication in this case is whether the prayer for buying up in a suit filed not by the transferee of the deed executed by the other co-sharers of the disputed holding is maintainable or not.

12. It is relevant here to quote the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act which runs as follows:

"4.(1) Where a share of a dwelling-house belonging to an undivided family has been transferred to a person who is not a member of such family and such transferee sues for partition, the Court shall, if any member of the family being a shareholder undertake to buy the share of such transferee, make a valuation of such share in such manner as it thinks fit and direct the sale of such share to such shareholder, and may give all necessary and proper directions in that behalf. (2) If in any case describes in sub-section (1) two or more members of the family being such shareholders severally undertake to buy such share, the Court shall follow the procedure prescribed by sub-section(2) of the last foregoing section."

Section 4 enables a co-sharer of an undivided family dwelling house to seek for buying up of the share of the transferee from a co-sharer selling his shares in undivided family dwelling house when the transferee sues for partition of his share. However, the expression "the transferee sues for partition" needs interpretation.

13. Section 4 shows that for its applicability at any stage of the proceeding between the parties, the following conditions are to be satisfied:

"(1)A co-owner having undivided share in the family dwelling house should effect transfer of his undivided interest therein;

(2)The transferee of such undivided interest of the co-owner should be an outsider of stranger to the family;

(3) Such transferee must sue for partition and separate possession of the undivided share transferred to him by the concerned co-owner;

(4)As against such a claim of the stranger transferee, any member of the family having undivided share in the dwelling house should put forward his claim of pre-emption by undertaking to buy out the share of such transferee; and

(5)While accepting such a claim for pre-emption by the existing co-owner of the dwelling house belonging to the undivided family, the Court should make a valuation of the transferred share belonging to the stranger transferee and make the claimant co-owner pay the value of the share of the transferee so as to enable the claimant co-owner to purchase by way of pre-emption the said transferred share of the stranger transferee in the dwelling house belonging to the undivided family so that the stranger transferee can have no more claim left for partition and separate possession of his share in the dwelling house and accordingly can be effectively denied entry in any part of such family dwelling house." (Ghanstesher Ghosh V. Madan Mohan Ghosh-DLR 1997 SC.471) .

14. Supreme Court of India in the aforesaid case has observed that amongst other conditions, section 4 requires for its applicability that such stranger purchaser sues for partition and only in that eventuality the right of buying up envisaged under section 4 of the Partition Act can be made available to other co-sharers. If the stranger purchaser is impleaded as a defendant, if as defendant seek execution for decree of partition filed by a co-sharer, then the stranger purchaser can be held to have initiated a legal action for redressal of his decretal right and at that stage any co-sharer can seek the remedy for buying up under section 4 of the Partition Act.

15. Supreme Court of India taking into consideration of Ghantesher Ghosh V. Madan Mohan Ghosh's case further observed in the case of Babu Lal V. Habibur Rahman Khan and others reported in (2000)5 SCC 662 that one of the basic conditions for applicability of section 4 as laid down by the aforesaid decision and also as expressly mentioned in the section is that the stranger-transferee must sue for partition and separate possession of the undivided share transferred to him by the co-owner concerned. It is, of course, true that in the said decision it was observed that even though the stranger-transferee of such undivided interest moves an execution application for separating his share by metes and bounds it would be treated to be application for suing for partition and it is not necessary that a separate suit should be filed by such stranger-transferee. In the case of Gautom Pal V Debi Rani (AIR 2001 SC 61) Indian Supreme Court further observed that at any stage before filing the petition under section 4 of the Act, the stranger purchaser impleaded as a defendant did not seek for separate allotment of his share, then the right of the co-sharer to apply under section 4 of the Act did not arise.

16. In our jurisdiction in the case of Maleka Khatun and others Vs. Amena Khatun and others reported in 59 DLR(AD) 69 it has been observed that the defendant in a suit for partition to avail the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act is required to establish that the person seeking partition is stranger purchaser from the co-sharer(s) of dwelling house of an undivided family.

<u>17. When a co-sharer of an undivided family dwelling house has filed the suit for partition of that dwelling house against another co-sharer, no right against another co-sharer accrues to the plaintiff co-sharer to seek the relief for pre-emption under section 4 of the Partition Act. Dwelling house belonging to an undivided family means family not decided qua dwelling house. The essence is that the house itself should be undivided although the co-sharers having defined shares. As long as there is a dwelling house which has not been divided qua the family it might be said to be a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family for the purpose of section 4(1) of the Act. The basic pre-requisites for an application under section 4 for exercising the right of buy up is that the property which is the subject matter of the application must be a dwelling house of an undivided family and the transferee must sue for partition.</u>

<u>18. Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 4 of the Partition Act are complimentary to each other and the terms "Undivided family" and "dwelling house" have the same meaning in both the sections. Section 44 is to maintain the integrity of the family dwelling-house which provides that the transferee of a dwelling house, if he/she is not a member of that family, gets no right to joint possession or common enjoyment of the house. The said provision adequately protects the family members against intrusion by an outsider into the dwelling house. The purchaser, though stranger, has certainly his title to the undivided share of the joint property by reason of his purchase but in enforcing his rights he is fettered to this extent that he cannot claim any joint possession in the undivided family dwelling house. That does not mean that the purchaser is without remedy. The purchaser has his remedy and he can sue for partition by metes and bounds and after such partition possesS. his own share, unless he is pre-empted under section 4 of the Partition Act. The only manner in which an outsider can get possession is to sue for possession and claim separation of his share. In that case section 4 of the Partition Act conies into play. In the case of Dorab Cowasji Warder V. Loomi Sorab Warder reported in (1990) 2 SCC 117 it was observed that even if the family is divided in status in the sense that they were holding the property as tenants in common but undivided qua the property, that is, the property had not been divided by metes and bounds, it would be within the provisions of section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act.</u>

19. In such view of the discussion made above, it is observed that to get an order of pre-emption under section 4 of the Partition Act three conditions are to be fulfilled, i.e. (1) the property must be dwelling house, (2) it must be the undivided family and then (3) the purchasers must file the partition suit. That is one of the basic conditions for applicability of section 4 of the Partition Act which has been expressly mentioned in the section is that the stranger transferee must sue for partition and separate possession of the undivided share transferred to him by the co-sharer. If the stranger moves execution application for separating his share by metes and bounds it would be treated to be application for suing for partition and it is not necessary that separate suit should be filed by such stranger transferee. "Such transferee sues for partition" includes idea of some action by transferee to secure partition even praying saham in suit for partition paying necessary court fees which is totally absent in this case. In this case the defendant No.5 appellant Shamsul Alain is the transferee of the land under partition and the suit has been Filed by Dr. Ashim Sarker who is not the transferee and appellant did not pray for any saham as yet in the said suit for partition, so the prayer for buying up by the plaintiff was not at all maintainable at the stage of the suit when the same was prayed for. The courts below have committed error of law in allowing the prayer for buying up.

20. Accordingly, we find substance in the appeal. Thus, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree passed by the courts below are hereby set aside. However, since the instant suit is a suit for partition, the plaintiff is entitled to get his share to the extent of .08 acre and the defendant No.4 is entitled to get saham to the extent of .07¼ acre as allotted by the trial Court.

End.
