full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J.: The Rule issued calling upon the Opposite Parties No. 1- 11 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 07.10.1995 passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Court, Kishoregonj in Other Class Appeal No. 260 of 1985 reversing those of dated 26.05.1985 passed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Kishoregonj in Other Class Suit No. 1051 of 1980 should not be set aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts giving raise to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell are as follows: One Noni Bala Das predecessor-in-interest of the present opposite parties No. 01-09 as plaintiff instituted the original Other Class Suit being No. 1051 of 1980 against the defendant-petitioners for a declaration that a compromise decree dated 07.10.1966 is collusive, illegal, fraudulent and the order dated 16.11.1978 regarding separation of holding passed by the Circle Officer (Rev.), Kishoregonj is fraudulent, illegal and void contending inter alia, that the suit land along with other lands had been owning and possessing by the plaintiff and the defendants. By way of amicable partition among the co-sharers of the case jote the plaintiff use to possess the suit property and at this stage the defendants No. 1- 3 and 10 in collusion with other defendants behind the back of the plaintiff, showing the plaintiff 2nd party and showing the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants-1st party created a false, collusive and anti-dated solenama on 07.10.1966. The further case of the plaintiff is such that without serving any notice upon the 2nd party the defendants managed to obtain a collusive service return and thereby in a Mutation Case No. 229(9)/1/78-79 they have mutated their names collusively and in fact in that mutation proceedings the plaintiff never obtained any notice. Subsequently, knowing about the mutation order the plaintiff filed an objection which was illegally rejected at the instance of the defendants. It is the contention of the plaintiff that in respect of the suit property in the year 1943 and 1957 there has been two registered ‘solenama’ deed among the co-sharers of the suit holding and in pursuant of those ‘solenama’ deeds the co-sharers after getting their separate shaham were possessing their portion of land. The plaintiff-opposite party never executed the ‘solenama’ dated 07.10.1966 and in that ‘solenama’ all the co-sharers were not impleaded parties. One of the sister of plaintiff namely Kusum Bala migrated to India long before 20/21 years of the disputed solenama' and in that solenama' the name of Girish Chandra Das was illegal inserted in order to grab a Cinema Hall situated in plot No.9036 and that the `solenama' dated 07.10.1966 was created by the defendants No.1, 3 and 10 in order to deprive the plaintiff. It was also contended in the pleadings of the plaintiff that there was no talk of solenama' in respect of the land of plot No.9036 in exchange of the land of plot No. 9136 and the plaintiff never surrendered her interest and title of the land appertaining to plot No.9036, but the defendants in order to grab the property in the name of surrender of title and interest in respect of the land of plot No.9036 in lieu of the land of plot No.9136 created the disputed solenama' . The plaintiff knowing about the disputed solenama' and the mutation in favour of the defendants on 20.12.1979 from the office of the concerned `Tahshir finally came to learn about the misdeed of the defendants which constrained the plaintiff to institute the original suit. 3. The contrary case of the defendant-respondent-petitioners in short is thus that the property-in-dispute originally belonged to the plaintiff and the defendants in ejmali and subsequently for the sake of peaceful possession to remove the inconvenience among the co-sharers of the suit holding a solenama' was executed on 07.10.1966 and in that solenama' the plaintiff put her signature and the said solenama' has been acted upon after its proper execution. The further case of the defendant-petitioners is such that two solenama' deed among the co-sharers in respect of their paternal property were made in the year 1943 and 1957, but in fact; those solenarna' were not acted upon. The subsequent solenama' dated 07.10.1966 was a genuine solenama' and it was executed properly by the parties to the suit in respect of their paternal property and by this amicable solenama' in the year 1966 the plaintiff-opposite party give up her interest and title of the land of plot No.9036 in favour of the defendant-petitioners and in exchange of that land the plaintiff obtained 1/2 of the land in plot No.9136 along with its standing structure. The further case of the defendant-petitioners is such that by the said amicable arrangement pursuant to the solenama' dated 07.10.1966 the defendants No.1-3 and 7 acquired 16 annas share in the plot No.9036 and thereafter, they constructed a Cinema Hall in front of their dwelling house. Subsequently, they mutated their name after proper service of notice in the office of the concerned Circle Officer (Rev.), Kishoregonj in Mutation Case No.229(9)/1/1978-79, but the plaintiff out of ill-motive suppressing the facts filed the suit on false allegations.

4. During trial of the original suit the learned trial court after taking evidences from the sides of the respective parties dismissed the suit on contest by its judgment and decree dated 26.05.1985.

5. Being aggrieved the plaintiff preferred an Other Class Appeal No.260 of 1985 in the court of learned District Judge, Kishoregonj, which was transmitted to the Court of learned the then Sub-ordinate Judge, Kishoregonj for hearing and disposal and the learned appellate court on hearing the appeal allowed the same and set aside the judgment and dismissal decree passed by the learned trial court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 07.10.1995.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree the defendant-respondent-petitioners have preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule with an interim order of stay.

7. During hearing of this Rule Mr. A.K.M. Shamshed, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioners while Mr. Kamrul Alam (Kamal) the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

8. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned appellate court during disposal of the appeal committed illegality and irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Kishoregonj failed to assess the evidence on record in its true perspective and also failed to appreciate the actual proposition of law. The learned Advocate also submits that there was no material in support of the plaintiff's contention that the `solenama ' of the year 1943 and 1957 were acted upon and according to those solenama' the plaintiff exercised her title and possession in the land. The learned trial court during disposal of the original suit rightly after proper sifting of evidence arrived at a decision that the 'solenma' of the year 1943 and 1957 are collusive and not acted upon and thereafter in the year 1966 among the co-sharers of the suit holding for the sake of their possession and interest they executed a solenama on 07.10.1966 which was properly executed by the plaintiff and pursuant to that solenama' the parties to the suit obtained their possession amicably. The learned Advocate submits that the evidence adduced from the sides of the respective parties were not properly evaluated by the learned appellate court and the learned appellate court without rebutting the findings of the trial court adverting evidence on records, reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and at the time of disposal of the appeal there has been misreading and non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate referring some decisions submits that the plaintiff during trial of the original suit failed to produce any particular, which was necessary in case of misrepresentation, fraud, breach of trust and undue influence. But the learned appellate court failed to appreciate that, and under Order VI Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure the impugned judgment and decree is bad-in-law. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the original suit as framed was not maintainable as the plaintiff having no legal character and right to sue instituted the original suit, but the learned appellate court failed to realize that and as such, the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

9. As against the aforesaid submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule controverted the argument advanced from the side of the petitioners and submits that in passing the impugned judgment and decree the learned appellate court committed no illegality or irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that, there has been no misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by dint of which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with. The learned Advocate further submits that under the provisions laid down in Order X1,1, Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned court of appeal below after proper assessment of evidence in its true perspective and appreciation of relevant law reversed the findings of the trial court and after rebutting the observation and decision of the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Kishoregonj adverting evidence on records reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial court by the impugned judgment and decree. The learned Advocate submits that the specific element of fraud, misrepresentation and undue influence has been well proved from the side of the plaintiff-opposite parties and the particulars were given specifically under Order VI, Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the plaintiff-opposite party in her pleadings as well as in the evidence adduced from her side. The learned Advocate argued that, from the cross-examination of the defendant's witnesses all the particulars of misrepresentation, fraud, breach of trust, willful default and undue influence has been proved and the learned appellate court rightly and properly in his observation and findings pointed out all the particulars and material evidence on the basis of which the judgment and decree was passed by the appellate court and as such there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Kishoregonj. The learned Advocate on citation of different decisions of this Court. and our Apex Court argued that the elements of fraud which have been mentioned in the plaint in paragraph No.05, has been properly proved by sufficient evidence and there has been clear description as to how the fraud was committed upon the mother of the opposite party No.7, who was the plaintiff to the original suit. The learned Advocate lastly submits that, there is no illegality or infirmity in the impugned judgment and decree by which it can be held that the learned court of appeal below during disposal of the appeal committed any unlawful act and as such the Rule is liable to be discharged.

10. In order to appreciate the submission advanced from the sides of the respective parties having gone through the pleadings of the parties in the plaint and in the written statement and the judgment and decree passed by the trial court in Other Class Suit No. 1051 of 1980, the subsequent judgment and decree passed by the appellate court on 07.10.1995 in Other Appeal No. 260 of 1985, the evidence adduced from the sides of the respective parties both oral and documentary including all other relevant papers it transpires that, it is an admitted position that the suit jote originally belonged to the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff and the defendants and they had been owning and possessing the property. The suit jote which is the paternal property of the parties to the suit admittedly was not partitioned by metes and bounds and it is the case of the plaintiff that in respect of the entire property of the suit jote in the year 1943 and 1957 there were two registered solenama deed among the co-sharers of the suit holding and according to those two solenama' deeds the parties to the suit amicably possessing the property of the suit holding. It has been specifically contended by the plaintiff in the pleadings that in order to deprive her subsequently the defendants No.1, 3 and 10 in collusion with other defendants managed to create a forged 'solenama in the year 1966. It was further alleged that on 07.10.1966 that `solenama' (aposhnama) was created by the defendants and in that aposhnama' the plaintiff never put her signature or LTI whatsoever and all the co-sharers of the suit holding were not impleaded parties to that `aposhnama' . Besides this, one of the daughter of the plaintiff namely Kushum Bala migrated to India 20/21 years prior to 1966, but in the solenama' her name has been collusively inserted and the signature was created. It was further contended from the side of the plaintiff that the suit Cinema Hall is situated in plot No.9036 in respect of which the `aposhnama' in the year 1966 was created by the defendants. It was shown in that collusive `solenama' that in lieu of the land appertaining to plot No.9136, the land of plot No.9036 was given to the defendants and this land was devolved by the defendants.

11. To substantiate the respective cases of the parties both the parties led evidences and the plaintiff examined 03 witnesses in order to succeed. On the other hand, the defendant-petitioners to substantiate their case have examined 04 witnesses. Besides the oral evidence the plaintiffs to the suit produced documentary evidences which have been marked as Exhibits No.1-17 after its formal proof.

12. Vis-à-vis; the defendants also submitted some documentary evidences and all the documents have been marked as Exhibits.

13. In order to prove the case of the defendant-petitioners that by their family arrangement pursuant to the `solenama' dated 07.10.1966 the defendants No.1-3 and 7 acquired the entire 16 annas share in the suit plot No.9036 in which they have allegedly constructed a Cinema Hall and also constructed their dwelling house in the back portion of that Cinema Hall, they have adduced 04 witnesses.

14. P.W.1. the plaintiff herself Noni Bala Das in her examination-in-chief testified that the property was the ejmali property of her and the defendants, who are the co-sharers of the suit holding and possessed the suit property pursuant to 02(two) registered `solenama' deeds of the year 1943 and 1957. P.W.1 also testified in her testimony that, still she possess the suit land and reside therein on the basis of those `solenama' deeds. With regard to the allegation raised by her in her pleadings as cited in paragraph No. 3 and 4 of the plaint, she has categorically stated at a stage that in the unregistered `solenama' of the year 1966 she did not put her signature. She has denied specifically that the `solenama' deed of the year 1966 is correct and it was written by a scribe of Bikrampur in her presence. She also denied specifically in her testimony that she obtained notice of Mutation Case No. 229(9)/1/78-79 and all the co-sharers in that mutation proceedings were duly notified. P.W.1 testified in her examination-in-chief that she did not sign any notice of the mutation case and she came to know about the false mutation case subsequently. Thereafter, she sent her son to the concerned `Tahsil' office in order to know the matter definitely. The plaintiff also testified specifically that she filed an objection before the concerned Circle Officer (Rev.) against the mutation case which was rejected. Thereafter, she has filed the present suit. She also denied that the `solenama' dated 07.10.1966 was executed in presence of her son. In respect of the Cinema Hall which is admittedly situated in plot No.9036, the plaintiff Noni Bala Das in her testimony testified that, Gonesh Pal viz. the defendant No.1 renovated the Cinema Hall by the money of rent which he realized in advance from the tenants. In a reply to a question from the side of the defendants, the plaintiff testified at a stage of her cross-examination that it is not a fact that in pursuant to earlier `solenama' deeds which are registered, no possession was delivered in favour of the co-sharers of the suit holding and in compliance of the subsequent `solenama' dated 07.10.1966 everything was done.

15. P.W.2 M.A. Mannan is a hand-writing Expert, who has submitted his report comparing the signature of the plaintiff Noni Bala Das and the report of this witness has been identified by him which has been marked as Exhibit-1 dated 04.04.1984. During cross-examination this witness categorically testified that the signature of the executant of the deed of the year 1966 does not tally with the signature as it appears in the deed of 1957, 1974 and 1983 and the signature of the disputed `solenama' deed is also not consistent with the specimen signature which was given by the plaintiff Noni Bala Das in the court room in the year 1983. In a reply to a question from the side of the defendants the hand-writing Expert specifically testified that he has also compared the signatures of the deeds of 1957, 1974 and 1983 with each other and he denied categorically that he did not compare the signature of the deeds of 1957, 1974 and 1983 with each other. He also denied specifically that his report is not prepared on scientific method.

16. P.W. 3 Girindra Sarker is the possession witness of the plaintiff. This witness in his testimony testified that he knows the parties and the suit land for the last 26/27 years. This witness also knows the Cinema Hall namely 'Universal Cinema' inasmuch as he was an employ of that Cinema Hall earlier. During cross-examination this witness testified that, when he was the employee of that Cinema Hall, the name of that Cinema Hall was `Moni Mongal Hall' and subsequently its name has been changed to 'Universal Cinema Hall' and one Sunil Chandra hired that Hall.

17. On the other hand, D.W.1 is the defendant No.1 Ganesh Chandra Pal. This witness in his testimony testified that the suit land originally belonged to their predecessors Kunju Mohon and others, and Morna Pal, Kunja Pal were the owner of 08 annas share and the remaining 08 annas had been owning and possessing by Nodi Ram Das and others. The defendant No.1 also testified that there was an amicable partition followed by solenama' on 10.07.1943 regarding plot No.9036, but they did not possess actually according to the saham of the aforesaid amicable partition of the year 1943. He has purchased the plot.No.9146 in the year 1955 from one Nalini Kanta and others and there was separate solenama' in the year 1957 amongst all the heirs and the heirs have obtained separate saham in respect of the suit holding. The plaintiff obtained 02 annas share and Kushum Bala obtained 02 annas share in the suit jote according to the solenama' deed of the year 1957. The suit Cinema Hall was allocated in the share of 02 annas but actually the co-sharers of the suit holding did not possess as per terms of that soknama' deed which was executed and registered in the year 1957. The defendant No.1 in his testimony also testified that in the year 1966 the solenama' which was filed after execution of the parties including the plaintiff, that was duly effected and all the co-sharers went into possession of the property pursuant to that solenama of the year 1966. D.W.1 in his examination-in-chief testified at a stage that the plaintiff Noni Bala has no title and possession in the suit plot No.9036. D.W.1 admitted that he filed an injunction suit against Noni Bala and others being No.633 of 1980 and that suit was dismissed and against that dismissal decree he preferred an appeal which is pending for disposal.

18. During cross-examination the defendant No.1 frankly testified that it is a fact that these two families had joint business in Tongibari and Kishoregonj. The defendant No.1 has also admitted in his cross-examination that the landed properties were also in ejmali. In a reply to a question from the side of the plaintiff the defendant No.1 testified that, there was amicable partition before 1966 in respect of their ejmali property and that was in the year 1943 followed by a registered deed. D.w.1 also testified in his cross-examination that their ejmali property and business were partitioned in the year 1943 and in that partition they got 08 annas share, Rajani Kanta and others got 04 annas share and Shyama Sunduri got 04 annas share. The defendant No.1 at a stage of his cross-examination admitted that the partition deed and its recital of the year 1943 are correct. He also testified that after the solenama of the year 1943 they have purchased some property in ejmali. D.W.1 in his cross-examination also conceded that Kushum Bala left this country for India prior to 1957 forever. The defendant No.1 in a reply to a question from the side of the plaintiff also conceded that he did not implead all the co-sharers in his `solenama' and he cannot say the area of property which was ejinali in 'Das' family and 'Pal' family. He also cannot say as to how much land he obtained by dint of the 'solenama' of the year 1966. With regard to the disputed 'solenama' of the year 1966 the defendant No.1 Gonesh Chandra expressed his inability to state the value of the stamp paper which was purchased by him. He has admitted that the cartridge papers were purchased from "Tongibari but lie cannot remember the year and date of that purchase and also cannot remember the date of execution of the disputed 'solenama' D.W.1 in the last portion of his cross-examination replied in a question from the side of the plaintiff in the following way, "Kushumbala also gets a share and her share is lying with us."

19. D.W. 2 Shailendra Ch. Sarker, is a businessman of Kishoregonj town. This witness is the attesting witness of the impugned 'solenama' of 1966. In the examination-in-chief this witness stated about the alleged signature of Noni Bala in the 'solenama' dated 07.10.1966. This witness claimed that in his presence the plaintiff put her signature in the 'solenama' and the other witnesses namely Abinash Chandra and Kala Chand were also present at that time and Kala Chand is now dead.

20. During cross-examination this witness testified at a stage that lie was not present when the deed was written. This witness also testified in his cross-examination that in the disputed deed the husband of Noni Bala and her son were not witness. D.W.2 admitted that he did not find Noni Bala prior to that `shalish' and execution of the solenama'.

21. D.W.3 Abdur Rashid Miah is a deed writer of Kishoregonj Sub-registry office. This witness testified in his examination-in-chief that he knows Noni Bala and her sons and lie wrote a deed of Noni Bala by which she disinherited her son. During cross-examination D.W.3 testified at a stage that he knows all the members of Noni Bala's family as the youngest son of Noni Bala happens to be his friend, but he cannot say the name of his that friend! D.W.3 in a reply to a question in his cross-examination testified that he wrote the disputed solenama' as per draft of an .Advocate, but he cannot say, whose draft it was!

22. The last witness of the defendant-petitioners Abinash Chandra Saha is a witness of the disputed 'solenama' of the year 1966. This witness testified that he is a businessman of Kishoregonj. This witness has expressed his inability to state that as to whether Noni l3ala put her signature in the 'solenama' before or after the presence him (D.W.4). During cross-examination D.W.4 frankly conceded that he is a tenant under the defendant No.1 for the last 31/32 years and there was an agreement between him and Gonesh Pal for purchasing the premises in which he is running his business at present. He cannot remember about the person of Kishoregonj, who was present at the time of disputed 'solenama'. At a stage of his cross-examination D.W.4 admitted that in his presence nothing was written and only one Kali Chand and Kalu Sarker put their signature in presence of him (this witness).

<u>23. On meticulous assessment of evidences and the case records I find that the matter of adjudication between the parties to the suit was properly addressed by the appellate court in its true perspective and also properly appraised the evidence on record in his observation and findings, and committed no wrong in relying the plaintiff's witnesses and discarding the evidentiary value of the defendant's witnesses for want of their credibility.</u>

24. "In the instant suit, the matter in controversy between the parties is the solenama' dated 07.10.1966 prior to which admittedly there were two registered deed in respect of compromise of the concerned parties with regard to their paternal property in which the suit property is located. It is the specific assertion of the plaintiff-opposite party that in the solenama' of the year 1966 she did not put her signature and behind her back it was collusively created. With regard to the pleading's case of the parties both the parties inasmuch as led evidences, the court of appeal below in his observation and findings adverting evidence on records vividly, rightly rebutted the findings of the trial court and thereafter arrived at a conclusive decision that the 'solenama' of the year 1966 is a collusive instrument by dint of which the subsequent mutation proceedings of defendant's Mutation Case No.229(9)/1/1978-79 was ended in the office of the Circle Officer (Rev.), Kishoregonj and in this proceedings there is nothing on record to show that the service was done properly or that the notice was ever served upon the plaintiff-opposite party, who was admittedly a party to that proceedings.

25. In the instant case, I have come across that under section 45 of the Evidence Act, 1872 there lies an Expert's opinion and the Expert was examined by the learned court below. The Expert opinion go to show that the signature as it appears in the disputed `solenama' is not consistent and identical with the actual signature of the plaintiff-opposite party and that the signature of the disputed solenama' (Exhibit-`E') is the product of different individual.

<u>26. Section 45 of the Evidence Act, (I of 1872) contemplates that the opinion of the Expert is not conclusive, nevertheless; it bears a strong prima-facie arguable case in favour of the party in whose favour the report lies. The Expert under the purview of section 45 of the Evidence Act, (1 of 1872) is empowered to compare and analyse the signature which is disputed and he is also empowered to give his decision after comparing and analysing the same, and such authentic report is no doubt a substantive piece of evidence. [Ref. 1978 BLD (AD) 142]</u>

27. Having regard to the facts, circumstances and discussions referred to above along with the decisions cited from the sides of the respective parties, I have every reason to inclined such a view that in disposing the appeal there is no such illegality or infirmity or misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with.

28. In the result, the Rule having no merit be discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 07.10.1995 passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Kishoregonj in Other Class Appeal No. 260 of 1985 reversing those of dated 26.05.1985 passed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Kishoregonj in Other Class Suit No. 1051 of 1980 is hereby affirmed.

29. Let the order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule be vacated.

30. Communicate the judgment and order at once and send down the lower court's records immediately.

End.

Rupa Das ------ Petitioner
vs
Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Bangladesh Secretariat, Ramna, Dhaka and others ---------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J : On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh filed by the petitioner, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Memo No. বি এম এন্ড ডিসি/১০-এফ-২০১৭-১৮ dated 6-7-2017 issued by the respondent No. 3, Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (Annexure-'K' to the Writ Petition) purporting that no registration would be accorded to her and the Memo No. একা-৫৪৯/৫৮১২ dated 18-7-2017 issued by the respondent No. 5, University of Chittagong (Annexure-'N' to the Writ Petition) cancelling her admission and registration should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The case of the petitioner, as set out in the Writ Petition, in short, is as follows:

An advertisement for admission test for all Government and Non-Government Medical Colleges was published in "The Daily Prothorn Alo" on 31-8-2013. In the said advertisement, it was clearly stipulated that only those students who took science subjects and scored Grade Point Average (GPA) of minimum 8-00 in his/her SSC and HSC Examinations with at least GPA-3.5 in either of the aforementioned examinations are eligible to sit for the admission test. The petitioner having the abovementioned required score sat for the admission test for MBBS course for the session 2013-2014. The result of the admission test was published online and made available to everybody. In the result sheet, her name appeared at serial No. 1712 having roll No. 201818 and she scored 109.38 out of 200 marks. She applied to the respondent No. 8-BGC Trust Medical College, Chandanaish, Chittagong for admission to 1st year, MBBS course and accordingly she submitted all the relevant papers and documents required therefor. Thereafter she was admitted to 1st year, MBBS course for the session 2013-2014 and began her studies in the college. Meanwhile she completed her 3rd year MBBS course and passed the 1st Professional Course Examination. All of a sudden, during the 2nd Professional Course Examination around May 2017, she was notified by the respondent No. 8 that the respondents had raised questions about her admission qualification. In fact, the entire admission procedure was completed by the respondent No. 8 based on all the original papers and documents submitted at the time of application for admission to the college including the admission test result sheet published online which were checked and verified by the college authority. Having being fully satisfied, the respondent No. 8 forwarded those to the respondent No. 4 (Directorate of Health Services). Having been found everything in order, the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (respondent No. 2) recommended the petitioner to the respondent No. 5-Chittagong University for issuance of registration in her favour. Accordingly on compliance with all necessary formalities, the Chittagong University found the petitioner eligible for admission as a student of MBBS course and gave her registration/identification No. 550 of 2013-2014 session.

3. However, a complaint was lodged by one journalist with the respondent No. 2 (BMDC) against the petitioner on 1-2-2017. It was alleged in the complaint that the petitioner had scored 109.38 marks in the admission test and her merit position was 61242; but the papers and documents submitted by the respondent No. 8 showed that the petitioner had scored 127.38 marks and accordingly her merit position was 45244 in the admission test. Thereafter a probe into the petitioner's admission test result was initiated, though the documents submitted by her clearly showed that she had got 109.38 out of 200 marks. On 19-6-2017, the petitioner received a letter from the respondent No. 8 asking her to submit the original score sheet of the admission test to its office urgently. The admission test result was available online and furthermore, the result was verified by the respondent No. 8 at the time of her admission. In fact, the verification was not only done by the college; but it was also done by the respondent No. 4 (Directorate of Health Services) which authenticated the result of the petitioner by attesting it. The admission committee of the respondent No. 8 prepared a checking and verification report and submitted it to the respondent No. 4. The respondent No. 4 found that the said report was incorrect and inconsistent with the admission result sheet, so far as it related to the petitioner. Subsequently the respondent No. 8 received a letter dated 6-7-2017 from the respondent No. 3 stating that as the petitioner had scored 109.38 marks in the admission test, she was found disqualified and accordingly she would not be given any registration number. On 12-7-2017, the respondent No. 8 issued a show cause notice upon the petitioner asking her to reply within 7 (seven) working days as to why her admission to the college would not be cancelled for submitting inconsistent papers and documents at the time of her admission. She replied to the show cause notice on 18-7-2017 stating that she did not submit any forged or manipulated documents at the time of her admission to MBBS course for the session 2013-2014. If any fraud was committed at the relevant point of time, it was the respondent No. 8 which did so in order to enroll a huge number of students into MBBS course out of sheer greed for money. She did never submit any documents showing that she had obtained 127.38 out of 200 marks in the admission test. Anyway, the respondent No. 5 vide Memo No. এক-৫৪৯/৫৮১২ dated 18-7-2017 cancelled the admission and registration of the petitioner even without considering the reply to the show cause notice which was provided to the college on the same date (18-7-2017). Thereafter the result of the 3rd year examination was published; but her result was withheld. Moreover, the respondent No. 8 has not been allowing her to continue her studies in the medical college. Given the above circumstances, the impugned Memo No. বি এম এন্ড ডি সি/১০ এফ-২০১৭/১৮ dated 6-7-2017 and Memo No. একা-৫৪৯/৫৮১২ dated 18-7-2017 are without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

4. The case of the respondent No. 3 and the respondent No. 4, as set out in their respective Affidavits-in-Opposition being identical in nature, is described below in a nutshell:

The Writ Petition involves resolution of disputed questions of facts which cannot be decided without investigation and trial and therefore the Writ Petition is not maintainable. However, the respondent No. 3 is the Registrar of the BMDC which is constituted under section 3 of বাংলাদেশ মেডিকেল ও ডেন্টাল কাউন্সিল আইন, ২০১০ (hereinafter referred to as the Act of 2010). By dint of section 5 of the Act of 2010, it is the statutory mandate of the respondent No. 3 to accord registration or refuse to accord registration due to any irregularity/illegality committed by any student and hence the impugned decision of the respondent No. 3 is legitimate and lawful. This is because, the decision was taken after conducting necessary inquiries and crosschecking the result with the record of the Directorate of Health Services. Furthermore, the respondent No. 5 (University of Chittagong) cancelled the admission and registration of the petitioner only after confirmation that she had submitted false papers and documents during her admission to MBBS course in the BGC Trust Medical College. The petitioner provided false and fabricated information with regard to her merit score and merit position in order to get herself admitted to the respondent No. 8 college. The question is not whether she was qualified to sit for the admission test; rather the question is whether she secured the required marks in the admission test to qualify herself to get admitted to MBBS course in the respondent No. 8 college.

5. Admittedly the petitioner failed to achieve the minimum benchmark of 120 marks in the admission test; but by resorting to forgery and manipulation, she got herself admitted to the respondent No. 8 college showing her merit score as 127.38 instead of 109.38. On 6-2-2017, the BMDC received a complaint from one Mamunur Rashid, a senior journalist of "The Daily Samakal", alleging that the petitioner had got herself admitted to MBBS course in the respondent No. 8 college for the academic year 2013-2014 by illegally increasing her test score and merit score, though her actual test score was below the benchmark. On receipt of this letter from Mamunur Rashid, the BMDC initiated necessary inquiries and ultimately found that the petitioner had scored 109.38 marks as per the result sheet published online by the Directorate of Health Services. Anyway, the respondent No. 8 supplied the merit score card of the petitioner which was apparently attested by one Dr. Md Emdadul Huq, Assistant Director (Medical Education), Directorate of Health Services, Mohakhali, Dhaka. From a plain reading of the advertisement dated 10-11-2013 (Annexure-'2-A'), the respondent No. 8 college invited applications from the candidates who had merit score of 120 and above in the admission test. But the petitioner, being fully aware of her merit score of 109.38, filled in an admission form of the college for her admission to MBBS course for the academic session 2013-2014. The respondent No. 4 by the Memo No. ডিজিএইচএস/এমই/এমবিবিএস-২০১৩-১৪ শিঃ বর্ষ (অংশ)/৯১৩ dated 29-6-2017 informed the respondent No. 3 that the correct merit score and merit position of the petitioner were 109.38 and 61242 respectively. Thus upon confirmation of the merit score by the respondent No. 4, the respondent No. 3 by the impugned Memo No. বি এম এন্ড ডি সি/১০-এফ-২০১৭/১৮ dated 6-7-2017 (Annexure-'K' to the Writ Petition) informed the Principal of the respondent No. 8 college that no registration would be given to the petitioner by the BMDC. The petitioner concealed her true identity and merit score and thus defrauded the respondent No. 8 college, attended classes and appeared in various examinations till date. She defrauded the college for a number of years until the fraud was detected very recently. She was allowed to get herself admitted to the college based on the declaration and forged documents submitted by herself. As fraud vitiates everything, she is not entitled to any relief sought for in this Writ Petition. She cannot be allowed to enjoy the fruit of her own fraud. As she is the beneficiary of fraud, she cannot claim that she did not have a square deal before the respondents. As the petitioner has not come up with clean hands, she ought to be shown the door both in law and equity. So the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

6. The case of the respondent No. 8, as set out in the Affidavit-in-Opposition, briefly, runs as under:

The respondent No. 8 is BGC Trust Medical College situated under Police Station Chandanaish, District- Chittagong. However, the respondent No. 8 college published an advertisement in "The Daily Purbokon" and "The Daily Samakal" for admission to MBBS course (1st year) for the session 2013- 2014 from those candidates who obtained a minimum of 120 marks in the admission test conducted by the respondent No. 4 (Directorate of Health Services). The petitioner purchased the application form bearing serial No. 903 and submitted the same to the respondent No. 8 after supplying the required information along with all other academic certificates, score sheets etc. as required for admission. The respondent No. 8 after tallying the information as provided by the petitioner in the application form with the submitted documents found her competent/eligible for admission and prepared a list of eligible candidates for admission. The respondent No. 8 formed a three-member committee to recheck and verify the information given in the application forms with the documents submitted by the candidates. The three-member committee accordingly re-checked and verified the information with the submitted documents of the eligible candidates and sent a list of such checking and verification to the respondent No. 8. As per the said verification list, the information supplied by the petitioner in the application form was found in order according to her submitted documents. Thereafter according to the requirement of the respondent No. 5 (Chittagong University), all the documents of the eligible candidates were sent to the respondent No. 4 for verification and attestation. After getting the documents of the eligible candidates including those of the petitioner attested by the respondent No. 4, the respondent No. 8 invited them for admission to MBBS course for the academic session 2013-2014. After receipt of the required fees from the students, the respondent No. 8 sent the attested documents to the respondent No. 5 (Chittagong University) for their final admission and registration for MBBS course (1st year) for the academic year 2013-2014. Upon completion of registrations and receipt of registration numbers from the Chittagong University, the academic session of the admitted students commenced.

7. Be that as it may, at the instance of one Mamunur Rashid, a senior journalist of "The Daily Samakal", necessary inquiries were held and ultimately it was found that the petitioner had scored 109.38 in place of 127.38 out of 200 marks in the admission test. In other words, as per the advertisement for admission to the medical college, the petitioner was disqualified for admission in view of the fact that she had scored 109.38 marks which were below the benchmark of 120. Afterwards the respondent No. 8 received a letter dated 6-7-2017 from the respondent No. 3 stating that no registration would be accorded to the petitioner. After receipt of the said letter dated 6-7-2017 from the respondent No. 3, the respondent No. 8 by a notice dated 12-7-2017 asked the petitioner to show cause as to why her admission should not be cancelled for submitting discrepant documents at the time of her admission. The petitioner replied to the show cause notice by a letter dated 18-7-2017; but the reply was found unsatisfactory. Thereafter the Chittagong University by its letter dated 18-7-2017 informed the respondent No. 8 of the cancellation of admission and registration of the petitioner for getting herself admitted to the medical college by submitting forged and fabricated documents. Then the respondent No. 8 by its letter dated 24-7-2017 cancelled the admission of the petitioner. The medical college authority was misled by the petitioner on production of forged and fraudulent documents at the time of her admission to MBBS course for the session 2013-2014. The college authority was never a party to the fraud committed by the petitioner. So the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

8. In the Affidavits-in-Reply both dated 15-5-2018 filed by the petitioner against the Affidavits-in-Opposition of the respondent Nos. 3 and 8, it has been stated that the petitioner did not submit any false or fabricated admission test result while applying for admission to the respondent No. 8 college. She filled in the admission form herself in capital letters as instructed therein. At the top left-hand corner of the form, there is a box under the caption "Result of Written Admission Test" wherein the session, merit score and merit position of the candidate concerned are written. The petitioner did not write anything in that corner box of the form as she was not required to do so. The college authority filled in the top left-hand corner box after verifying her result which was published online. Her name was in the waiting list and subsequently she was admitted to the medical college therefrom. During the academic session 2013-2014, most of the medical colleges of the country accepted application forms from the students who scored less than 120 marks in the admission test. Like the petitioner, those students were admitted to various private medical colleges of Bangladesh. Anyway, the respondent No. 8 constituted a three-member committee which verified the papers and documents submitted by the petitioner and others. In the merit score column of the report of the three-member committee, the petitioner was quoted to have scored 127.38 marks in the admission test. This score was not provided by her and the admission test result which was published online clearly stated that she had scored 109.38 marks. She did not tamper with her result nor did she make any false statement in respect of her admission score. The three-member committee after verifying her admission score intentionally put a false score (127.38) against her name. So the college authority is responsible for the perpetration of fraud as regards her admission to 1st year MBBS course for the academic session 2013- 2014.

9. By filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition on behalf of the respondent No. 8 against the application of the petitioner for direction dated 15-5-2018, the respondent No. 8 has specifically stated that the petitioner herself filled in the admission form on 10-8-2016 with the false and inflated merit score for getting professional registration from the BMDC. It is crystal clear from the filled in form (Annexure-'X-21') that the petitioner bearing roll No. 201818 carried her merit score as 127.38 and merit position as 45244 instead of her actual merit score of 109.38 and merit position of 61242.

10. At the outset, Mr Masood R Sobhan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that after successfully completing three academic years and passing all the examinations, the sudden cancellation of the admission and registration of the petitioner and disallowing her to continue her studies, through no fault of her own, are mala fide and therefore the impugned letters dated 6-07-2017 and 18-7-2017 are without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

11. Mr Masood R. Sobhan further submits that the registration of the petitioner was cancelled by the Chittagong University without issuing any show cause notice and the reply dated 18-7-2017 furnished by the petitioner in response to the show cause notice issued by the respondent No. 8 was not taken into account whatsoever without any justifiable reason.

12. Mr Masood R. Sobhan next submits that the sudden cancellation of the admission and registration of the petitioner without any valid reason will totally jeopardize her life and educational career thus violating her fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution and therefore the impugned letters dated 6-7-2017 and 18-7-2017 are without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

13. Mr Masood R Sobhan also submits that the petitioner did not commit any fraud in relation to her admission to 1st year MBBS course for the session 2013-2014 and the fraud was perpetrated by the respondent No. 8-college and in that view of the matter, the petitioner is entitled to continue her studies in the respondent No. 8-college.

14. Mr Masood R. Sobhan further submits that although the petitioner is a beneficiary of the fraud, yet the fact remains that she did not play any role in the forgery resorted to by the college authority at the time of her admission and, as such, she is not responsible for her illegal admission to the college.

15. Mr Masood R Sobhan lastly submits that regard being had to the decisions in the cases of Registrar, University of Chittagong, Chittagong vs Niger Sultana Naina handed down by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal Nos. 3027-3029 of 2016 and Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka vs The University of Dhaka represented by the Vice-Chancellor, Shahbag, Dhaka rendered by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 147 of 2015 with Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal Nos. 1110 and 1111 of 2015, the petitioner cannot be victimized and so she may be allowed to continue her studies in the medical college.

16. Per contra, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 3, submits that in view of Clause 14 of Annexure-'A' to the Writ Petition, the Writ Petition is not maintainable.

17. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam also submits that as the resolution of the dispute involves questions of facts and adducing of evidence and as it is a matter of evidence and trial, the Writ Court sitting under Article 102 of the Constitution cannot go into those questions and that being so, the Writ Petition is not maintainable.

18. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam next submits that indisputably the result of the admission test of the petitioner and others for admission to 1st year MBBS course for the academic session 2013-2014 was published online and the petitioner admittedly scored 109.38 out of 200 marks and knowing full well that she was not qualified to make any application for admission to the respondent No. 8 college in view of the benchmark of 120, even then she made an application for admission to the college out of bad faith.

19. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam further submits that the petitioner submitted the application for admission in the prescribed form to the medical college authority and the top left-hand corner box of Annexure-A-1' was filled in by the college authority on the basis of Annexure-'X-2' (corresponding to Annexure-1-1-1') supplied by the petitioner herself and as Annexure-'X-2' was supplied by the petitioner herself, the college authority cannot be blamed for the wrong score and merit position written in the aforementioned box of Annexure-'X-1'.

20. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam also submits that Annexure-'X-21' dated 10-8-2016 was filled in by the petitioner herself which was addressed to the BMDC for her registration as a medical student and in that Annexure- 'X-21', it is clearly and unambiguously written as her merit score of 127.38 and merit position of 45244 instead of her merit score of 109.38 and merit position of 61242 and this Annexure-'X-21' is confirmatory of the perpetration of fraud by her.

21. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam next submits that admittedly the advertisement issued by the respondent No. 8 college for admission to MBBS course stipulated that the minimum requirement for admission to the college was 120 marks, but it does not stand to reason and logic as to why the petitioner submitted her application to the college for admission and ultimately she was kept in the waiting list wherefrom she was admitted thereto and this very submission of the application for admission to the college by her goes to show that she was a party to the fraud.

22. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam also submits that the petitioner has not come up with clean hands before this Court inasmuch as she is a party to the fraud and by submitting false and fabricated documents showing her merit score of 127.38 and merit position of 45244, she got herself admitted to the college and since fraud vitiates everything, she cannot be allowed to reap the fruit of her fraud.

23. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam further submits that the BMDC acted within its jurisdiction and power conferred upon it under section 5(11) read with sections 5(20) and (24) of বাংলাদেশ মেডিকেল ও ডেন্টাল কাউন্সিল আইন, ২০১০ which enable the BMDC to accord registration or refuse to accord registration due to any irregularity/illegality committed by any student and since undeniably the petitioner did not obtain the required merit score for getting admission to the medical college and since she obtained admission thereto by way of perpetration of fraud, the BMDC conducted necessary inquiries and crosschecked the result of the admission test with the record of the Directorate of Health Services and upon giving an opportunity to her to present her case, the BMDC issued the impugned letter dated 6-7-2017 refusing to grant registration to her.

24. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam next submits that it is a settled principle of law that no one is allowed to take advantage of his own wrong and the same principle has been enunciated in the cases of the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Secretariat Building, Dhaka vs Mrs Momtaz Begum, 10 MLR (AD) 23 = 10 BLC (AD) 23 and Principal, Fulbaria College, Mymensingh vs Md Helaluddin, 32 BLD (AD) 11 = 64 DLR (AD) 35 and in this perspective, the petitioner cannot capitalize on the fraud perpetrated by her in the matter of her admission to the respondent No. 8 college.

25. Mr Md Ekramul Hoque, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 4, adopts the sub-missions advanced by Mr Tanjib-ul Alam.

26. Mr Md Ashik-al-Jalil, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 8 college, submits that it is undisputed that the petitioner scored 109.38 out of 200 marks and the benchmark for admission to medical colleges for the session 2013-2014 was 120 and being fully aware of her score of 109.38, she submitted her application to the respondent No. 8 college for admission when admittedly the required benchmark of 120 was specifically stated in the notice of the college as evidenced by Annexure-'X' and this conduct of the petitioner indicates that she was a party to the fraud.

27. Mr Md Ashik-al-Jalil also submits that on the basis of Annexure-'H-1', the respondent No. 8 college made the entries at the top left-hand corner box of the prescribed form as evidenced by Annexure-'X-l' and had the petitioner not supplied the Annexure-'H-1', the college authority would not have written the fictitious marks of 127.38 and merit position of 45244 in the box and in order to skirt the liability deliberately, she did not consciously annex Annexure-'X' to the Writ Petition and this conduct of the petitioner unerringly shows that she was very much concerned with the perpetration of fraud at the time of her admission to 1st year MBBS course in the college during the session 2013-2014.

28. Mr Md Ashik-al Jalil also submits that the verification and checking of the application form along with the documents submitted by the petitioner for the purpose of her admission to the college were done by a three-member committee and the committee relied upon the documents submitted by the petitioner, in particular, Annexure-'H-1' which was attested by one Dr Md Emdadul Huq, Assistant Director (Medical Education), Directorate of Health Services, Mohakhali, Dhaka and given this scenario, the fraud perpetrated at the time of her admission to the college could not be detected earlier.

29. We have perused the Writ Petition, Affidavits-in-Opposition, Affidavits-in-Reply and relevant Annexures annexed thereto and heard the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr Masood R. Sobhan and the counter-submissions of the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 3 Mr Tanjib-ul Alam and the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 8 Mr Md Ashik-al-Jalil.

30. There is no gainsaying the fact that the petitioner took the admission test for MBBS course for the session 2013-2014 and her merit score and merit position were 109.38 and 61242 respectively. Needless to say, the benchmark for admission to 1st year MBBS course was 120 as evidenced by Annexure-'X'. Although admittedly the petitioner's merit score was 109.38 having merit position 61242, yet she submitted her application in the prescribed form to the respondent No. 8 college. In this connection, Annexure-'H-1' to the Writ Petition may be gone into. A reference to Annexure-'H-1' reveals that the merit score of the petitioner was 127.38 and her merit position was 45244. It may be recalled that this Annexure-'H-1' was attested by one Dr. Md Emdadul Huq, Assistant Director (Medical Education), Directorate of Health Services, Mohakhali, Dhaka and it was supplied to the college authority by the petitioner herself for the purpose of her admission. However, it is the candid assertion of Mr Md Ashik-al-Jalil that the top left-hand corner box of Annexure-'X-1' was filled in by the college authority on the basis of Annexure-'H-1'. The submission of this Annexure-H-1' to the college authority by the petitioner herself is not disputed. What is more, the Annexure-'X-21' dated 10-8-2016 was also admittedly filled in by the petitioner herself. In that Annexure-'X-21', her merit score was shown as 127.38 and merit position was shown as 45244 in place of her actual merit score 109.38 and merit position 61242. The Annexures-H-1' and `X-21', if considered together, will conclusively indicate that the petitioner was privy to the fraud committed during the time of her admission to 1st year MBBS course in the college during the session 2013-2014.

31. It is the contention of Mr Masood R. Sobhan that the petitioner was not served with any show cause notice by the Chittagong University (respondent No. 5) prior to cancellation of her admission and registration as a student of the medical college (respondent No. 8) and on that score, the same is tainted with bad faith or mala fides. In this context, it may be pointed out that fraud vitiates everything.

32. In the decision in the case of The State of Chhattisgarh vs Dhirjo Kumar Sengar reported in (2009) 13 SCC 600, it was held in paragraphs 19, 20 and 21:

"19. The respondent keeping in view the constitutional scheme has not only committed a fraud on the Department, but also committed a fraud on the Constitution. As commission of fraud by him has categorically been proved, in our opinion the principles of natural justice were not required to be complied with.

20. Mr Gupta has relied upon a large number of decisions of this Court, viz., Inderpreet Singh Kahlon vs State of Punjab, ((2006) 11 SCC 356); Mohd. Sartaj vs State of UP, ((2006) 2 SCC 315); Jaswant Singh vs State of MP, ((2002) 9 SCC 700) and State of MP vs Shyama Pardhi, ((1996) 7 SCC 118) to contend that audi alteram partem doctrine should have been complied with.

21. In these cases, requirement to Comply with the principles of natural justice has been emphasised. The legal principles carve-out therein are unexceptional. But, in this case, we are concerned with a case of fraud. Fraud, as is well known, vitiates all solemn acts. (Ram Chandra Singh vs Savitri Devi reported in ((2003) 8 SCC 319), Tanna & Moth vs CIT reported in ((2007) 7 SCC 434) and Rani Atoka Dudhoria vs Goutam Dudhoria reported in ((2009) 13 SCC 569). The High Court, therefore, must be held to have committed a serious error in passing the impugned judgment."

33. Reverting to the case in hand, we have already found that the petitioner was the perpetrator of fraud during the time of her admission to 1st year MBBS course in the medical college for the session 2013-2014. It may be reiterated that it is a settled principle of law that no one is allowed to take advantage of his own wrong. This principle also finds support from the decisions in the cases of the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Secretariat Building, Dhaka vs Mrs Momtaz Begum, 10 MLR (AD) 23 = 10 BLC (AD) 23 and Principal, Fulbaria College, Mymensingh vs Md Helaluddin, 32 BLD (AD) 11 = 64 DLR (AD) 35 relied on by Mr Tanjib-ul Alam.

<u>34. After admission of the petitioner to 1st year MBBS course in the respondent No. 8-college, everything went off without any hitch and she continued her studies for three years in a row. Thereafter all of a sudden, a whistleblower, namely, one Mamunur Rashid, a senior journalist of "The Daily Samakal", lodged a complaint dated 1-2-2017 with the BMDC about the perpetration of fraud relating to admission of the petitioner to the respondent No. 8 college for the session 2013-2014. On receipt of that complaint, the BMDC caused necessary inquiries by cross-checking her result of the admission test with the record available with the conducting authority, that is to say, Directorate of Health Services and found her alleged merit score of 127.38 and merit position of 45244 fictitious and baseless. Since the petitioner secured her admission to the medical college by means of fraud, she is not entitled to any prior show cause notice at all. So on this question, the contention of Mr Masood R Sobhan stands discarded.</u>

35. However, if the petitioner is allowed to continue her studies in the medical college on the basis of the fictitious result submitted to the college authority during the time of her admission and to the BMDC at a subsequent stage for her registration, that will amount to putting a premium on the perpetration of fraud. A Court of law cannot put any premium on the fraud perpetrated by any person. The college authority, that is to say, the respondent No. 8 should have cross-checked the result of the petitioner submitted at the time of her admission with reference to the result available both with the BMDC and the Directorate of Health Services of Bangladesh. The college authority might have played a nefarious role in the perpetration of fraud as claimed by Mr Masood R Sobhan; but that has not been proved at all. So we refrain from penalizing the respondent No. 8 on this count.

36. It is curious to note that one Dr. Md Emdadul Huq, Assistant Director (Medical Education), Directorate of Health Services, Mohakhali, Dhaka attested Annexure-'H-1' to the Writ Petition showing the merit score of the petitioner as 127.38 and her merit position as 45244 in place of her actual merit score of 109.38 and merit position of 61242. It is the admitted position that the college authority relied upon Annexure-'H-l' which was attested by Dr. Md Emdadul Huq. This being the state of affairs, it is quite incomprehensible and unfathomable as to why the BMDC failed to refer the malfeasance of Dr. Md Emdadul Huq to the Directorate of Health Services for initiating necessary punitive steps against him. Besides, the Directorate of Health Services ought to have taken punitive actions against Dr. Md Emdadul Huq suo motu for such malfeasance. The inaction of both the BMDC and the Directorate of Health Services in this regard is deprecated.

37. The reliance of the petitioner on the decisions in. the cases of Registrar, University of Chittagong, Chittagong vs Niger Sultana Naima rendered by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal Nos. 3027-3029 of 2016 and Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka vs The University of Dhaka represented by the Vice-Chancellor, Shahbag, Dhaka made by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 147 of 2015 with Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal Nos. 1110 and 1111 of 2015 does not appear to be of any avail to her inasmuch as the facts and circumstances of those cases are quite distinguishable from those of the present case.

38. In the instant case, the petitioner has been found to be privy to the fraud and as she is privy to the fraud, she cannot derive any benefit out of that fraud. In a case of almost similar nature, this Bench adjudicated upon the Writ Petition No. 16016 of 2016 and discharged the Rule issued therein on 24-5-2017 on the ground that the petitioners of that Writ Petition were privy to the fraud and that judgment of the High Court Division was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Division by its judgment dated 2-1-2018 passed in Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No. 4056 of 2017.

<u>39. As the hands of the petitioner are tainted with fraud, she cannot invoke the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. There goes a time-honoured legal dictum-'One who seeks equity must come with clean hands'. It should be borne in mind that a Writ Court is undoubtedly a Court of Equity too. Since the hands of the petitioner are unclean, she must be shown the door under Article 102 of the Constitution. Over and above, Clause 14 of Annexure-'A' to the Writ Petition is to the effect that—"নির্বাচিত প্রার্থীদের দেওয়া তথ্য অসম্পূর্ণ অথবা ভুল প্রমাণিত হলে, তার ভর্তি বাতিল বলে গণ্য হবে।" So we find that the Writ Petition is incompetent.</u>

40. From the foregoing discussions and in view of the facts and circumstances of the case, we find no merit in the Rule. The Rule, therefore, fails. But as the petitioner was a party to the fraud, she should be penalized by way of exemplary costs.

41. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged with costs of Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) only. The Directorate of Health Services is directed to take necessary punitive steps against Dr Md Emdadul Huq, Assistant Director (Medical Education), Directorate of Health Services, Mohakhali, Dhaka for falsely attesting Annexure-'H-1' to the Writ Petition showing the merit score of the petitioner as 127.38 and her merit position as 45244 in place of her actual merit score of 109.38 and merit position of 61242 immediately.

Let a copy of the judgment be immediately transmitted to each of the respondents for information and necessary action.

End.
