Jahangirnagar University and others  ---------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed J : This Rule Nisi was issued on 4-11-2018 calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the publication of a separate merit list for Madrasah students in respect of the First Year (Honours) Admission Examinations (2018-2019) of the Faculty of Arts and Humanities (Unit-C) of Jahangirnagar University (Annexures-H(8) & H(9)) and the non-inclusion of the names of Madrasah students in the merit lists prepared by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities of Jahangirnagar University for successful candidates from the 'Science' and 'Humanities' streams in respect of the said Admission Examinations shall not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect, and as to why the Respondents shall not be directed to complete the admission process by incorporating the names of all Madrasah students, including the Petitioners, in the merit list prepared by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities (Unit-C) of Jahangirnagar University for candidates from the 'Science' and 'Humanities' streams and/or such other or further Order or Orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. This Court at the primary stage had also to dispose of an Application for Stay dated 18-11-2018 predicated on developments at the heels of this Court's Rule issuing Order of 4-11- 2018. On 4-11-2018 in addition to the prayer for a Rule Nisi the Petitioners had additionally sought a direction upon the Respondent No. 6, the Dean, Faculty of Arts of Humanities of Jahangirnagar University to publish the merit list of successful candidates from the 'Science' and 'Humanities' streams in respect of the First year (Honours) Admission Examinations (2018-2019) of the Faculty of Arts and Humanities (Unit-C) by incorporating the names of Madrasah students. The Court, however, was at the time disinclined to so intervene pursuant to that prayer primarily on the ground that this would tantamount to granting the substantive relief and pre-judging the Rule Nisi. The Court's expectation, on the other hand, was also of the concerned University authority keeping the examination /selection process in abeyance up until the Rule Nisi being substantively disposed of.

3. It so transpired, however, and as was evident from the Application for Stay dated 18-11-2018, that two weeks into the issuance of the Rule Nisi, as had been served on the Respondents by Special Messenger, the Faculty of Arts and Humanities of Jahangirnagar University had scheduled interviews of successful candidates on the basis of the merit lists the legality of which are under challenge in the instant Writ Petition. This Court was apprised further that the interviews were scheduled for 18, 19, 20 and 22-11-2018. It was asserted that the Applicant-Petitioner through Counsel had issued a legal notice dated 17-11-2018 upon the Respondents by Special Messenger requesting a halt to the viva-voce examinations but that this had been to no avail.

4. The learned Advocate for the Applicant-Petitioner, Mr Imran Siddiq submitted that should the interview process have continued as scheduled the Rule Nisi would be rendered infructuous and that the interview process in itself in that regard merited treatment as an interference with the administration of justice. The prayer, accordingly, was for staying altogether the holding of the viva-voce examinations in respect of the First Year (Honours) Admission Examination (2018-2019) of the Faculty of Arts and Humanities (Unit-C) of Jahangirnagar University.

5. An Affidavit-in-Reply on behalf of the Respondent Nos. 1-6 to the said Application for Stay seeking effectively to oppose the intervention so sought by the Applicant-Petitioner brought on record the fact that the viva-voce examination dates had already been set prior to the issuance of the Rule Nisi at a meeting of the University Central Admission Committee on 31-10-2018. Ms Nahid Mahtab, representing the Respondents, further alerted this Court to the fact that allowing the prayer for stay would potentially affect the entire admission process and jeopardize the admission prospects of 18,000 students then awaiting selection through the examination process. This Court was also apprised that the Applicant-Petitioner Mr Sajjadul Islam, being one of the three Petitioners, had already appeared in the viva-voce examination on 18-11-2018 along with 23 other male Madrasah students.

6. Upon a consideration of the above, this Court on 19-11-2018 deemed it prudent to inter-vene, albeit in a limited manner, in disposal of the Application for Stay. Accordingly, the Respondent Nos. 3 to 6 were directed to reserve a seat each in three departments being (i) Journalism and Media Studies, (ii) International Relations and (iii) History, being a total of 3 seats, until further directions/Orders from this Court.

7. It is to be noted at the outset that the Writ Petition initially filed by three Petitioners has now come to represent the pleadings and claims of the sole petitioner, being the Petitioner No. 1 Sajjadul Islam. By an Order of the Court dated 2-1-2019, as per a prayer to that effect, the other two Petitioners had their names struck off this case in evidence of their withdrawal from these proceedings.

8. In this Writ Petition, the Petitioner has challenged the legality of the publication of a separate merit list for Madrasah students in respect of the First Year (Honours) Admission Test (2018-2019) of the Faculty of Arts and Humanities of Jahangirnagar University and the non-inclusion of the names of Madrasah students in the merit lists prepared by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities for successful candidates from the 'Science' and 'Humanities' streams of higher secondary education.

9. The publication of separate merit lists for different groups of students as categorised by the University authorities (i.e., Humanities/ Science/Commerce/ Madrasah) is directly linked to caps on the number of seats offered to the various groups. This is because Clause 2(Chha) of the Admissions Circular dated 16-8-2018 clearly provides that the number of candidates in the merit list shall be ten times the total number of available seats. Thus, the publication of names of 770 candidates in the Merit List titled 'Male Candidates (Humanities)' indicates that the University authorities has fixed the number of seats available for Male Candidates (Humanities) to 77, while the publication of a separate merit list for 110 Madrasah students indicates that the University authorities has restricted the number of seats available to Madrasah students to only 11. Aggrieved by such caps on the seats being offered to Madrasah students, the Petitioners filed the instant Writ Petition.

10. The Petitioner's contention that the University authorities have placed caps on the number of seats available to Madrasah students has been confirmed by a series of documents in evidence of decisions of distribution of seats taken by various Departmental Academic Committees as appended to the Respondents' Affidavit in Opposition. The Petitioner asserts, accordingly, that the total number of seats in the Faculty of Arts and Humanities available for Madrasah students has been restricted to only 9.

11. It is noted at the outset that the Rule Nisi that has been issued in the instant Writ Petition is confined to the question of legality of separate classification of Madrasah students. The Petitioner is not aggrieved by nor has he challenged the classification that has been made by the different departments of the Faculty of Arts and Humanities on the basis of the disciplinary backgrounds of the various candidates (i.e., Science/Arts/Commerce). Thus, all questions relating to the legality of such classification as well as the propriety, reasonableness and validity of fixation of a specific number of seats for candidates coming from Science/Arts/Commerce background (i.e., fixing, for instance, the ratio of candidates from Humanities background as 55% and that from Science background as 35% for the Department of International Relations) are beyond the scope of the Rule.

12. Given the limited scope of the Rule, the Petitioner's arguments have been confined to the question of legality of separate classification and capping of seats for Madrasah students

13. The Petitioner argues that the impugned action of the University in publishing separate merit lists and the capping of seats for Madrasah students is liable to be declared without lawful authority and of no legal effect for the following reasons:

(I)	Capping of seats and publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students not sanctioned by the Jahangirnagar University Act, 1973 ("The Act") and the University Ordinance, 1993 ("The Ordinance");

(II)	Capping of seats and publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students violate Article 27 of the Constitution; and

(III)	Capping of seats and separate merit lists for Madrasah students undermine merit in violation of Clause 7 of the Ordinance.

14. It is on these limited grounds that the Petitioner has sought an intervention of this Court in exercise of its powers under Article 102 of the Constitution.

I. Capping of seats and publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students not sanctioned by law:

15. The Petitioner submits that the Act and the Ordinance do not in any manner permit the University authorities to impose any restrictions on the admission of Madrasah students to the University by publishing a separate merit list for Madrasah students and fixing the number of seats available to them, details of which are set out below.

16. The conditions under which students are to be admitted to the University are set out in the Act and the Ordinance. Section 42(1) of the Act provides that admission to the University shall be made by the University Admission Committee, while section 42(2) provides that additional qualifications may be prescribed by the University Ordinance to govern the admission of students to the University over and above the basic eligibility requirement of completion of higher secondary level examinations. It is stated that there is no provision in the Act nor has any additional qualifications been prescribed by the Ordinance which permit the University authorities to fix a cap on the number of seats available for Madrasah students.

17. The constitution and powers of the University Admission Committee (as referred to in section 42 of the Act) are set out in detail in sections 2 and 3 of the Ordinance respectively. Section 3(Ka) of the Ordinance empowers the Admissions Committee to determine the minimum eligibility conditions for admission to the University, while section 3(Ga) of the Ordinance empowers the Admissions Committee to determine the procedure to be adopted by the Departmental Admission Committees for admission of students to the University. In exercise of its powers under section 3 of the Ordinance, the Admissions Committee issued the Admissions Circular dated 16-8-2018 to regulate the admission of students to the University for the Academic Year (2018-2019). Clause 1 of the said Circular contains the minimum eligibility requirements for admission to various departments (as contemplated under section 3(Ka) of the Ordinance), while Clause 2, in particular Clause 2(Chha), of the Circular provides the procedure to be followed by the Departmental Admissions Committee for admission of students to the University (as contemplated under section 3(Ga) of the Ordinance). The Petitioner asserts that no provision of the Circular dated 16-8-2018, as has been issued by the Admissions Committee in exercise of its powers under section 42 of the Act read with section 3 of the Ordinance, allows the capping of seats for Madrasah students and the publication of separate merit lists. As such, the Petitioner submits, the publication of the separate merit list and the capping of seats for Madrasah students by the University's Faculty of Arts and Humanities, being devoid of legal sanction, is liable to be declared without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

18. The Petitioner points out that section 3(Gha) of the Ordinance empowers the Admissions Committee to determine the numbers of seats to be offered in a particular Academic Year and the allocation of seats between the various departments. In exercise of its powers under section 3(Gha), the Admissions Committee adopted a resolution on 12-8-2018 fixing the total number of seats to be offered by each Department and Faculty of the University. However, as is evident from the records, the Admissions Committee has not fixed the number of seats to be offered to Madrasah students in a particular department as it has not been so empowered under section 3(Gha). The learned Advocate for the Petitioner, Mr Imran Siddiq submits that, however, if section 3(Gha) of the Ordinance were to be appropriately amended by the Syndicate, the Admissions Committee could arguably determine the number of seats to be allocated to Madrasah students in any particular department. Even then, Mr Siddiq submits further, the authority would be reserved to the University Admission Committee and not the individual Departments themselves.

II. Capping of seats for Madrasah students and publication of separate merit lists violate Article 27 of the Constitution.

19. The Petitioner agitates further that even assuming without conceding that the publication of separate merit lists/capping of seats for Madrasah students is sanctioned by law, such action, being in violation of Article 27 of the Constitution, is liable to be declared without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

20. It is stated that by virtue of a notification dated 23-2-1986 issued by the Ministry of Education, Alim graduates have been placed at par with students who have passed Intermediate Examinations. The equivalency of Alim Examination to HSC Examinations, Mr Siddiq apprises this Court, has also been recognised by this Court in Writ Petition No. 7944 of 2009 wherein it has been held that 'the Alim Certificate is equivalent to HSC standard ' Pursuant to such equivalency circular dated 23-2-1986, all public universities, including Jahangirnagar University treat Alim graduates as being at par with candidates who have passed Intermediate examinations. This is made evident to this Court from the Admissions Circular dated 16-8-2018 issued by the Admissions Committee which in determining the eligibility conditions refers to the aggregate GPA obtained in ‘মাধ্যমি/সমমান এবং উচ্চমাধ্যমিক/সমমান পরীক্ষা’. Mr Siddiq explains that the term has been used to refer to 'Alim' and `Dakhil' as being equivalent to 'HSC' and 'SSC' respectively. In this regard, it is to be noted that Alim (Science) is treated as equivalent to HSC (Science) while Alim (General) is treated as equivalent to HSC (Humanities) (a fact which has not been denied by the Respondents) as well as the Admissions Circular dated 16-8-2018 which contemplates Alien (General) candidates as falling within the category of ‘উচ্চমাধ্যমিক মানবিক’.

21. The Petitioner now contends that having accepted Alim graduates as being at par with candidates who have passed Intermediate examinations, the action of the University in treating Madrasah students as a separate category of students and publishing a separate merit list and capping the number of seats for Madrasah students violates the twin test of equality inherent in Article 27 of the Constitution, i.e., that the classification must be based on 'permissible criteria' or 'intelligible differentia' and that such classification must have a reasonable nexus with the object to be thereby achieved. It is noted that in the case of Sheikh Abdus Sabur vs Returning Officer, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 30, the Appellate Division held in paragraph 29 as follows:

The term 'equal protection of law' is used to mean that all persons or things are not equal in all cases and that persons similarly situated should be treated alike. Equal protection is the guarantee that similar people will be dealt with in a similar way and that people of different circumstances will not be treated as if they were the same and  if these differences are identified, then the persons or things may be classified into different categories according to those distinctions; this is what is called 'permissible criteria' or 'intelligible differentia'  To stand the test of equality, a classification, besides being based on intelligible differentia, must have reasonable nexus with the object the legislature intends to achieve by making the classification...'

It is submitted in this context that Madrasah students being at par with HSC students and having passed the common entrance examinations (where they are tested to the same degree of proficiency and skill) are required to be treated in the same manner as HSC students. Separate classification of Madrasah students in these circumstances is not, therefore, based on any permissible criteria nor does it have any nexus with the object to be achieved of selecting the best candidates for admission to the University. As such, the separate categorisation of Madrasah students violates Article 27 of the Constitution.

22. The Petitioner also relies on the judgment of the Supreme Court of India in the case of the State of Andhra Pradesh and others vs Balaram, reported in AIR 1972 SC 1375, wherein it has been held that classification of candidates on the basis of their academic backgrounds after they have completed the common entrance examinations violates the equality clause. The Supreme Court held as follows:

'It is open to the State to prescribe the sources from which the candidates are declared eligible for applying for admission to the Medical College; but when once a common Entrance Test has been prescribed for all the candidates on the basis of which selection is to be made, the rule providing that 40% of the sets will have to be reserved for Higher Secondary Course (Multi-purpose) candidates is arbitrary. In the first place, after a common test has been prescribed, there cannot be a valid classification of the Pre-University Course and Higher Secondary Course (Multi-purpose) candidates. Even assuming that such a classification is valid, the said classification has no reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved, namely selecting the best candidates for admission to the Medical Colleges'.

Furthermore, similar observations were made by the Supreme Court of India in the case of AIIMS Students Union vs AIIMS reported in AIR 2001 (SC) 3252 at paragraph 53, wherein it was held as follows:

' The impugned reservation, obnoxious to merit, fails to satisfy the twin test under Article 14. Having taken a common entrance test, there is no intelligible differentia which distinguishes  the institutional candidates from others;  and there is no nexus sought to be achieved with the objects of AIIMS by such reservation------

Mediocracy over meritocracy cuts at the roots of justice and hurts right to equality. Protective push or prop by way of reservation or classification must withstand the test of Article 14. Any over-generous approach to a section of the beneficiaries, if it has the effect of destroying another's right to education, more so by pushing a mediocre over a meritorious belies the hope of our Founding Fathers on which they structured the great document of Constitu-tion, and so must fall to the ground...'

III. Capping of seats for Madrasah students undermines merit in violation of Clause 7 of the Ordinance and Clause Khha)(1) of the Admission Circular.

23. The Petitioner has averred that Alim graduates who have scored much higher in the Admission Examinations (2018-2019) than candidates who have passed Intermediate examinations are being denied a place in the University on account of the cap placed on the number of seats available for Madrasah students. It is pointed out, for instance, the Petitioner who scored a total of 59.425 in the Admission Examinations being an Alim (General) graduate has not been offered a seat in the University's Faculty of Arts and Humanities. However, as many as 32 candidates from the Merit List of 'Male Candidates (Humanities)' (who had passed Intermediate examinations) had been offered seats by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities although they all scored less than the Petitioner in the Admission Examinations. Thus, as a result of the publication of the separate merit lists and the capping of seats for Madrasah students, candidates who are less meritorious are securing admission to the University. As such, the Petitioner argues, the impugned action of the University in restricting admission of Madrasah students undermines merit in violation of Clause 7 of the Ordinance and Clause 2(Chha)(1) of the Circular dated 16-8-2018.

24. It is at this juncture that Mr Imran Siddiq has submitted that in view of the fact that the admissions process for the Academic Year 2018-2019 has been completed, the Petitioner did not pray for any Order from this Court which would be tantamount to nullifying the entire admission process. However, since the question of legality of separate merit lists for Madrasah students arises every year, the Petitioner, sought an adjudication by this Court by laying down an authoritative interpretation of Article 27 of the Constitution and section 42 of the Act read with sections 3, 5 and 7 of the Ordinance which will serve as a guidance for the University in subsequent academic years.

25. Mr Siddiq submits further that as regards the Petitioner it has been admitted by the University that he is qualified to be admitted to the Department of Journalism and Media Studies. Moreover, a seat in the said Department has already been kept reserved for him by the Order of this Court dated 19-11-2018. As such, the prayer is for this Court to direct the University authorities to admit the Petitioner to the Department of Journalism and Media Studies immediately.

26. In the circumstances, the Petitioner prayed that the Rule be made absolute in part by:

(i) declaring the publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and directing that in subsequent academic years the names of Madrasah students be included in the merit lists prepared in respect of candidates from HSC academic background; and

(ii) directing the Respondents to admit the Petitioner to the Department of Journalism and Media Studies.

27. The Respondent No. 1, Jahangirnagar University, a residential university, responded to the Rule and asserted that in view of provision of section 40 of the Act each of its students shall reside in a designated Residential Hall. Accordingly, total seats for admission in the University depend upon availability of seats in such Halls which varies from year to year.

28. The learned Advocate for the University, Ms. Nahid Mahtab explains that the admission process is regulated by the Admission Committee formed by the Academic Council under section 42 of the Act and the Ordinance wherein the power and function of Admission Committee of University and Academic Committee of each department has been described. Ms. Mahtab submits that the University Academic Committee is authorized to fix seats for students from various groups seeking admission in the department and the recommendations of the Academic Committee of each department is forwarded to the Admission Committee through the Dean of each Faculty for facilitating the admission process. Prior to initiation of the admission process the Academic Committee of each department fixes the criteria of admission qualification in the department in view of provision of section 5 read with section 3(ga) of the Ordinance. As for example, the Department of International Relations in its Academic Meeting dated 22-7-2018 decided to distribute seats among groups by giving preference to the students of Humanities. As per that decision 55% seats were allocated for students of Humanities Group, 35% seats for Science Group, 10% for Commerce and other groups.

29. Afterwards, the University Admission Committee in it's meeting dated 12-8-2018 decided to admit 376 students in the Faculty of Arts and Humanities (C-Unit) and also fixed seats among the departments. As per the decision 60 seats were allocated for Department of Bangla, 70 for Department of English, 60 for Department of History 50 for Department of Philosophy, 26 for Department of Drama, 30 for Department of Archaeology, 70 for Department of International Relations and 36 seats were allocated for Department of Journalism and Media Studies.

30. Subsequently, the University authority published the circular for admission of students for admission in 376 seats of C-Unit and as many as 46, 671 students of Humanities, Science, Commerce and other groups participated in the Admission Test out of whom 3,579 examinees qualified. Ms Mahtab submits that it is only after completion of the admission test that the Writ Petitioner filed the instant Writ Petition and obtained the Rule Nisi.

31. Ms Mahtab submits further in reiteration that in view of section 42(1) of the Act the admission of students to the University shall be made by the Academic Committee appointed for that purpose by the Academic Council and in view of provisions of section 5 read with section 3(ga) of the Ordinance the Academic Committee has authority to take decision for distribution of seats among groups and accordingly as per the University's requirement the University Admission Committee conducted the examination for admission of students and the University by following all provisions and completed the admission process, thereby, negating any prospects for a favourable consideration and disposal of this Rule Nisi.

32. Ms Mahtab argues that the decision to adopt classifications is an internal administrative policy of the University which should not be interfered with since it has been taken by following rules and without any mala fide intention and for the benefit of all students from different groups. Ms Mahtab stresses further that the classification is purely a 'beneficial classification' since in fact after publication of a separate merit list for male Madrasah students the Petitioner has secured an opportunity to choose either International Relations or Media and Journalism Studies whereas if a combined merit list was published that would not necessarily have been the case and the Petitioner would not get any subject to choose from. Ms Mahtab, accordingly, submits that as the decision of publication of separate merit list for Madrasah students has been taken for the benefit of Madrasah students and has enured to the benefit, for instance, of the Petitioner the Rule Nisi may be found to be without any substance and be discharged.

33. Additionally, Ms Mahtab draws on the maxim "factum infectum fiery nequit" i.e., "what is done cannot be undone" which she argues to be relevant to the present Writ Petition given that the admission process has been acted upon and thousands of new entrants have taken admission into the University, thereby, necessitating a rejection of the Petitioner's claims in the greater interest.

34. In reply, Mr Siddiq argued satisfactorily that the Respondents' argument that section 5 read with section 3(Ga) of the Ordinance allows the Departmental Admission Committee to fix the number of seats available for Madrasah students is completely misconceived inasmuch as section 5 of the Ordinance merely provides that the Departmental Admission Committee shall perform its responsibilities in the manner required under section 3(Ga). This Court finds that section 3(Ga) of the Ordinance is an empowering provision which allows the University Admission Committee to determine the procedure to be adopted by the Departmental Admission Committees in the admission of students. In that regard, it is noted that the Admissions Circular dated 16-8-2018, which was issued pursuant to section 3(Ga) and sets out the admission procedure to be followed by the Departmental Admission Committees, does not contemplate that the latter will fix the number of seats available for Madrasah students. As such, this Court finds, there is indeed no legal sanction for the decision of the various departments to place a cap on the number of seats available for Madrasah students. Within the scheme of the applicable law it is imperative for the Departmental Committees to function according to procedure set out by University Admission Committee under section 3(Ga). In the facts, the Departmental Admission Committees evidently have transgressed their authority in determining capping limits without due prior sanction of not only the University Admission Committee but indeed the law itself. Resultantly, the very act of limiting the number of seats available to students with a Madrasah background is found to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

35. In response to the argument of the Respondents that the separate classification of Madrasah students is not hit by Article 27 as it is in the nature of a 'beneficial classification', Mr Siddiq has argued that there is to the contrary ample evidence to show that Madrasah students are being denied admission to the University by virtue of their separate categorisation, although candidates who have scored much less than them are being offered seats at the University.

36. Furthermore, as Mr Siddiq points out, for the Academic Year 2018-2019, the University authorities have already determined the various categories of candidates in respect of whom a policy of 'beneficial classification' has been sanctioned, which includes freedom fighters' children, backward and Dalit communities, physically challenged individuals etc. There is a separate application process for admission to the University in such reserved categories. Madrasah students do not fall within any of the aforesaid categories of candidates earmarked by the University by way of 'beneficial classification'. As such, the argument that the separate categorisation of Madrasah students is in the nature of a beneficial classification is found by this Court to be misconceived and flawed.

37. Finally, it has aptly been pointed out by the Petitioner that it is only, and curiously so, the Faculty of Arts and Humanities that has resorted to the policy of separate categorisation of Madrasah students. It is difficult for this Court to understand why a policy of 'beneficial classification' for Madrasah students should be pursued by only one Faculty and not uniformly by other Faculties of the University in unison. In other words the true rationale behind this ostensible 'beneficial classification' remains elusive to this Court even notwithstanding the University's insistent invocation of the same.

38. The Petitioner also disputes the argument of the Respondents that meritocracy is not being undermined inasmuch as the student who secured the 9th position in the Merit List for Male Madrasah students scored 60.51 whereas the same score was obtained by the 'student who secured the 58th position in the Merit List for Male Candidates (Humanities). This Court finds this argument of the Respondents to be misconceived inasmuch as it does not take into consideration the phenomenon of capping of seats. Thus, and as sufficiently explained to this Court by Mr Siddiq, because of the cap of 9 seats for Madrasah students, no one from amongst Madrasah candidates who scored less than 60.51 would be allowed a place in the University. However, since a total of 72 seats are available for candidates from the Merit List of Male Candidates (Humanities), as many as 14 candidates from the said merit list would be able to obtain admission to the University although they scored much less than 60.51.

39. This Court, taking stock of submissions and arguments placed on both sides, finds the emphasis on a merit-based admission process by both sides to be inescapable. The question that is moot, however, is whether the system, by no means universal even within the University, devised by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities is beneficial, hence, equitable and legal or not. The University would have this Court believe that it is so. The Petitioner, on the other hand, decries the same to be outright discriminatory and, therefore, hostile to Madrasah students as a class. As Mr Imran Siddiq explains, and satisfactorily so, the intent is in the math, and it just does not add up. Taking the case of the Petitioner Sajjadul Islam, for instance, it is noted that he scored a total of 59.425 marks but risked being denied a place although as many as 32 candidates who have scored for less, but drawn from other groups, were preferentially offered places in the University. The spectre of the 'cap' placed, and arbitrarily so without any legal sanction as discussed above, on the number of seats available for Madrasah students has, therefore, loomed large in this case leading to the inequity and discrimination in the intake of students by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities (Unit-C) of the University. In other words, the reduced number of seats, arbitrarily and peremptorily, introduced selectively within the University is found to operate greatly to the prejudice of Madrasah students disentitling them to compete on an equal footing with University entrants of other diverse backgrounds notwithstanding that they qualify eminently under a purely merit- based entrance and elimination mechanism to be treated at par. The arbitrarily conjured 'capping' mechanism by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities invidiously reeks of introducing a 'no-demand' element in the admission selection process. Indeed, the University Act and Ordinance provide no sanction or accommodation for such a criterion to gain currency. It is now, therefore, for this Court to declare, hereby, the same to be without lawful authority and no legal effect in order that it does not gain a further foothold.

<u>40. Moreover, the case law scrutinized and applied by this Court as above amply attest to the prevalence of a 'level-playing field' in any admission process. The tests for example of 'permissible criteria' and 'intelligible differentia' coupled with the 'reasonable nexus' standard all aim at upholding in the facts that which is contemplated in Article 27 of the Constitution. That is, the purpose of merit lists is to identify and select the most meritorious of candidates. But in the instant case, the merit lists as devised or drawn up fail to achieve that purpose but rather yield an opposite result. That, as is evident in the discussions above, this Court cannot condone.</u>

41. As the judicial precedents examined above declaredly endorse, common entrance tests must serve as a vehicle to create a level-playing field and once that hurdle is overcome by the aspirant examinee the examining authority will have administratively crossed the Rubicon with no avenue left to harp on pre-test differences in educational backgrounds. Never, therefore, has the proposition that genetic blemishes and birthmarks disappear upon fusion into a common stream (See, State of J & K vs Triloki Nath Khosa, reported in (1974) 1 SCC 19 & 1974 SCC & S) 49) proved to be more axiomatic than when applied to the instant facts and circumstances. Predicated on these compelling grounds, our findings, therefore, are in favour of the Petitioner.

42. Resultantly, the Rule is made absolute-in-part. Accordingly, it is declared that the publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students by the University's Faculty of Arts and Humanities is without lawful authority and of no legal effect and the University is directed that in subsequent academic years the names of Madrasah students shall be included in the merit lists prepared in respect of candidates from HSC academic backgrounds.

43. Furthermore, bearing in mind certain developments noted in this Court's earlier Order dated 19-11-2018 and the fact that the Petitioner has taken up an offer for enrolment in the University's English Department but with plea of preference stated by him of rather now being granted a place in the Department of Journalism and Media Studies, this Court, hereby, orders that the Order of reservation of 19-11-2018 is, hereby, lifted subject only to a seat in the Department of Journalism and Media Studies being offered to the Petitioner. The remaining three other seats in the Departments of International Relations, History and now English (now being vacated by the Petitioner in light of this Judgment and Order) should now be filled up by deserving aspirants at the earliest in accordance with applicable law and regulations. Ms Nahid Mahtab is, hereby, directed to issue a lawyer's certificate to that effect to the concerned Respondents forthwith.

44. There is no Order as to costs.

Communicate this Order at once.

End.

Islamic University, Kushtia - Jhenidah, Bangladesh, represented by its Vice-Chancellor and others --------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury J : The concept of "due process of law", which has found a place in our Constitution in Article 31 under the heading "Right to protection of law", has come up once again before this Court for consideration. From one perspective, the issue is quiet simple and straight forward; yet, from another perspective, it is rather complex, involving various dimensions, not just legal, but social and administrative as well.

2. 88 writ petitioners, all being students of 1st year in the Department of Mathematics and Department of Statistics, Islamic University, Kushtia have challenged the legality of Decision No. 196, taken at the 233rd Meeting of the Syndicate of Islamic University, Kushtia, held on 6-3-2017 cancelling the result of the admission test of the 1st year students of F Unit in respect of the academic session 2016-2017 and directing to hold the admission test, afresh, for the 1st year students of F Unit, as per circular contained in Memo No.২/শিক্ষা/ইবি-২০১৭/৬১৬ dated 8-3-2017 issued by respondent No. 3, published in the daily Bangladesh Protidin on 10-3-2017 as evidenced by Annexure F.

3. At the time of issuance of the Rule on 13-3-2017, although a prayer was made in the writ petition itself and also by the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners to postpone the re-admission test, this Court declined to grant the prayer. Rather, the respondents were directed to proceed with the admission test scheduled to be held on 16-3-2017 and the petitioners were also directed to take part in the admission test. It has to be brought on record that the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners readily agreed to abide by the Court's directive upon the petitioners to take part in the re-admission test in order to demonstrate their bonafide.

4. Certain facts, which are undisputed, need to be recorded at the very outset.

5. The petitioners, who are the students of the Department of Statistics and the Department of Mathematics, The Islamic University, Jhenaidah, Kushtia (briefly, the University), appeared in the admission test of F Unit held on 7-12-2016. The result was published on the following day i.e. on 8-12-2016. Subsequently, the process of admission started on 16-1-2017 when the students, including the petitioners, who had qualified in the admission test, were directed by the University to pay the fees and other charges in order to complete the admission procedure. The 88 petitioners and the remaining 12 students, who are not before us (totaling 100), duly paid the fees and other charges through the Bank, as directed by the University. Thereafter, the classes of the 1st year students of both the departments namely, Mathematics and Statistics departments, commenced on and from 30-1-2016.

6. While the petitioners along with the other students were attending the classes regularly, the University authorities took a mock test of all the students on 14-2-2017. However, without any further steps or directive, the students of both the Departments were allowed to continue with their classes.

7. On 6-3-2017, the University authorities issued the impugned order contained in Decision No. 196, taken at the 233rd Meeting of the Syndicate, cancelling the result of the 1st year admission test of F Unit and directing to hold a fresh admission test of 1st year students of 'F' unit. Being aggrieved thereby, the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule.

8. The Rule is being opposed by respondent Nos. 1-5 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition.

9. Mr Md Ruhul Quddus, the learned Advocate appears along with Mr Khaled Mahmudur Rahman, Mr Akter Rasul, Ms. Nusrat Yeasmin, and Mr Mossaddek Billah, Advocates on behalf of the petitioners, while Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appears with Mr Syed Quamrul Hossain, the learned Advocate on behalf of respondent Nos. 1-5.

10. Having placed the instant application together with the Annexures, Mr Md Ruhul Quddus, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the impugned action of the respondents in cancelling the result of the 1st year admission test of F unit is not tenable in law for the simple reason that the same was passed in gross violation of Article 31 of the Constitution, which provides for the right to protection of law. Moreover, according to Mr Quddus, the impugned decision was taken in utter disregard to the well-settled principle of natural justice. The learned Advocate submits that if a person is accused of a crime which carries "capital punishment", even in that case, the accused is dealt with in accordance with law. However, in the instant case, the petitioners were completely kept in the dark and no prior notice was served upon the petitioners and therefore, the impugned order was passed behind their back. He further submits that this is not a simple order cancelling the result of the admission test held on 7-12-2016, but an "administrative order", which has grave consequences for the students in as much as, they would be prevented from pursuing their academic career in any public or private University. Therefore, according to Mr Quddus, the impugned order had the effect of causing "academic death" of the petitioners.

11. The learned Advocate submits that even if it is accepted, but not conceded, that the allegation of leakage of question paper, as alleged by the University, is correct, that by itself cannot absolve the University from giving an opportunity to the petitioners to be heard before passing the impugned order. He submits forcefully that none of the petitioners had any involvement with the alleged leakage of question paper. Referring to the Inquiry Report filed by the University through the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 12-4-2017 Mr Quddus submits emphatically that it is evident from the said Report that as many as 4-5 teachers and staff of the University were involved in the said incident. However, not a single student belonging to the 1st year F Unit, in either Mathematics Department or the Statistics Department, was found to be involved with the incident in question.

12. Mr Quddus contends that the students of "F" unit, who had qualified in the admission test held on 7-12-2016, were directed to pay the fees on the very same date on which the University formed an Inquiry Committee to inquire into the matter. Therefore, according to the learned Advocate, the University authorities came to know of the matter at a very early stage, only when the result had been published. Despite being fully aware of the matter and having initiated an inquiry into the same, but without waiting for its outcome, the University Authority directed the students to complete their admission process and also allowed them to start their respective classes from 30-1-2017.

13. The learned Advocate contends that by their own conduct, the University authorities are, at the least, guilty of waiver and acquiescence. Mr Quddus concludes his submission by submitting that if the arbitrary and malafide decision of the University is allowed to stand, it would destroy the future prospect of the petitioners by causing "academic death" at the very early stage their career.

14. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appears in his personal capacity, and not as the Attorney-General, along with Mr Syed Quamrul Hossain, the learned Advocate in opposition to the Rule.

15. Mr Alam submits that the Inquiry Committee was formed on 16-1-2017 immediately after the University became aware of the matter, which first came to light through the newspaper report, published on 4-1-2017 Referring to the writ petition itself, Mr Alam submits that although the admission of 100 students was cancelled, only 88 have appeared before this Court, out of whom only 2 writ petitioners have filed necessary documents evidencing their admission in the University, while the rest have not annexed any documents to prove their standing. According to Mr Alam, the petitioners have accepted the impugned decision by their own conduct by taking part in the subsequent re-admission test held on 16-3-2017.

16. Referring to the re-admission test result, which has been annexed in the affidavit of compliance dated 23-3-2017, Mr Alam submits that out of 88 petitioners before this Court, only 29 petitioners have been able to secure their names in the merit list of 100 successful students. Although the names of 11 other petitioners have appeared in the 1st waiting list containing 100 names, the names of the remaining 48 petitioners do not appear in the result published by the University.

17. Mr Alam submits that admittedly the question papers were leaked before holding of the 1st admission test on 7-12-2016, as is evident from the Inquiry Report submitted to the Syndicate on 4-3-2017. Therefore, according to Mr Alam, since the matter of leakage of question paper has been established by the University upon holding a full fledged inquiry, the petitioners, whose admission test result has been cancelled, cannot be allowed to benefit from a wrongful act, even though all of them may not have any link with such act. He submits that no person can claim to be benefitted from a wrongful act.

18. Mr Alam next submits that merely by attending classes, the petitioners cannot be said to have been vested with a legal right. On the contrary, he contends that the students, who have taken part in the subsequent admission test and qualified, now have a legitimate expectation to pursue their academic career in the University. Mr Alam submits that if the Rule is made absolute and the petitioners' admission result, test published on 8-12-2016, is held to be valid, that would create both academic and administrative complications as there are only 100 seats in the Statistics and Mathematics Departments, each having 50 seats. Therefore, any additional number of students cannot be accommodated in the present academic year without prior approval and sanction from the University Grants Commission (UGC).

19. Referring to paragraph 3 of the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 12-3-2017, Mr Alam submits that in the Admission Form given to the students at the time of admission, it has been clearly stated in the Form itself that the University Authority has every right to cancel the admission of any student at any moment and no question can be raised regarding such action.

20. Mr Alam submits that since the factum of leakage of question paper has been established beyond any reasonable doubt by the Inquiry Committee, it cannot be said that the cancellation of the 1st year admission test of F Unit, held on 7-12-2016, by the Syndicate is without lawful authority and consequently the Rule is liable to be discharged.

21. As indicated at the very outset of this judgment, the concept of "due process of law", as enshrined in Article 31 of our Constitution, is central for determination of the issue before us.

22. Let us now refers to Article 31 of the Constitution, which reads as under:

"31. To enjoy the protection of the law, and to be treated in accordance with law, and only in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen, wherever he may be, and of every other person for the time being within Bangladesh, and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law."

23. From the language of Article 31, it is evident that the Constitution not only confers upon a person the right to protection of law, but seeks to ensure the same by prohibiting any action detrimental to one's life, liberty, reputation or property, save and except in accordance with law. This constitutional guarantees, as envisaged by Article 31, is referred to as "the due process of law".

24. The concept of "due process of law" involves two distinct elements. The first element imposes a mandatory duty upon the Authority concerned to appraise the person of the charge or offence for which a proceeding is being initiated against him. Not only that, judicial pronouncements have gone, to the extent to hold that even the proposed punishment must be indicated to the person concerned at the very initial stage. The second element requires that the person, who is so charged, should be afforded an opportunity to file a reply/representation to the Authority in respect of the said allegation or charge. Non-compliance or non-observance of the second element is bound to give a "telling blow" to any subsequent action of the Authority.

25. Now, let us have an over view of the matter before us. The whole issue arose following the leakage of the question paper of the admission test of 'F' Unit. Admittedly, the question papers were leaked prior to holding of the admission test on 7-12-2016. The result was published on the following day. Even if it is accepted for the sake of argument that the University Authority had no knowledge about the matter prior to holding of the admission test, quite clearly, the University Authorities became fully aware of the matter, as early as 4-1-2017, when the newspaper report was published, as acknowledged by Mr Alam himself. Thereafter, the Inquiry Committee was formed on 16-1-2017 to investigate into the matter. Being fully aware of the matter and having started an inquiry into the same, the University Authorities, on the very same date, i.e. on 16-1-2017, initiated the actual process of admission by directing the students to deposit their fees and other charges. The matter did not end there. The University authorities completed the admission procedure and allowed the students, including the present petitioners, to start their academic career in the University by holding the 1st year classes on and from 30-1-2017. It was not until 6-3-2017, i.e., after a period of two and half months, that the impugned order was passed. All this while, the University Authorities did not take any step to suspend the classes and prevent the petitioners from attending the classes. Rather, despite initiation and continuation of the inquiry, the University Authorities allowed the petitioners to attend their classes in their respective departments.

26. On the other hand, the petitioners, having duly qualified in the admission test and having paid their admission fees and other charges and having completed the admission procedure, started their classes on and from 30-1-2017 It is not until the issuance of the impugned order on 6-3-2017 that the petitioners were officially intimated about the matter. There is not a single document on record nor is there any statement in the affidavit-in-opposition to the effect that on any date prior to 6-3-2017, the petitioners were notified about the proceeding or that they were issued show cause notice or that some explanation was sought from the petitioners. Therefore, upto 6-3-2017, the petitioners were totally kept in the dark and they had no prior notice about the proceeding or the inquiry, which culminated in the issuance of the impugned order.

27. The issue of leakage of question paper is undoubtedly a very serious matter which, in our view, cannot be condoned in any manner. The persons involved with such heinous act should be punished very severely, without any sympathy. Having said that, it has to be borne in mind that no person can be condemned unheard. In other words, a person against whom an action is proposed to be taken which is detrimental to his life, liberty and/or property, should be afforded an opportunity of stating his case before the concerned authority.

28. From Annexure 3 of the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 12-4-2017, filed on behalf of respondent Nos. 1-5, being the Report of the Inquiry Committee (তদন্ত কমিটির প্রতিবেদন), it appears that the Inquiry Committee did not find the involvement of any of the students of F Unit, who had appeared in the admission test on 6-12-2016. On the contrary, the Report discloses the complicity and involvement of some senior academic staff of the University. The only student, who has been named in the said report, appears to be a student of the Master Degree in the Department of Mathematics.

29. It is on record that the Inquiry Report has not been made available to any of the petitioner before us, although it is on the basis of this very report that the impugned Decision No. 196 was taken by the Syndicate on 6-3-2017 cancelling the admission test result of F unit, held on 6-12-2016.

30. During the course of his submission, the learned Advocate for the respondents has provided several official correspondences made by the University, although the same has not been filed by way of affidavit-in-opposition, despite a directive by this Court to do so. However, we take judicial notice of the same.

31. It appears from the letter dated 9-3-2017 issued vide প্রশাঃ ইবি/২০১৭/৩০৫২, under the signature of the Registrar (Acting) and addressed to one Md Saiful Islam, Senior Auditor, Finance and Accounts Department, Islami University, Kushtia, that pursuant to a written complaint filed by a student organization on 20-1-2017, the University Authorities constituted a Inquiry Committee. The letter reads as under:
