full_judgment:
Md. Iqbal Kabir, J: 

1. This appeal has been presented, at the instance of the defendants/appellants against the judgment and decree dated 31.01.2006 passed by the Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Money Suit No. 28 of 2003. 

2. The facts relevant for disposal of the appeal are that the plaintiff filed the aforesaid Money Suit for compensation, stating inter alia that the plaintiff Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation here in after called BADC engaged with the development of agriculture under the Ministry of Agriculture entered into an agreement for Group Term Insurance on 05.08.1990 known as Contract No. 0181/90 with the defendant No.2, Delta Life Insurance Company Ltd. The Contract was initially effective from 01.07.1990 to 30.06.1993, extendable annually upon mutual consent of the parties. The said contract No. 0181/90 was remained in force until 30-06-1994 and thereafter, both the parties made a Memorandum of Understanding herein after called (MOU) and as per the MOU the said contract was extended from 01.11.1994 to 30.06.1995. The plaintiff corporation demanded some claim against their employees. But the settlement of the aforesaid claims having remained unsettled, thereafter, a tripartite meeting was held amongst the plaintiff corporation and the company that is the defendant No.1 and the Controller of Insurance (defendant No.3). The meeting was convened at the instance of the plaintiff Corporation and it was Chaired by the defendant No.3. 

3. Pursuant to the decisions the defendants made settlement of 11 claims out of 19, remaining 8 claims which amounting of Tk. 5,01,165/, remained un settled, while company do not make such payment the plaintiff made representation for the same. The defendants are also responsible to pay the said amount as per clause 2 of the contract, though it has also mentioned in the tripartite agreement. While defendants failed to settle the claims as per the tripartite agreement and contract, then the plaintiff made several remainder about the payment. This inaction of the defendants hampered the livelihood of the poor employees of the plaintiff. Thereafter, on 31-07-01 the plaintiff corporation issued a legal notice upon the defendants, demanding payment of the amount of Tk. 5,01,165/- on insurance claims and Tk.6,00,000/- as compensation for having not been paid the claims money to the poor staff members of the plaintiff corporation intentionally, which led to their suffering and harassment and by this notice threatened to take legal action. In response to the reply of the notice the plaintiff corporation issued another notice stating that since defendants failed to pay the insurance claims made by the plaintiff corporation, there is no scope to renew the new insurance contract. On the contrary the defendants were in breach of the contract for which they became liable to pay damages to the Corporation having not executed the terms and obligation laid down in the contract and MOU. Subsequently one legal notice was published in ‘the Daily Inquilab’ dated 17.02.2002 by the plaintiff corporation asking to pay the insurance claims along with compensation money all together Tk. 11, 01, 165/ within 15 days from the receipt of the notice.

4. The suit was contested by the defendants by filing the written statements contending inter alia that the plaintiff company entered into a contract for Group Term Insurance on 05.08.1990 known as contract no. 0181/90 with the defendant No.2, Delta Life Insurance Company Ltd. which was effective from 01.07.1990 to 30.06.1995, extendable annually upon mutual consent of the parties. The said contract No. 0181/90 was remained in force until 14.11.1994 and by a Memorandum of Understanding the said contract extended from 01.11.1994 to 30.06.1995, subject to the condition that if any claim had not been submitted by the plaintiff corporation within 31.01.1995 it would not qualify for settlement. The defendant No.1 has made a settlement of 374 claims totaling an amount of taka 3,84,79,005/- of the plaintiff corporation and when only 22 claims remained outstanding the said defendants paid 14 of those claims whereby only 8 claims were left for settlement. 

5. The plaintiff corporation submitted eight claims for settlement to the defendant No.1, the particulars of which are as follows: i) Atul Tudu, Tk. 58,680/; ii) Shukra Chandra, Tk.95,130/; iii) Sultan Ahmed, Tk.89,460/, iv) Habibullah Kazi, Tk.1,25,820/; v) Khoka Mia, Tk.17,325/, vi) Emadul Haq, Tk.50,400/,; vii) Abdul Khaleque, Tk.16,200/,; and viii) Abdul Motaleb, Tk.48,150/- all together Tk. 5,01,165/- (Taka five lac one thousand one hundred and sixty five) only. 

6. Out of the above mentioned eight claims (i) to (v) were submitted to the defendant No.1 beyond the time limit prescribed in MOU, which is part of the Contract No.0181/90; claims mentioned at no (vi) and (vii) could not be settled as the plaintiff Corporation demanded payment at an enhanced rate, without making payment of the increased premium at the applicable rate corresponding to the said demand of enhancement, and the claim shown at item (viii) as aforesaid was made for the reason of amputation of one leg of the assured due to Buerger’s disease which does not fall within the purview of the contract as it is stipulated therein that such claim could be made only for disability arising from accident. 

7. The trial court examined one witnesses on behalf of the plaintiff and one witness on behalf of the defendants and by the impugned judgment decreed the suit. 

8. The plaintiff examined only one witness who is Mr. Mohammad Ismail stated in his examination in chief that plaintiff has filed money suit calming Tk. 11, 01,165/. The Group Term contract No. is 58/90. This contract was remained in force until 30-06-93, later on it was extended for further one year. As per contract the defendants are responsible for all risk. This witness further stated that as per fixed rate they gave the premium. Since defendant refused to pay the insurance claims, hence on 15.11.94 a MoU has been made in between plaintiff and defendants. As per the said MoU, it has decided that plaintiff made all his claim within 31st January, 95 and defendant will pay the claim with 28th February, 95. But defendant failed to pay. As per MoU the defendant settled 11 insurance claims and reaming 8 were not settled. On 25th January 97, a tripartite meeting was held amongst the plaintiff corporation and the Company, this meeting had decided about payment, but defendant not willing to pay the claims. The plaintiff corporation submitted eight claims for settlement and all together the claim is Tk, 5,01,165/. As per the contract dated 28th February, 95 the defendants are responsible to pay the claim within that period but when they failed, the corporation made two separate representations before the controller of insurance. Thereafter,a tripartite agreement was signed on 25th January, 97 and 22nd February, 97 wherein it was decided that defandent will pay the insurance claims, failing which the plaintiff made several remainder letter. Thereafter, on 31-07-01 the plaintiff corporation issued a legal notice upon these defendants demanding payment of the amount of Tk. 5, 01,165/- against insurance claims and Tk.6, 00,000/- as compensation for having not been paid the claim money of the poor staff members of the plaintiff corporation intentionally. On 16th September, 01, the defendants refused to pay the said amount. Then to reduce the damage of the employees of corporation legal advisor of the plaintiff corporation issued another legal notice on 04th December, 01 claiming Tk. 11, 01, 165/. Thereafter, plaintiff corporation published the said legal notice in the daily news paper namely ‘The Daily Inquilab’ on 17. 02.2002, but the defendant did not pay heed to it, hence this suit. To support the claim, he submitted some documents. 

9. In his cross examination this witness stated that he is an accounts officer and service holder of BADC. After obtaining the consent from the concerned authority he made this witness. He stated that on 5th August, 90 the contract was executed in-between plaintiff corporation and Delta Life Insurance Ltd, at that time he was not present. He informed that the total claim including the compensation was of Tk. 11,01,165/, out of that Insurance claim was of Tk. 5,01,165/. He also denied the defence suggestions that the contract would be failed if the claim dose not made in specific time; new Group Term insurance contract would be made; plaintiff breach the condition of the contract; as per the condition of the contract plaintiffs failed to make the claims in time. Claims are not acceptable. 

10. The defendants examined only one witness, who is Mr. Asif Iqbal, Joint Vice-President of the Company stated in his examination inchief that for the employees and the officers of the Corporation, Insurance Contract was made in between the BADC and Delta Life Insurance Ltd. The Group Term contract No. is 181/90 dated 5th August, 90. (Exhibit-(L), The contract began on 1st July, 1991, remain valid until 30th June, 93. After this contract another MOU was made in between the plaintiff corporation and the defendant on 1st November, 94 (exhibit-M) and that was remain valid till 30th June, 94. Condition No.2 of the MOU suggest that every claim have to be made within stipulated time. But the claims were not submitted with in that stipulated time. The plaintiff corporation issued the legal notice and the company on 16th September, 01, made reply against on it (Exhibit-N), On 17th, February, 02, that legal notice was published in daily Inquilab, against which on 21st February, 02 defendants made a protest through publishing a Notice in daily Inquilab. (Exhibit-.O).The defendant made payment against 11 claims out of 19 claims. Out of eight claims (i) to (v) were submitted their claims beyond the time limit prescribed in MOU which is part of the Contract.; claims no (vi) and (vii) could not be settled as the plaintiff Corporation demanded payment at an enhanced rate: since they failed to make payment of the premium in enhence rate, the claim (viii) as aforesaid was made for the reason of amputation of one leg of the assured due to Berger’s disease which does not fall within the purview of the contract as it is stipulated therein that such claim could be made only for disability arising from accident. In support certificate was produced, (Exhibit-P). On 11th October, 98, it was duly informed to the Controller (Exhibit-Q), There is no reason to file this suit. This suit has been filed only to harass the defendants; plaintiff cannot get any relief from this suit. This DW also denied the suggestions made by the plaintiff that the plaintiff is entitled the get the relief from this suit.

11. In his cross examination he stated that the Company has been registered under Joint Stock Company, and have Article of Association. BADC and Delta Life Insurance Ltd entered into a contract, which was effective from 01.07.1990 to 30.06.1993. Lateron it was extended for one year that is till 30th June, 94. MOU has been signed on 1st November, 94. It was remained valid from 1st November, 94, to 30th June, 95. As per MOU the defendant made their payment within 28th February, 95, if plaintiff submitted their claims within time. It is not true that the claims have not submitted as per schedule time. Plaintiff submitted their claims before the Controller of Insurance and through him a contract has been signed in between the plaintiff and defendants. It is not true that 8 claims out of 19 have not purposely been fulfilled by the defendants. The defendants made reply against the letters submitted by the plaintiff, it is not true that company have breach the conditions of MOU and contract. It is not true that company have to fulfill the 8 claims. The claims made by Hossain Gazi has been fulfilled later on. It is not true that Motaleb Miah may get his claim as because he fall in an accident but due to operation has fallen in Buerger’s disease. 

12. The trial court examined the witnesses as well as documents produced by the plaintiff and the defendants, the fact and circumstances of the case and evidence both oral and documentary on record and found that plaintiff has succeeded to prove his case. Upon consideration of the evidences on record the trial court, decreed the suit. 

13. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree the contesting defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have preferred this appeal. 

14. We have heard the learned Advocate Mr. M A Azim Khair along with Mr. Abul Kalam Azad who appeared on behalf of the appellants and submitted that trial court erred in law in passing the impugned judgment and decree. 

15. Learned advocate for the appellant, submitted that contract No. 0181/90 was remained in force until 30-06-1994 and by a MoU the said contract was extended from 01.11.1994 to 30.06.1995, subject to the condition that if any claim had not been submitted by the plaintiff corporation those have to be made and submitted within 31.01.1995, otherwise it would not qualify for settlement. 20. We have gone through the evidences on record, heard the learned advocate for the appellants and examine the relevant facts and circumstances and evidences. On the other hand no one appears to oppose the appeal, although this item was in the list since long along with the name of the learned lawyers of both the parties. 

21. On our careful scrutiny it is found from the MoU that: 

বাংলাদেশ কৃষি উন্নয়ন কর্পোরেশন ও মেসার্স ডেলটা লাইফ ইনসিওরেন্স কোম্পানি লিমিটেড-এর মধ্যে দ্বিপাক্ষিক সমঝোতাপত্র।

২। যেহেতু উভয় পক্ষের মধ্যে বকেয়া দাবি ও বকেয়া বীমা প্রিমিয়াম পরিশোধে অচলাবস্থা নিরসনকল্লে এই সমঝোতাপত্রের উদ্বব হয়, সেহেতু ২৩-১০-৯৪ ইং তারিখে উভয় পক্ষের প্রতিনিধিদের উপস্থিতিতে বিস্তারিত আলোচনান্ডে নিম্নলিখিত শর্তাধীনে উভয় পক্ষের সম্মতিক্রমে অত্র সমঝোতাপত্র সম্পাদনের ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করা হইল।

(খ) সমঝোতা পত্রের শর্তাবলীঃ

১। এই চুক্তিনামা ০১/১১/৯৪ ইং তারিখ হইতে ৩০/০৬/৯৫ ইং তারিখ পর্যন্ত বলবত থাকিবে। প্রয়োজনবোধে পরবর্তীতে উভয় পক্ষের সম্মতিক্রমে অত্র সমঝোতাপত্রের সময় সীমা বৃদ্ধি করা যাইবে ।

২। প্রয়োজনীয় কাগজ পত্র এবং তথ্যাদি সঠিক পাওয়া গেলে কোম্পানি প্রতি সন্তাহে গড়ে ৫ (পাঁচ) টি বীমা দাবি করপোরেশন কর্তৃক দাখিলকৃত তালিকার ক্রমানুষায়ী পরিশোধ করিবে এবং ২৮/০২/৯৫ ইং তারিখের মধ্যে বকেয়া বীমা দাবি পরিশোধ করিবে ।

বীমা দাবির ক্ষেত্রে কোন অজর আপত্তি থাকিলে, দাবি প্রাপ্তির ১০ (দশ) দিনের মধ্যে কোম্পানি সুনির্দিষ্ট আপত্তি সমেত উহা করপোরেশন এর নিকট পাঠাইবেন। করপোরেশন উক্ত আপপ্তি প্রাপ্তির ১০(দশ) দিনের মধ্যে আপত্তি যথাফতভাবে নিষ্পত্তিপূর্বক প্রয়োজনীয় কাগজপত্র ও তথ্যাদিসহ কোম্পানির নিকট পাঠাইবেন।

আপত্তি মিটানোর ৭ (সাত) দিনের মধ্যে কোম্পানি বীমা দাবি পরিশোধ করিতে বাধ্য থাকিবে। করপোরেশন কর্তৃক কোন বীমা দাবি ইতিমধ্যে কোম্পানির নিকট দাখিল করা না হইয়া থাকিলে সর্বশেষ ৩১শে জানুয়ারী, ৯৫ ইং এর মধ্যে অবশ্যই দাখিল করিতে হইবে |

22. Apart from that the contract as well as the MoU suggested that if there is any dispute raised between the parties they are at liberty to settle the matter through arbitration and in this connection the Contract and MoU stated as follows:

“গ্রুপ সাময়িক জীবন বীমা চুক্তি নং ০১৮১/৯০”

অনুচ্ছেদ-১৬ মধ্যস্থৃতাকারী নিযোগঃ ১৯৪০ সালের মধ্যস্থৃতাকারী আইন অনুসারে এই চুক্তিনামায় যে কোন শর্ত /শর্তসৃমহ (আংশিক এবং /অথবা সামগ্রিক) বা গ্রুপ সাময়িক জীবন বীমা সংক্রান্ত কোন বিষয়ে উভয় পক্ষের মধ্যে মতানৈক্য হইলে সংশ্লিষ্ট অনুচ্ছেদের সঠিক ব্যাখ্যা এবং/ অথবা ঔরূপ মতানৈক্য নিরসনের জন্য উভয় পক্ষের সমঝোতা সাপেক্ষে একজন মধ্যস্থতাকারী, আর ষদি উভয় পক্ষ একমত হইতে না পারে তবে উভয় পক্ষ একজন করিয়া মোট দু'জন মধ্যস্থতাকারী নিয়োগ করিবে । উক্ত বিষয়ে মধ্যন্থৃতাকারী (গণ) এর রায়/ সিদ্ধান্ত
উভয় পক্ষ মানিয়া লইতে বাধ্য থাকিবে

(খ) সমঝোতাপত্রের শর্তাবলীঃ

৫। সমঝোভাপত্র বা উহার সহিত সংশ্লিষ্ট বিষয়ে উভয় পক্ষের মধ্যে কোন বিরোধ বা মতদৈততা দেখা দিলে উভয় পক্ষের মধ্যে সম্পাদিত গ্রুপ সাময়িক জীবন বীমা চুক্তি (চুক্তি নং-০১৮১/৯০) এর ১৬ নং অনুচ্ছেদ অনুযায়ী উহা নিরসন করা হইবে । সালিশের শুনানী অন্য কোথাও নির্ধারিত না হইলে, ঢাকাতেই অনুষ্ঠিত হইবে |

স্মারক নং হিসাব/যৌবী/৩১৭/৯৫/২৭৫ তারিখঃ-৩০.০১.১৯৯৫ইং

24. In this connection the provision of the contract stated as follows:

খ) দুর্ঘটনা বীমাঃ দুঘটনার পতিত হইয়া সম্পূর্ন বাহ্যিক এবং দৃশ্যমান আঘাতের কারণে তাৎক্ষনিক এবং/ অথবা দূর্ঘটনার সঠিক সময় হইতে ৯০ দিনের যধ্যে কর্পোরেশনের বীমাকৃত কোন সদস্যের মৃত্যু হইলে কোম্পানী দুর্ঘটনা মৃত্যু দাবীর সমপরিমাণ টাকা কর্গোরেশন কে অতিরিক্ত পরিশোধ করিবে । এবং তৎক্ষনাত মৃত বীমাকৃত সদস্যের বীমা ঝুঁকির পরিসমান্তি ঘটিবে।

গ) পঙ্গুত্বের বীমাঃ যদি বীমাকৃত কোন সদস্য দুর্ঘটনাজনিত কারণে সম্পূর্ণ বাহ্যিক এবং দৃশ্যমান আঘাতে আক্রান্ত হন এবং দুর্ঘটনার সময় হইতে ৯০ দিন পরও দুর্ঘটনা জনিত আঘাত নিরাময় না হয় এবং দুর্ঘটনা জনিত সরাসরি আঘাতের কারণে এবং/অথবা এই আঘাতের সহিত অন্যকোন ব্যাধি সম্পর্কযুক্ত না হইয়া শুধুমাত্র দুর্ঘটনায় আক্রান্ত হইয়া যে আঘাতের সৃষ্টি হইয়াছিল সেই কারণে চোখের দৃষ্টি শক্তি সম্পূর্ণ লোপ পাইলে এবং/ অথবা অন্যকোন অংগ খোয়া বা সম্পূর্ন নষ্ট হইলে পরে বর্ণিত সাধারণ নিয়মাবলীর আওতায় কোম্পানী নিম্নে বর্ণিত বীমা অংক বা আংশিক বীমা অংক কর্পোরেশনকে পরিশোধ করিবেঃ

25. We have examined the record and found that there is no tripartite agreement, but there is a meeting minutes and the decision of the meeting does not support to meet up the claims in favour of the plaintiff beyond the scope of MoU. The decision of the meeting as follows:

“বিষয়ঃ ডেল্টা লাইফ ইনস্যুরেন্স কোম্পানি লিমিটেড ও বাংলাদেশ কৃষি উন্নয়ন কর্পোরেশনের মধ্যে গ্রুপ বীমার দাবী পরিশোধ সংক্রান্ত গত ২৫.০১.৯৭ এবং পরবর্তীতে ২২.০২.৯৭ ইং তারিখের অনুষ্ঠিত বর্ধিত সভার কার্য বিবরণীঃ

সভায় সার্বিক বিষয়ে আলোচনাল্ডে সর্বসম্মতিক্রমে এই সিদ্ধান্ত গৃহীত হয় যে, ডেল্টা লাইফ ইনস্যুরেন্স কোম্পানী লিমিটেড ৩০-০৬.৯৪ ইং তারিখ পর্যন্ত সময়ের মধ্যে বিএডিসি কর্তৃক উত্থাপিত সকল বীমা দাবি পলিসির চুক্তি শর্ত মোতাবেক অনতিবিলম্বে পারিশোধের ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করবে এবং বিএডিসি ভবিষ্যতে তাদের সকল গ্রুপ বীমা ডেন্টা লাইফ ইনস্যুরেন্স কোম্পানির সাথে সম্পাদন করার জন্য যথাসাধ্য চেষ্টা করবেন এই জন্য যে, বিএডিসির এ যাবৎ উত্থাপিত দাবীসমূহ পরিশোধে ডেল্টা লাইফ ইনস্যুরেন্স আর্থিকভাবে বেশ ক্ষতিগ্রস্থ হয়েছে।"

26. On our careful scrutiny it is evident from the statement made by the P.W. that plaintiff deposited their claims within stipulated time mentioned in the MoU, plaintiff witness also denied the suggestion made by the defendants lawyer that they do not deposited claims within time, in this connection P.W. produced some documents. But the oral evidence does not supported by the documentary evidence shown as exhibits. Those documents suggested that claims have been submitted after expiry of the time limited mentioned in the MoU. On the other hand the defence witness stated that the plaintiff failed to submit their claims within time and they do not deposite their premium in an enhanced rate. In support thereof this defendant’s witness produced some documents which were shown as exhibits, those exhibit also support the oral evidence made by the DW. 

27. The finding of the trial court is that since there was a contract and MoU and the plaintiff submitted their claims and made several reminder as a results defendants have to settle their claims and have to make payment. But the records suggested that the oral evidence of the plaintiff does not support the documentary evidence produced by the plaintiff. On the other hand defendant case has been proved through the exhibits produced by the defendant as a result we can say mere submitting of claims and issuance of reminder are not enough to settle the claim. The finding of the trial court is thus not correct hence it is necessary to interfere. 

28. From the above circumstances, examining the rules, law and contract. We find that the plaintiff made the claims No.I-V, on 31.01.95. But as per the provision of the contract and MoU these claims ought to have been submitted within 31st January, 95. For the others claim the plaintiff claimed in an enhanced rate without depositing their premium at the enhanced rate. Apart form that they do not comply with the other obligations which are also laid dawn in the contract. 

29. In support of the claims no (i) to (vii), we find that nothing was wrong in not adjusting the claims by the defendant and the submission made by the advocate for the appellants are the valid submissions and we find substance in his submission. It is found that contract No. 0181/90 was in force until 30-06-1994. By the MoU the said contract was extended from 01.11.1994 to 30.06.1995, it needs to mention here that the MoU has been signed only to resolve the previous claim to which premium was paid, wherein a condition was laid down that any remaining claim have to be submitted by the plaintiff corporation within 31.01.1995, otherwise it would not qualify for settlement. It is evident from the record that alleged 5 climes out of 8 the claim of ( i) Atul Tudu, Tk. 58,680/; dated 06.05.95, Exhibit-1(N) ii) Shukra Chandra, Tk.95,130/; dated 06.05.95,Exhibit-1(O) iii) Sultan Ahmed, Tk.89,460/,dated 09.05.95 Exhibit-1(P) iv) Habibullah Kazi, Tk.1,25,820/; dated18.06.95 Exhibit-1(Q) v) Khoka Mia, Tk.17,325/, dated 18.06.95 Exhibit-1(L) respectively, were made after long times from due date, in breach of the contractual time limit set in MoU. The claims no (vi) and (vii) the plaintiff Corporation demanded payment at an enhanced rate but against those they do not deposit their premium in enhanced rate, as a result they cannot claim those at enhanced rate and the defendant has rightly refused to pay the enhance amount. 

30. Regarding the claim (No.viii) we find that the accident has taken place during the contract period and thereafter he took treatment and failed to succeed as a result he suffered a lot and finally he lost one of his legs, which was also held within the time frame of contract and MoU and claims was made within stipulated time mentioned in MoU. So there is nothing wrong to get the benefit of the insurance claim. At the same time the advocate for the appellant also agreed to pay the claim No viii. In such situation, we are of the opinion that Abdul Motaleb is entitled to get his claim. In this connection we further observed that his claim was made within time in the year 1995, but it was refused illegally and thereby he suffered a huge loss. 

31. We further observed that the court has no discretion in the matter awarding compensation. However considering the sufferings of the applicant as well as upon taking the considered view of agreement made by the appellants advocate, we are of the opinion that the interest of justice will be served if the appellants are directed to pay the claim of Abdul Motalib along with interest at the rate of 6% of his claim from the date of institution of the suit till date. 

32. On an overall consideration of the entire matter, we find that the trial court committed illegality in decreeing the suit in full. We find substance in the appeal. In the result, the appeal is allowed in part with the observation and direction made herein above. 

33. In the result, the appeal is allowed in part. The impugned judgment and decree dated 31.01.2006 (decree drawn on 06-02-06) passed by the Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Money Suit No. 28 of 2003 is hereby set aside in part. 

34. The defendant appellant are directed to pay the claim against claim No. viii of Abdul Motalib in terms of decree along with interest at the rate of 6% of the decretal amount from the date of institution of the suit up to realization of the claim. 

35. Let the lower Court record along with the copy of this Judgment be transmitted down and the order also be communicated to the authority concern at once.

End.

Mr. Md. Ibrahim Molla, Advocate ----- for the petitioners

parties:
Md. Tofazzal Hossain and ors
Vs.
Shamima Aktar and ors
full_judgment:
Khondker Musa Khaled, J:- This Rule, arising out of an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, is directed against the judgment and decree dated 23.9.1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 253 of 1995 setting aside those of the learned Assistant Judge, Dohar, Dhaka, who decreed the Title Suit No. 21 of 1994 (the original number being Title Suit No. 86 of 1992). 

2. The relevant facts necessary for disposal of the rule, are the petitioners-plaintiffs instituted the above noted title suit for declaration of title in 'Ka' schedule land and recovery of Khas possession in the `Kha' schedule land shown in the plaint against the opposite parties-defendants with the contentions that Sheikh Jobbar Ali was owner of 1/2 share in the lands of the suit holding and Abed Ali had a share to the extent of less than 1/12 share in the land measuring .52 acres as recorded in P.S. and S.A. Plot No. 979. He was in exclusive possession in the said Plot by way of amicable partition and the P.S. Khatian No. 138 was recorded accordingly. The previous owner Sheikh Jobbar Ali died leaving two sons in Abdul Sattar, Fazu Mia and two daughters namely Mosammat Amironnessa and Samirunnessa. One son and one daughter of the previous owner namely Abdus Sattar and Amirunnessa sold .22 acres of land out of .52 acres of the suit plot to Chini Mia by a registered kobala dated 26.8.1961. The name of the said purchaser was duly recorded in the S.A. Khatian and R.S. Khatian. Therefore, Chini Mia transferred .473 acres (Ka Schedule) to the plaintiffs by a registered kobala dated 26.6.1979. The plaintiffs started possession through cultivation of vegetable in some portion and also erected a tin shed on some area. On 6.9.1991, all on a sudden, the defendant 2 dispossessed the plaintiffs by force from the `Kha' schedule land measuring `o330 acres out of the "Ka' schedule land and dismantled the dwelling structure of the plaintiffs therefrom. As such, the plaintiffs filed the present suit. 

3. The defendants 1-2 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the entire lands in the suit plot No. 979 belonged to Abed Ali on the basis of amicable partition, who died leaving his wife Fulmati and three sons namely Abdul Hai, Afzal and Taher Ali and also two daughters Suratunnessa and Arafatunessa. The heirs of the previous owner Abed Ali transferred 10 Kathas of land to Ashraf Bepari and Hossain bepari in the year 1987, 3 Kathas of land to Nasima Begum alias Shiuli Begum and 3 kathas of land to Manik Fakir on 22.11.1990. Again they transferred 4 Kathas of land to the predecessor of the defendant No. 1. namely Afsaruddin, Abdul Wahed, Md. Gyashuddin and Md. Abul and handed over possession to the purchasers. Again, they transferred 3 kathas of land to Abdul Aziz Master on 22.4.1991. Subsequently, Afsaruddin and other sold 2½ Kathas of land to the defendant 1 by a registered kobala dated 30.4.1991. Accordingly, the defendant I has been possessing by raising a dwelling but thereon. The plaintiffs have no title to and possession in the suit property to succeed in the suit. 

4. At the trial, the plaintiffs examined 8 witnesses and the defendants adduced 4. Both the parties produced documents in support of their respective claim; and the learned Assistant Judge, considering the evidence on record, decreed the suit with the findings that the plaintiffs-petitioners were in possession of 'Ka' schedule land on the basis of purchase and they were subsequently dispossessed by the defendants from some portion of land shown in the schedule 'Kim'. The defendants (opposite party) filed Title Appeal No. 253/93 against the judgment of the trial court which was ultimately heard by the learned Subordinate Judge and he allowed the appeal on setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court only on the ground that since both the parties are co-sharers in the ejmali suit land, every co-sharers having interest in every inch of the undivided lands, the plaintiffs are not entitled to get a decree of exclusive title and possession in the suit land without partition in respect of the shares of the parties. Being aggrieved by the said judgment of reversal passed by the Appellate Court, the plaintiffs preferred this present revisional application. 

5. Mr. Md. Ibrahim Mollah, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the appellate court did not set aside the judgment of the trial court considering merit of the case on the basis of evidence on record and as such committed error of law in not considering the pleadings and evidences of the respective parties. He submits further that when both the parties pleaded about previous amicable partition and their exclusive possession in the suit plots, the appellate court unnecessarily introduced a new case of having ejmali possession and dismissed the suit with the finding that without partition of the suit land, the plaintiffs are not entitled to establish title and get recovery of possession. It is submitted that the trial court has elaborately discussed the evidence and found the plaintiffs case of acquiring title and facts relating to possession and dispossession true, but the appellate court without taking those findings into consideration, dismissed the suit on the sole ground of non-maintainability on the ground of having ejmali possession in the suit holding, which was not the contention of either party. Moreover, when the plaintiffs purchased the suit land earlier from the admitted co-sharer and got possession in the specific portion of purchased land in the year 1979, the defendants cannot dispossess them in the year 1991 by taking a kobala from the heirs of another co-sharer Abed Ali, who had hardly saleable interest in the lands in view of his earlier transfers to many persons in excess of his shares. When it has been established by the evidence that the plaintiffs dispossessed from the suit land by the defendants in the year 1991, they are legally entitled to get their possession restored and thereafter, the aggrieved party, if necessary, may prefer to file a suit for partition. In support of his contention, he referred to the case decision reported in 12 DLR 708 and 11 DLR (SC) 78. It is submitted further that the appellate Court committed serious error of law resulting- error in arriving at a proper decision due to non-consideration of evidence and non-reversal of findings given by the trial Court and also for bringing a new case of ejmali possession not agitated by any of the parties. 

6. Mr. Md. Emdadul Haque Azad, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties 1 and 2 defendants, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly for that when both parties have been claiming interest from the previous admitted co-sharers of the joma, they are co-sharer of the case holding and the suit of the petitioner-plaintiffs in the present form is not maintainable without effecting partition. According to his contention, the appellate Court has given decision in the right direction in views of legal question and as such, the impugned judgment and decree need not be interfered with. 

7. On hearing submissions made by both the learned Advocates and going through the case records, it appears that both the parties relied upon P.S. Khatian No. 138 (exhibits. 4 and A) in respect of previous ownership of the suit plot No. 979 measuring an area of .52 acres. According to the plaintiffs case, their predecessor-in-interest Sheikh Jobbar Ali was exclusive owner of entire suit plot by amicable partition while the defendants claimed through the predecessor Abed Ali, another P.S. recorded co-sharer who is said to have acquired exclusive ownership in the suit lands by amicable partition Exhibit. 4, P.S. Khatian No. 138 shows that the said holding was comprised of at area of 6.66 acres in as many as 14 plots including the suit plot No. 979, and the predecessor of the plaintiffs Sheikh Jobbar Ali had /8/ annas share and Abed Ali, predecessor-in-interest of the defendants, had 1 anna, 3. gandas, 1 kara, I kranti share in the suit holding along with so many other co-sharers. In the said admitted P.S. Khatian, possession of the co-sharers is found to have been written specifically against each of the plots. It is evident that Sheikh Jobbar Ali had exclusive possession in the entire suit plot bearing No. 979 as per remarks noted in the P.S. Khatian. Similarly, Abed Ali is also found to have possessed some other plots in respect of his small portion of share as recorded in the admitted khatian Plaintiffs vendor Chini Mia purchased.22 acres out of .52 acres of land in the suit plot from the 2 heirs of Sheikh Jobbar Ali by a registered Kobala dated 28.8.1961 which is marked exhibit. Apparently, those vendors had transferable right in the portion of lands out of the suit plot, if the recording of P.S. Khatian is considered to be correct. So, they had sold less than 1/2 portion of the lands contained in the suit plot, on the basis of the purchase by exhibit. 1. It appears that the name of Chini Mia was also recorded in the subsequently prepared S.A. Khatian No. 164 (Exhibit. 2 and Kha). It appears from the S.A. Khatian that though the same lands of 14 plots of the P.S. Khatian No. 138 were recorded in one holding but unlike P.S. Khatian specific share of the co-sharers and their possession in the lands have not been shown. However, the name of the aforesaid purchaser Chini Mia has been duly inserted in the S.A. Khatian on the basis of his purchase deed Exhibit. 1. Presumably, he had possession in .22 acres of land out of suit plot otherwise his name would not have been recorded. He subsequently transferred 13½ chataks equivalent to .0473 acres (Ka Shedule) to the plaintiffs by a registered kobala dated 26.6.1979 (Exhibit. 3). Though the defendants have taken plea that Abed Ali, their predecessor-in-interest, got exclusive ownership and possession in the entire .52 acres of the suit plot by amicable partition, there is no evidence to that effect, rather the P.S. Khatian No. 138 which has been admitted in evidence in the instance of both the parties and on which they have placed reliance, stands in support of the contention of the plaintiffs to the effect that their predecessor Sheikh Jobbar Ali had exclusive ownership and possession in the lands of the disputed suit plot on the basis of amicable arrangement. In addition to the said admitted documentary evidence, the plaintiffs examined 8 P.Ws. including the plaintiff, his vendor Chini Mia and scribe of the kobala. Out of the total P.Ws. examined, P.Ws. 1-7, gave testimony about plaintiffs possession by purchase and subsequent occurrence of dispossession, which were elaborately discussed by the trial court in the right direction. 

8. On the other hand, the defendants submitted only 2 registered kobalas dated 22.11.1990 and 30.4.1991 (Exhibits. Ga and Gha). Heirs of Abed Ali at first transferred 4 kathas of land from the suit plot to Afsaruddin and 3 others by the exhibit. `Ga' on 22.11.1990 and thereafter the defendants 3 and others again sold 2½ Kathas of land out of the said 4 Kathas to the defendant I on 30.4.1991 vide exhibit. Gha. After the said purchase, the dispute appears to have been cropped up in between the parties resulting initiation of criminal and civil litigations.

9. The defendant examined 4 witnesses including the defendant 2 Md. Unus (D.W.1), defendant-3 Afsaruddin (D.W.2) and D.W. 3 Md. Rafique is an attesting witness and friend of defendant-I. The defendant-1. The remaining witness D.W.4 Afsu Mia categorically admitted during cross-examination that the plaintiffs vendor Chini Mia had been in possession of the suit land before 15-20 years by purchasing the same from the heirs of Sheikh Jobbat. Ali and that he used to possess by cultivation. He could not deny that the plaintiffs purchased the suit land from Chini Mia by saying that he did not know if Chini Mia transferred the land to the Plaintiffs. The defendants have no document of possession except the purchase deeds of the year 1990-91. There is no evidence in respect of possession of Abed Ali's heirs from whom the defendants have claimed, to be in successive possession. If the suit was under the ownership and possession of Abed Ali's heirs, it would not have been possible to get possession by Chini Mia on the basis of purchase from the heirs of P.S. recorded tenant Sheikh Jobbar Ali. The defendants could neither submit the transfer deed of M.A. Aziz Master dated 22.4.1990 nor the said purchaser came to depose about his possession by purchase from the heirs of Abed Ali. 

10. In view of the aforesaid evidence on record, the learned Assistant Judge appears to have rightly decided that the plaintiffs acquired title and possession in the suit land by the earlier purchase and that they held possession in the 'Ka' schedule land. But subsequently the defendants dispossessed them in the year 1991 long after execution and registration of the plaintiffs purchase deed. But the learned Subordinate Judge, without considering and controverting those findings of the trial court based on evidence, dismissed the suit by introducing a new ground to the effect that since both the parties were co-sharers in the suit holding, which had not been partitioned by metes and bounds, the plaintiffs cannot get decree for declaration their exclusive title and recovery of Khas possession. Neither of the parties raised the question of undivided share at the time of trial and no pleading to that effect is available. It is true that the S.A. Khatian was recorded in the name of Chini Mia, predecessor of the plaintiffs, along with many others including some of the heirs of Abed Ali and Sk. A. Jobber and the said purchase land of the plaintiffs has not yet been separated by mutating the names of the plaintiffs. But the fact remains that the specific possession of Sheikh Jobbar Ali against the suit Plot in P.S. Khatian has not been challenged by saying that the share and possession of Sheikh Jobbar Ali was wrongly inserted in the said P.S. Khatian (exhibit. Kha), Moreover, the plaintiffs are found to have been in possession since 1979 and the defendants subsequently dispossessed them in 1990-91 by taking kobala from the heirs of Abed Ali, whose title and possession in the lands sold is yet to be established. Because, he had a very small share in the entire suit holding as recorded in the P.S. Khatian. Even, if, it is conceded that Abed Ali's heirs had some interest in the suit plot, the extent of their share is required to be established first and then the new purchasers like the defendants can be allowed to take possession from other co-sharers through the process of law. In this respect, the case decisions reported in 11 D.L.R. (SC). 78 and 12 D.L.R. 708 can be relied upon. It is held in those decisions that the possession of specific portion of lands by the purchaser in joint possession is entitled to get possession thereof till the lands are partitioned. In the present case, if the defendants want to seek relief on the basis of their purchase deeds, they are legally entitled to seek partition to get their share, even if any, through the court. In no way, they can be allowed to take law in their own hands and invade possession of other co-sharers in the lands. 

11. Having due regard to the facts, circumstances and decree have been passed by the appellate court without reversing the findings and decision of the trial court in respect of title, possession and dispossession of the parties, and the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have committed error of law in not considering the evidence and findings and introduced a new ground which was not even an issue in the suit. As such, his decision in dismissing the suit on the aforesaid ground of non-maintainability has become erroneous resulting failure of justice. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and decree are not legally sustainable. 

In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree of the appellate Court are set aside and those of the trial Court restored.

Send down the lower Court records at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J: By filing two separate applications, the defendant No. 2 (Director General of Food, Ministry of Food, Government of Bangladesh) and the defendant No. 5 (the PEC limited, an Indian Government entity) are praying to this Court for vacating the interim Order of Injunction passed by this Court on 28-6-2018, by which the defendant No. 2 has been restrained from making any payment to the defendant No. 3 (the Supreme Container Line, who chartered the Vessel MV RAINBOW FAIRY from the plaintiff of this suit). And, by filing another application the plaintiff is praying for temporary injunction against the defendant No. 2 restraining him to make any further payment to the defendant No. 5.

2. The background facts of filing these applications are that Topcom Holdings Limited, who is the disponent owner of the vessel MV RAINBOW FAIRY, as the plaintiff, filed the instant Admiralty Suit against the defendants for realization of its outstanding freight/hire under the time-charter party dated 18-1-2018 for an amount of USD 274,677.98, equivalent to BDT 2,32,10,289.31. At the time of admission of the suit on 28-6-2018, the plaintiff also filed an application for temporary injunction restraining the defendant No. 2 from making any further payment of the outstanding amount of freight to the defendant No. 3 till disposal of the instant suit. After hearing the aforesaid application, the same was allowed. Now, the defendant Nos. 2 & 5 have come up with their respective applications for vacating the said Order of Injunction and the plaintiff has filed an application for modification of the Order dated 28-6-2018 to the effect that defendant Nos. 2 & 8 shall be restrained from making any payment to the defendant No. 5 (i.e. at the time of admission, Injunction Order was passed against the defendant No. 3, now the plaintiff prays for passing the same Order against the defendant No. 5, instead of the defendant No. 3).

Factual averments made by the respondent Nos. 2 & 5.

3. In the applications filed by the defendant Nos. 2 & 5, it is stated, inter alia, that under the Government to Government (G to G) negotiations, contract No. DGF/PEC-01 dated 25-10-2017 was signed between the DG, Food, Government of Bangladesh (defendant No. 2) and the PEC Limited, an enterprise of the Government of India (defendant No. 5) to purchase 1,00,000 Metric Tons (mt) non-basmati parboiled rice from India; that pursuant thereto, the Letter of Credit (L/C) No. 033017010569 was opened by the defendant No. 2 with Sonali Bank Limited (defendant No. 8) on 1-11-2017 in favour of the defendant No. 5; that Bill of Lading was signed for and on behalf of the vessel MV RAINBOW FAIRY; that the freight has been paid in advance; that as per the contract dated 25-10-2017 signed by the Bangladesh Government and the Indian exporter, the ship (the plaintiff) with the rice arrived at the Chittagong Port on 23-5-2018 and after completing the formalities with the customs and other authorities, offloading of rice started on 2-6-2018 and ended on 21-6-2018 and, thereafter, the vessel sailed out from the Chittagong Port on 25-6-2018.

4. It is further stated that the plaintiff did not submit the original copy of the charter party or any certified copy thereof before this Court, the plaintiff has merely submitted a printed copy of the Form NYPE/93; that through the addendum No. I. the plaintiff seeks to show that there is existence of the charter party dated 18-1-2018, but it relates to a different vessel named MV ORCHID; that for the sake of argument, even if the said charter party is taken to be for the vessel MV RAINBOW FAIRY, the said charter party dated 18-1-2018 provides a "guarantee clause" of the performance of the defendant No. 3 and condition No. 6 of its addendum No. 1 provides that the disponent owner (the plaintiff) does not have any objections if the Supreme Container Line (defendant No. 3) receives freight payment on the basis of services performed.

5. It is further stated that although only 5% of the total L/C money amounting to USD 2,62,762 currently is due to be paid through the L/C opening Bank, but this Court's Order has stopped further exports and imports between the Bangladesh Government and the said Indian Government's enterprise; that the defendant No. 5 is not being allowed to enter into new business/ contract with the Bangladesh Government; that due to the Order of Injunction passed by this Court, the defendant No. 5 is to pay 12% interest as per the Rules framed by the Central Bank of India; that the defendant No. 5 failed to supply 2,00,000 mts of rice to Bangladesh as the Indian Bank did not provide loan facility because of the fact that the previous loan has not yet been adjusted and, consequently, the defendant No. 5 has been bearing interest incurred thereon on top of losing new business; that they have sent e-mail and letter by registered post to the address of the defendant No. 3 with a request to contest this suit so that they may be relieved of the hassle they are facing in dealing with this suit owing to the alleged fault of the defendant No. 3, but till date they have not heard anything from the defendant No. 3.

Factual statements of the plaintiff:

6. In the Written Objection filed by the plaintiff, it is stated that although the Fixture Note dated 18-1-2018 mentions the name of MV ORCHID as the performing vessel, however, the addendum No. 4 dated 19-4-2018 clearly shows that the above-named MV ORCHID was replaced by the plaintiff-vessel MV RAINBOW FAIRY as the performing vessel; that the plaintiff has not been paid off its freight by the defendant No. 3; that the claim of the plaintiff requires to be either admitted or denied by the defendant No. 3 who is yet to appear before this Court.

Submissions advanced and the arguments made by the learned Advocates for the respondent Nos. 2 & 5:

7. Placing the provisions of section 5(1)(a) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 (shortly, the Admiralty Court Act) before this Court and, side by side, taking me through the Fixture Note and the Four Addenda thereto, the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 2, Mr Md Syed Hasan Zubair and the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 5, Mr Ashadullah, at the very outset submit that the factual contentions of these two defendants being the same, their submissions may be recorded as joint submissions. They, thus, jointly submit that in the light of the fact that Fixture Note with the four addenda were executed in India between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 and since the main grievance and allegation is only against the defendant No. 3 and, further, given the fact that the place of business of the defendant No. 3 is in Mumbai, India, the jurisdiction of the suit falls outside Bangladesh territory as per section 5(1)(a) [ktilta0)()] of the Admiralty Court Act. They strenuously submit that the charter party having been executed outside Bangladesh territory between two foreign parties, namely, the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3, and the other defendants of the suit admittedly being not party to the said charter party, they were illegally made defendants to the suit by the plaintiff with a motive to make them scapegoat, so that the defendant Nos. 2 & 5 become compelled to contact the defendant No. 3 towards ensuring the presence of the defendant No. 3 before this Court. They submit that since the defendant No. 5 has paid off the freight in advance to the defendant No. 3, the outstanding 5% L/C money lying with the defendant No. 2 is the payment against the rice purchased by the defendant No. 2 from the defendant No. 5. They argue that had it been the scenario that the defendant No. 5 would pay the freight to the defendant No. 3 out of this 5% outstanding L/C money, the plaintiff would have been justified to seek Order of Restraint upon the outstanding 5% money.

8. They submit that since it is evident that the Form NYPE/93, which has been produced before this Court, was not executed by the aforesaid parties to the contract; it is not a contract at all and, thus, not binding upon the defendants of the suit. They further submit that, even for the sake of argument if the template of the Form NYPE/93 is taken to be a valid one, since the Clause No. 40 of the said prescribed Form NYPE/93 provides for arbitration in case of any dispute arising out of the said contract, the plaintiff is required to approach the arbitration forum and, hence, the present suit is not maintainable. They next submit that the contract was signed between Bangladesh and India for export and import of rice, which is the commercial dealing between Bangladesh and India, and the Order of Injunction in fact restrained the performance of international contractual obligations arising out of international trade. They submit that the Order of Injunction virtually stopped the payment of L/C money relating to international trade and non-payment of L/C money may cause serious repercussions on the international trade of the country inasmuch as payment of the L/C money cannot be stopped by way of injunction as per the provisions of various International Banking and Trading Laws, such as UCP-600, UCC, URC-522 and ISBP (International Standard Banking Practice).

9. They submit that the 'maritime lien' contemplates against ship/vessel; not against the freight or damages and, that is why, 'maritime lien' compels the ship for payment of a claim founded upon the maritime law when a judicial proceeding is taken under the Admiralty Court Act against the vessel. He submits that since the vessel MV RAINBOW FAIRY left the Chittagong Port on 25-6-2018 after discharging the rice as per the Bill of Lading, and since the plaintiff filed the suit for charges and damages asserting the same as the 'maritime lien', institution of the suit for money decree in the name of the Admiralty Suit is a fraud upon the statute, as apparently the present suit is cunningly filed for avoiding Court-fees of a significant amount of money which would have required for institution of a Money Suit.

13. Upon hearing the learned Advocates for both the sides and perusal of the relevant laws, it appears to this Court that since these applications are regarding granting or vacating temporary injunction, it would be useful if it be learnt as to under what legal provisions as well as under what factual circumstances a Court grants temporary injunction and when it may be vacated/varied/ modified.

14. Section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act and Rule 3 of the Admiralty Rules, 1912 (Admiralty Rules) make it mandatory for the litigants to comply with the provisions of the Code of the Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) in drawing up, subscribing and verifying a plaint, and Rule 35 of the Admiralty Rules mandates this Court to resort to the CPC for execution of a decree. The Admiralty Court Act and the Admiralty Rules, however, do not contain any prohibitory provision as to application of the other Rules of the CPC; rather Rules 51 & 60 of the Admiralty Rules herald that the provisions of the CPC shall be applicable where the Admiralty Rules do not contain any Rule to cover the situation and, more so, the last part of Rule 60 of the Admiralty Rules empowers this Court to pass any Order which the Judge may think fit and proper. It leads me to conclude that subject to the provisions of the Admiralty Rules, not only the provisions of the CPC but also any other Rules and Practice are applicable in the Admiralty Court. Since the Admiralty Rules do not contain any Rule to deal with the prayer for Restraint, Status quo, Stay and other necessary interim Order/Direction, obviously the provisions of the CPC should be resorted to adjudicate upon the prayers of the parties to this suit.

15. Having obtained nod as to taking recourse to the provisions of the CPC, now I may look at the relevant provisions of the CPC for dealing with these applications. The relevant provisions are Order XXXIX, rules 1 & 4, which run as follows:

Order XXXIX, rule 1(1) Case in which temporary injunction may be granted. (1) Where in any suit it is proved by affidavit or otherwise—

(a) that any property in dispute in a suit is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated by any party to the suit, or wrongfully sold in execution of a decree, or

(b) that the defendant threatens, or intends, to remove or dispose of his property with a view to defraud his creditors,

the Court may by order grant a temporary injunction to restrain such act, or make such other order for the purpose of staying and preventing the wasting, damaging, alienation, sale, removal or disposition of the property as the Court thinks fit, until the disposal of the suit or until further orders.

Order XXXIX, rule 4 Order for injunction may be discharged, varied or set aside. Any order for an injunction may be discharged, or varied, or set aside by the Court, on an application made thereto by any party dissatisfied with such order.

<u>16. From a plain reading of the provisions of Order XXXIX, rule 1, all that I understand is that after institution of the suit, when it would appear to the Court that if the temporary injunction is not granted, the suit itself may be infructuous or great hardship and prejudice may cause to the party, then, in order to keep the subject matter of the suit intact or for the purpose of preserving the rights of the parties, temporary injunction may be granted for a limited period or till the disposal of the suit. The cardinal principles for granting temporary injunction are that the applicant must satisfy the Court that (i) there is an arguable prima facie case, (ii) balance of inconvenience is in favour of the applicant and (iii) the applicant shall suffer irreparable loss and injury not commensurable in monetary terms unless the other party is restrained.</u>

17. And, from a plain reading of Order XXXIX, rule 4, it appears to me that when any party would successfully register its dissatisfaction with the Court by way of filing an application about the temporary injunction already granted, it is the discretionary power of the Court either to vacate the Injunction Order completely or to modify it.

18. Now, let me see whether there is a prima facie arguable case in favour of the plaintiff for granting temporary injunction restraining the defendant Nos. 2 & 8 from transmitting L/C money to the defendant No. 5 and/or continuing with the Order of Injunction granted earlier on 28-6-2018 or the same is liable to be vacated as per the prayer of these applicants (defendant Nos. 2 & 5). In order to adjudicate upon the issue as to whether there is a prima facie arguable case, I would, at first, go for examination of the following issues; (i) whether the money lying with the defendant Nos. 2 & 8 is payment against L/C, and whether it is for payment of price of the rice purchased from the defendant No. 5 or the said money is for payment of freight to the defendant No. 3 by the defendant No. 5, (ii) whether the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8 have been impleaded as the defendants of the suit lawfully or illegally and (iii) whether the plaintiff is competent to claim lien over the money to be paid by the defendant No. 2 to the defendant No. 5 for purchasing the rice. Further, since it is no more a res Integra that the plaintiff cannot have a prima facie case where the suit ex facie is not maintainable, I should venture scrutiny whether on the face of the plaint and the submitted papers the suit appears to be maintainable or not. For the examination of this aspect, I need to adjudicate upon the following issues; (iv) whether this Court lacks the jurisdiction in the backdrop of incorporation of the arbitration clause in the charter party, (v) whether there is any other efficacious forum available for the plaintiff and (vi) whether the payment of the Letter of Credit can be stopped by an Order of Injunction of the Court.

19. Although the issue Nos. i, ii and iii appear to be interlinked with each other requiring dealing with these three issues together, however, I would be taking them up serially one after another. Admittedly, the money, which is currently lying with the defendant Nos. 2 & 8 is L/C money. Evidently, the disputes have arisen out of the charter party dated 18-1-2018 executed between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 and, as per the claim of the plaintiff; the defendant No. 3 is responsible for making payment for using the vessel for a specified time inscribed in the charter party. It has been contended by the plaintiff that since the plaintiff has not received the hire of the vessel from the defendant No. 3 for the period during which the vessel carried the cargos of the defendant No. 5, the defendant No. 5 should pay the hire to the plaintiff out of the money lying with defendant Nos. 2 & 8, as the same being the freight payment, the plaintiff has got lien over it. The plaintiff has sought to make out a case that the money lying with the defendant Nos. 2 & 8 is not only the payment against the price of the purchased-rice, but it also includes the freight payment. Per contra, it has been contended by the defendant No. 5 that it had hired the vessel from the defendant No. 3 only for a particular voyage to carry the rice from India to Bangladesh, and the defendant No. 3 had agreed to engage with the shipper (Indian company) only on the condition that before sailing out of the Indian Port, the defendant No. 3 must be paid off its freight payment in advance and, accordingly, the defendant No. 5 have paid off the freight in advance. The logic behind advance freight payment by the defendant No. 5 to the defendant No. 3 is that, since by the charter party the plaintiff has given full authority to the defendant No. 3 to receive advance from any sub-charterer, the defendant No. 5 did not see any legal impediment to pay full freight in advance in enjoying the service of the vessel.

20. Following their above contentious arguments on this issue, I examined the relevant papers, namely (i) the template of the charter party, i.e the Form NYPE/93 (as the original or photocopy of the charter party dated 18-1-2018 has not been produced before this Court by the plaintiff), (ii) Fixture Note together with its four addenda and (iii) the Bill of Lading. Since all the above papers have been submitted by the plaintiff before this Court and the defendants are also not raising any question as to the authenticity of these papers, there is no impediment for me to rely on the same to come to a primary conclusion. It transpires that (a) the charter party was sealed between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 and there is no mentioning of the names of the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8 in any connection, not to speak of stating them as the parties to the charter party, (b) by condition No. 6 of the addendum No. 1 of the charter party, the defendant No. 3 has been categorically authorised by the plaintiff to receive freight payment from any person during the tenure of the charter party, (c) Bill of Lading was signed for and on behalf of the plaintiff and it states that the freight was paid in advance and the same was received on behalf of the plaintiff and (d) from the e-mail sent by the defendant No. 3 on 10-5-2018 at 17:31:20+530 to the shipper it is evident that the defendant No. 3 has acknowledged receipt of Indian Rupees 2,31,17,663.

21. Therefore, without prejudicing this Court's final findings of the fact to be arrived at upon taking evidence, I find that the defendant No. 5, following hiring the vessel from the defendant No. 3 for a voyage from Kandla Port of India to Chittagong Port of Bangladesh, has paid off freight payment in advance relying on the condition No. 6 of the first addendum to the Fixture Note to the defendant No. 3. Although it is an admitted position that the DG, Food of Bangladesh Government (defendant No. 2) is purchasing the rice from the Indian Government entity (defendant No. 5) on the basis of Costs, Insurance and Freight (CIF), but since prima facie it appears that the defendant No. 5 has paid off the freight payment in advance as per the terms of the charter party to the defendant No. 3, the primary view of this Court is that the money lying with the defendant Nos. 2 & 8 is the money for payment of price of the rice purchased by the Bangladesh Government from the defendant No. 5, not for making payment to the defendant No. 3.

22. Now, I need to see why the plaintiff has impleaded the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8 as the defendants in this suit, despite the plaintiff's own admission that the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8 are not the parties to the contract (charter party). The apparent reasons behind it, so far surfaced from the above discussions, are that the plaintiff believes and asserts that with this outstanding 5% L/C money, the defendant No. 5 would make the freight payment to the defendant No. 3 and since it is the belief of the plaintiff that as per clause 23 of the charter party, he got lien over the freight payment, this money should be handed over/transferred to the plaintiff by the defendant Nos. 2 & 8, instead of letting the money to be remitted to the defendant No. 3 by the defendant No. 5. In other words, since this money would ultimately go to the Bank account of the defendant No. 3 through defendant Nos. 2, 8 and 5, therefore, instead of handing over this money to the defendant No. 3, it should be transferred to the Bank account of the plaintiff and, as per the plaintiff, that is why the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8 are necessary parties to this suit. Although from the documents submitted before this Court, it primarily appears to this Court that the outstanding 5% L/C money is not going to be used for the purpose of making any payment to the defendant No. 3, however, until the claim of the advance payment of freight is required to be proved through examining the relevant witness in this Court by exhibiting the payment receipts/ documents in presence of defendant No. 5, and since the source of finance of the defendant No.5 is the defendant No.2 through defendant No.8, I hold the view that the presence of these three defendants, namely, 2, 5 & 8 are required in this suit.

23. The above resolution leads me to take up the issue as to whether the plaintiff can claim `lien' or 'maritime lien' over the outstanding 5% L/C money. For this purpose, I need to be acquainted with the statutory and dictionary meaning of the terms 'lien' and 'maritime lien'.

24. Although no Act of Parliament provides the definition of the term 'lien', sections 170, 171 and 221 of the Contract Act, 1872 (the Contract Act) states about 'lien'.

170. Bailee's particular lien—Where the bailee has in accordance with the purpose of the bailment, rendered any service involving the exercise of labour or skill in respect of the goods bailed, he has, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, a right to retain such goods until he receives due remuneration for the services he has rendered in respect of them.

171. General lien of bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys and policy-brokers-Bankers, factors, wharfiners, Advocate of the Supreme Court and policy-brokers may, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, retain, as a security for a general balance of account, any goods bailed to them; but no other persons have a right to retain, as a security for such balance, goods bailed to them, unless there is an express contract to that effect.

221. Agent's lien on principal's property—In the absence of any contract to the contrary, an agent is entitled to retain goods, papers and other property, whether moveable or immovable, of the principal received by him, until the amount due to himself for commission, disbursements and services in respect of the same has been paid or accounted for to him.

25. The above provisions of the Contract Act do not furnish the exact meaning of the word `lien'. However, the provisions suggest that 'lien' is a right of retaining any property, goods and money against the service rendered by any skilled/unskilled professional, or in exchange of or against the sale of any movable/ immovable property. 'Lien' is almost similar to `pledge', which has been defined in section 172 of the Contract Act in the following terms;

172. "Pledge", "pawnor" and "pawnee" defined—The bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called "pledge". The bailor is in this case called the "pawnor". The bailee is called the "pawnee".

26. Section 172 of the Contract Act defines `Pledge' as bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. The civil law recognizes two kinds of pledge, viz the "pignus" (pawn) in which possession of goods is actually delivered to the creditor or pawnee and "hypotheca" (hypothecation) where possession of the goods pledged remained with the debtor with the obligation as per contract.

27. Both in a pledge and in a lien the general property remains with the debtor and the creditor has only a special property. But the nature and extent of this special property in the two cases is quite different. A lien gives only a personal right to retain possession. The creditor holding this security cannot transfer it to any other person, nor can he himself enforce it by sale of his own motion, without the aid of judicial proceedings. A creditor holding a pledge may, on the other hand, transfer his interest to another, and he may himself enforce his security by sale without the aid of a Court.

28. The Black's Law Dictionary provides the definition of the word "Lien' in the following expressions: Lien: A legal right or interest that a creditor has in another's property, lasting until a debt or duty that it secures is satisfied. Typically, the creditor does not take possession of the property on which the lien has been obtained.

<u>29. Thus, from the statute and the dictionary, all that I understand about 'lien' is that a lien is the right to retain property belonging to a debtor until he has discharged a debt due to the retainer of the property. So, in 'lien', (i) there must be a debtor and a creditor (ii) there must be a property, goods, money belonging to the debtor and (iii) the creditor has directly or indirectly control or possession over the property, goods, money. This is known as 'common law lien'.</u>

30. In this suit, admittedly, the plaintiff is the creditor and the defendant No. 3 is his debtor; none of the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8 is the debtor to the plaintiff, nor the property, goods, money of the plaintiff's debtor (defendant No. 3) is in possession of the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8. Therefore, there is no scope for the plaintiff to claim Lien over this 5% L/C money. Had any property/goods/money of the charterer (defendant No. 3) been in the control/ possession of the defendant No. 5, the plaintiff could have claimed a 'common law lien' over the same.

31. When a 'common law lien' is created in connection with the dealings of a vessel, it may give rise to a `maritime claim'. The list of the `maritime claim' has been provided in clauses (a) to (r) of section 3(2) of the Admiralty Court Act, which is quoted below:

(a) any claim to the possession or ownership of a ship or to the ownership of any share thereof or for recovery of documents of title and ownership of a ship, including registration certificate, log book and such certificates as may be necessary for the operation or navigation of the ship;

(b) any question arising between the co-owners of a ship as to possession, employment or income of that ship;

(c) any claim in respect of a mortgage of or charge on a ship as to share therein;

(d) any claim for damage done by a ship;

(e) any claim for damages by a damaged ship;

(f) any claim for loss of life or personal injury sustained in consequence of any defect in a ship or in her apparel or equipment, or of the wrongful act, neglect or default of the owners, charterers or persons in possession or control of a ship or of the master or crew thereof or of any other person for whose wrongful acts, neglects or defaults the owners, charterers or persons in possession in the navigation or management of the ship, in the loading carriage or discharge of goods on, in or from the ship or in the embarkation or disembarkation of persons on, in or from the ship;

(g) any claim for loss of or damage to goods carried in a ship;

(h) any claim arising out of any agreement relating to the carriage of goods in a ship or to the use or hire of a ship;

(i) any claim in the nature of salvage of life from a ship or cargo or any property on board a ship or the ship itself or its apparel, whether services were rendered on the high sea or within territorial waters or inland waters or in a port, (including any claim arising by virtue of the application by or under section 12 of the Civil Aviation Ordinance, 1960, of the law relating to salvage to aircraft and their apparel and cargo);

(j) any claim as to towage in respect of a ship or an aircraft;

(k) any claim as to pilotage in respect of a ship or an aircraft;

(I) any claim in respect of goods or materials supplied to a ship for her operation or maintenance;

(m) any claim in respect of construction, repair or equipment of a ship or dock charges or dues.

(n) any claim for wages by a master or member of the crew of a ship or any claim for any money or property under the provisions of the Merchant Shipping Ordinance, 1983, hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance, or which is recoverable as wages in the Court of law;

(o) any claim by a master, shipper, charterer or agent in respect of disbursements made on account of or for the purpose of a ship;

(p) any claim arising out of an act which is or is claimed to be a general average act;

(q) any claim arising out of bottomry or respondentia;

(r) any claim for forfeiture or condemnation of a ship or of goods which are being or have been carried, or have been attempted to be carried, or for the restoration of a ship or any such goods after seizure, or for droits of Admiralty including any other power to grant reliefs as are provided under the provisions of the mentioned Ordinance or any other jurisdiction which was vested in the High Court Division as a Court of Admiralty immediately before commencement of this Act and any other jurisdiction as to any matter in connection with ships or aircraft which has by custom been exercised by the High Court Division as a Court of Admiralty.

32. Apparently, the plaintiff's grievance attracts clause (h) of section 3(2) of the Admiralty Court Act inasmuch as the plaintiff has instituted this suit for recovery of his hire from the charterer (defendant No. 3) and, thus, prima facie there is an existence of 'maritime claim' against the charterer (defendant No. 3).

<u>33. Since the plaintiff has sought to claim `maritime lien' over the defendant's money, it is incumbent upon me to see whether the above `maritime claim' can be termed as the 'maritime lien'. For the purpose of examining this issue, I need to be familiar with the meaning of the terminology 'maritime lien'. Black's Law Dictionary defines the expression 'maritime lien' in the following language;</u>

<u>Maritime Lien: (1831) A lien on a vessel, given to secure the claim of a creditor who provided maritime services to the vessel or who suffered an injury from the vessel's use.—Also termed tacit hypothecation.</u>

34. Griffith Price, in his book The Law of Maritime Liens 1 (1940) describes about the terminology 'maritime lien' in the following manner;

"The maritime lien has been described as one of the most striking peculiarities of Admiralty law, constituting a charge upon ships of a nature unknown alike to common law and equity. It arises by operation of law and exists as a claim upon the property, secret and invisible. A maritime lien may be defined as: (1) a privileged claim, (2) upon maritime property, (3) for service done to it or injury caused by it, (4) accruing from the moment when the claim attaches, (5) travelling with the property unconditionally, (6) enforced by means of an action in rem."

35. The international convention for the unification of certain Rules relating to the maritime liens and mortgages in 1967 held at Brussels, "having recognized the desirability of determining by agreement certain Rules relating to maritime liens and mortgages agreed as follows":

Article 4.-1. The following claims shall be secured by maritime liens on the vessel:

(i) wages and other sums due to the master, officers and other members of the vessel's complement in respect of their employment on the vessel;

(ii) port, canal and other, water way dues and pilotage dues;

(iii) claims against the owner in respect of loss of life or personal injury occurring, whether on land or on water, in direct connection with the operation of the vessel;

(iv) claims against the owner, based on tort and not capable of being based on contract, in respect of loss of or damage to property occurring, whether on land or on water, in direct connection with the operation of the vessel;

(v) claims for salvage, wreck removal and contribution in general average. The word "owner" mentioned in this paragraph shall be deemed to include the demise or other charterer, manager or operator of the vessel.

<u>36. From the provisions of section 3(2) of the Admiralty Court Act and from the definition of the 'maritime lien' as cited hereinabove, it is crystal clear that the terms "maritime lien" and `maritime claim' have been given two distinctive meanings. While all of the claims catalogued in section 3(2) of our Admiralty Court Act can be easily termed as 'maritime claims', but only few of them are recognized as 'maritime liens' as per the national laws and the international laws of today. It is the established principle across the maritime world that the parties to the charter party cannot by agreement confer status of 'maritime lien' which is by nature a mere 'maritime claim'. That is to say, although all 'maritime liens' are `maritime claims', but all 'maritime claims' are not 'maritime liens'. 'Maritime lien' is an important aspect of maritime law with the liability of contract that falls on ship and ships' equipment. In other words, it is a privileged claim upon a ship for service rendered to, or injuries caused by the ship.</u>

37. Apparently, in this suit there is a `maritime claim' against the defendant No. 3 and, after completion of trial it would be clear as to whether there is any 'maritime claim' against the defendant No. 5. But in no way is there any `maritime lien' against any of them. In view of my above prima facie finding that as of now apparently there is no 'maritime claim' against the defendant No. 5, hence there cannot be any question of 'maritime lien' against the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8.

38. I am, therefore, constrained to arrive at the conclusion that there is no prima facie case in favour of the plaintiff so far as against the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8.

39. Two cases have been referred to by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff in support of his prayer for granting/continuing with Order of temporary injunction. In the case of Care Shipping corporation vs Latin American Shipping Corporation, reported in (1983) 1 All ER 1121, the issue was whether the owner of the vessel can claim lien over the cargos and freight payment for recovery of his hire due to the sub-charterer and it was held that the lien on sub-freights conferred by clause 18 included a lien on any remuneration earned by the charterers from their employment of the vessel whether by way of voyage freight or time chartered hire. This cited case was purely with regard to retaining hire and freight; it was not a L/C money. So, the ratio laid down in this cited case is not applicable in this suit. In the case of Mareva Compania Naviera SA vs International Bulk Carriers SA, reported in (1975) Vo1.2 Lloyds Rep. 509, CA, the owner obtained an Order of injunction on the charterer's money, which the charterer had received as hire from his sub-charterer. The money was lying in the charterer's Bank account. More importantly, it was not the charterer's money against the sale of goods, as is the case in the present suit. Therefore, the facts of the cited case being different from the facts of the present case, I do not find the ratio of this cited case to be persuasive.

40. In view of this Court's conclusion that there is no prima facie case in favour of the plaintiff against the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8, there is no need to examine the maintainability of this suit against the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8. Nonetheless, in order to more effectively dispose of these applications, I intend to examine the issue Nos. iv, v & vi. I would take up the issue Nos. iv & v at first and, thereafter, the issue No. vi would be taken up for the reason to be noticed hereinafter. In order to deal with the issue Nos. iv & v this Court should be acquainted with the relevant provisions of the Admiralty Court Act by which the jurisdiction of the admiralty matters has been vested in this Court. The relevant provision is section 3 of the Admiralty Court Act, which is quoted below:

3. Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court Division:

(1) The High Court Division shall be a Court of Admiralty.

(2) The Admiralty Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine any of the following questions or claims, namely;

(a)
