41. From a plain reading of the above laws, it is my understanding that section 3(2)(h) [ধারা-৩(২)(জ) of the Admiralty Court Act provides that any person is competent to invoke the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court with a prayer for adjudication upon any question or claim which are enumerated in sub-sections 2(a) to 2(r) of section 3 [৩ ধারার উপ-ধারা-২(ক) থেকে ২(দ) পর্যান্ত] of the Admiralty Court Act, and section 3(5)(a) [ধারা-৩(৫)(ক)] of the Admiralty Court Act provides that all the provisions of section 3 of the Admiralty Court Act shall be applicable irrespective of the facts that whether the vessel is a local or foreign one, whether it is registered or unregistered and whether the usual abode or permanent address is in Bangladesh or outside.

42. With the above conclusion, a pertinent question crops up as to whether the provision of arbitration clause contained in the charter party has any overriding power over the admiralty jurisdiction. In order to find the answer, I had to go through the relevant provisions of the Arbitration Act, 2001 (the Arbitration Act) and from a concurrent reading of the provisions of sections 3 & 7 of the Arbitration Act, it appears that the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court on a dispute, which is required to be resolved through arbitration to be held in Bangladesh, has been made subservient to the provisions of the Arbitration Act; meaning that if any of the provisions of the Arbitration Act allows the Courts to entertain legal proceedings for adjudication upon a particular issue, only for that purpose the Courts are competent to hear and determine the said legal proceedings. Although the provisions of section 3 of the Arbitration Act stipulates that the provisions of the Act would be applicable only for those arbitration agreement which contain that the place of arbitration is Bangladesh, but there being no ouster clause as to application of the Arbitration Act for foreign arbitration, our Courts sometimes in a fit case entertain legal proceedings only in aid of the foreign arbitration tribunal. It means that if our Court is satisfied that by entertaining a legal proceeding, the Court is not going to be trying any dispute which is pending before the foreign tribunal; rather the Court's interference is needed for the time being to help the said tribunal, our Courts, in that scenario, finds it appropriate to entertain a legal proceeding. In this suit, the charter party stipulates that the seat of the arbitration would be either in New York in USA or London in UK and, that is why, the provisions of the Arbitration Act are apparently not applicable in this suit and, therefore, there is no legal bar for this Court to try this suit. However, had any of the defendants already been in the arbitration forum, in that scenario, upon an application by any party to the legal proceedings in this Admiralty Court, the Court might have halted the proceedings pending before it till disposal of the arbitration. Given the present scenario of the suit that none of the parties have approached the arbitration tribunal, this Court appears to be well competent to entertain and dispose of this suit.

43. In other words, since the Arbitration Act of Bangladesh does not prohibit trying this suit, and in view of the averments made by the plaintiff that the defendant No. 3, upon taking hire of the ship from the plaintiff, sent the vessel into Bangladeshi territory for delivery of the cargos on board the vessel, which is primarily supported by the documents submitted by the plaintiff, I find that the plaintiff has been able to make out a prima facie case of 'maritime claim' against the defendant No. 3 and, accordingly, I hold that this Court has the jurisdiction as per the provisions of section 3(2)(h) and 3(5)(a) of the Admiralty Court Act to hear and determine the claim. However, in the event of decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff, whether the plaintiff would be able to execute the decree in Bangladesh in the context of presently having no property attached herein this country- is altogether a different issue. It may be that upon obtaining a decree, the plaintiff may wait to attach any money of the defendant No.3 to be available in future in Bangladesh through any transaction by the defendant No.3 with any person/ company/Bank, or the plaintiff may try to execute the decree in a foreign country with whom Bangladesh has reciprocal arrangement for execution of decree.

44. Apparently, the better forum for the plaintiff is to approach the arbitration tribunal in New York or London inasmuch as the award of the aforesaid forum is executable in most of the countries of the world, including India, the country of the defendant No. 3. Also, the plaintiff could have invoked the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court in India in order to comfortably execute the decree, if it is passed in its favour.

45. Now, I would take up the issue No. vi, namely whether the payment of Letter of Credit can be stopped by an Order of injunction by the Court. A Letter of Credit is an irrevocable guarantee given by the issuing Bank (L/C opening Bank) to the negotiating Bank to the effect that upon receipt of the clean shipping documents from the side of the negotiating Bank, the specified amount of money as contained in the L/C shall be remitted without being influenced by any objection raised by any party, except the objection of fraud if it is alleged to have been committed by the seller with regard to the documents sent by him through the negotiating Bank. It is the globally-honoured practice that payment of the L/C money shall not be stopped by the issuing Bank except finding fraud with the documents inasmuch as it has serious implications in international trade. If the buyer has any objection with regard to the quality of goods or timeous performance, it should be dealt with as per the prevailing law of the country, but the buyer or his Bank (issuing Bank) must not retain the L/C money for the purpose of settling down the contractual issues between the buyer and the seller. Therefore, while it is the settled principle of law that a buyer or his Bank is not competent to withhold the payment of L/C, stopping the payment of L/C at the instance of a third party would be outright illegal. In this suit, there is no allegation of fraud against the seller (the defendant No. 5) in sending the clean shipping documents to the buyer (the defendant No. 2) and, therefore, the defendant Nos. 2 & 8 are legally bound to remit the L/C money to the defendant No. 5. In fact, in this suit there being no objection from the side of the buyer with regard to the goods, the buyer (defendant No. 2) and its Bank (the defendant No. 8) wish to send money to the seller (the defendant No. 5) at the earliest possible time. Therefore, the plaintiff; being not any party to the L/C or to the underlying contract to the L/C, is not competent to seek injunction upon the payment of L/C money.

46. It means that the plaintiff's suit against the defendant Nos. 2, 5 & 8 is though maintainable, temporary injunction cannot be granted upon the defendant Nos. 2 & 8 restraining them from transmitting the L/C money to the defendant No. 5. And, if the temporary injunction has already been granted, the same should be vacated.

47. Moreover, if the injunction is granted/ continued, the inconvenience which would be caused to the defendant No. 5 is greater than that of the plaintiff in that while the plaintiff would have the option to recover the money from the defendant No. 3 by execution of the decree, if any, at a favorable time or the plaintiff would be able to obtain an award from the arbitration tribunal, the defendant No. 5 would be suffering serious hardship by not being allowed by the Banks of Bangladesh and India to enter into new business. Also, if injunction is granted/ continued, the loss that is going to be suffered by the defendant No. 5 is apparently grave having enormous impact in his business given that he would be a Bank-defaulter, not only to the Banks of his country, but also to the foreign Banks. Since there is no prima facie case in favour of the plaintiff and the balance of inconvenience is also not in favour of the plaintiff and, further, there would be irreparable loss and injury to the defendant No.5, if injunction is granted/continued and, more importantly, the subject matter of injunction being the L/C money in which the plaintiff does not have any apparent ownership, this Court is not inclined to grant temporary injunction or to continue/extend the interim injunction already granted. However, it is a well-settled principle that granting or vacating the temporary injunction is a discretionary power of any Court, and a discretionary power is required to be exercised only in favour of those litigants who come before the Courts with clean hands. I would now briefly check whether these defendants, particularly the defendant No. 5, have approached this Court with clean hands.

48. From the Order Sheets of this suit, it transpires that the defendant No. 5 entered its appearance in this suit on 17-1-2019 only when this Court on 14-8-2018 had directed the defendant No. 2 to communicate with the defendant No. 3 through e-mail asking him to appear before this Court. It appears to this Court to be a bit mysterious that after sending an e-mail to respondent No. 3 on 30-9-2018, although the recipient of the e-mail (defendant No.3) did not appear before this Court but the defendant No.5 appeared in this suit on 17-1-2019. The aforesaid event leads this Court to believe, albeit superficially at this juncture, that the defendant No. 3 is in touch with the defendant No. 5.

49. In the light of the fact that as per the G to G contract, still a huge quantity of rice is yet to be exported by the defendant No. 5 to the Government of Bangladesh. Thus, law and equity demand that Order of temporary injunction may be vacated with the conditions that in course of trial of this suit if it is revealed that the defendant No. 3 has any financial transaction with the defendant No. 5 or the defendant No. 3 is in touch with the defendant No. 5 in any connection, the defendant Nos. 1, 2, 5 & 8 shall be duty bound to bring the fact to the notice of this Court or to the knowledge of the plaintiff, so that an appropriate Order may be passed in time. Further, the defendant No.5 must submit some sort of security, which may be a Bank Guarantee to this Court or a bond to the defendant No. 2 or to the defendant No. 8 so that after trial of the suit, if it is surfaced that there was connivance of defendant No. 5 with defendant No. 3, the Bank Guarantee/bond may be used towards partial execution of the decree. However, the moment the defendant No. 3 would appear in this suit, all these three defendants shall be relieved of the above conditions. In view of this Court's exercise of its discretionary power in favour of the defendant No. 5, it is expected that the defendant No. 5 shall show its bonafides in assisting this Court in effectively disposing of this suit either by depositing the above security or by producing the defendant No. 3 before this Court so that the conduct of the defendant No.5 of this suit does not appear to be dubious.

50. With the above findings of facts, examination of the laws and the conclusions arrived at on the issues framed by this Court, the applications filed by the defendant Nos. 2 & 5 for vacating the Order of interim injunction passed on 28-6-2018 by this Court are declared to have succeeded, subject to compliance of the following conditions;

(i) There shall be a standing direction (continuing mandamus) upon the defendant No. 5 that henceforth if the defendant No. 5 at any point in time receives any money from the defendant No. 3 in any connection, he must retain the same in his custody and inform this Court immediately.

(ii) The defendant Nos. 2 & 8 are directed to withhold payment of money if they ever receive any money from/for the defendant No. 3 and notify this Court immediately without fail.

(iii) The defendant No. 5 shall either furnish a Bank Guarantee of the equivalent amount of the money (i.e. the amount of money which is going to be released now) to this Court or in the alternative, the defendant No. 5 shall execute a bond in favour of the defendant No. 2 confirming that in course of completing the exportation of the rest of the quantity of rice to the defendant No. 2, the latter shall be competent to retain the equivalent amount of money at any point of time to satisfy any Order or decree passed by this Court.

(iv) The learned Advocate for the defendant No. 5 is directed to remain present in this Court without fail whenever this suit would appear in the 'Cause List' so that the suit may be expeditiously disposed of.

(v) The learned Advocate shall ensure the presence of any relevant witness of the defendant No. 5, if this Court intends to take his/her deposition as a Court Witness (C/W). In the event of failure to comply with this condition by the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 5, he shall be liable to furnish a written explanation before this Court.

51. In the result, the applications filed by the defendant Nos. 2 & 5 are allowed and the Order of interim injunction passed by this Court on 28-6-2018 restraining the defendant No. 2 from making any payment to the defendant No. 3 is vacated. Further, the application filed by the plaintiff praying for restraining the defendant Nos. 2 & 8 from making further payment to the defendant No. 5 is rejected.

52. If the defendant No. 5 wishes to file any Written Statement in this suit, he is directed to file it within 7 (seven) days from the date of receipt of this Judgment and Order.

53. The suit is fixed for framing issues on 22-5-2019. Let the matter appear in the list under the heading for 'Framing Issue' on 22-5-2019.

54. Before parting with this Judgment and Order, I find it pertinent to remind the learned members of the Bar that they, being the integral part of the Judiciary, should be more interested to dispose of the substantive matters pending before the Courts than showing their eagerness in obtaining the interim relief. Particularly, when any Court suggests that the substantive matter shall be heard on fast-track basis, the concerned Advocates should understand that while on the one side, the parties of the suit/case would get the aspired remedy, which would obviously include the interim relief, on the other, the Court would be able to reduce the number of backlog of cases. The learned Advocates should take into consideration the valuable time of the Courts that requires for adjudication upon the interim/ interlocutory matters. Instead of compelling the Courts to spend time in dealing with interlocutory matters, if the learned Advocates extend their co-operation to dispose of the substantive matter, the Judiciary will be able, to some extent, to cope with the prevailing backlog.

55. In this suit, after hearing the learned Advocate for the defendant No.5 on his application for vacating the Order of injunction, this Court had suggested that the suit shall be heard on priority basis by fixing the next date for framing issues. It was observed by this Court that if it surfaces upon examining the oral and documentary evidence that the suit is not maintainable against the defendant No. 5, then the suit would be proceeded only against the defendant No. 3. Had the learned Advocate conceded to the above suggestion of this Court, the defendant No.5 could have been permanently relieved of the hassle he is facing and on the other hand, this Court could have disposed of a substantive matter with the amount of time that required for disposing of these interim applications. Now, by getting the aspired relief in these applications, although the defendant No.5's L/C money would be released subject to depositing the equivalent amount of security, he remains entangled with the suit.

End.

full_judgment:
JBM Hassan J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the continuation of Artha Execution Case No. 18 of 2011 before the Artha Rin Adalat, 2nd Court, Dhaka on the basis of application of the respondent No.2 (Bank) being revived by order No. 8 dated 8-1-2014 which was concluded by a Solenama vide order No.7 dated 19-10-2011 (Annexure-D to the writ petition) should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect, and/or pass such other or further order of orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Relevant facts leading to issuance of the Rule Nisi are that the respondent No.2, Bank Asia Limited (the Bank) obtained a money decree amounting to Taka 1,10,50,363.01 by judgment and decree dated 19-4-2009 (decree signed on 23-4-2009). In pursuance of the said decree, the Bank filed 1st execution case No. 4 of 2010 on 3-1-2010 before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka (the Adalat) claiming decretal amount of Taka 1,27,23,940.65. In the said execution proceeding both the judgment debtor (borrower) and the decree-holder (the Bank) came to a settlement by Solenama, and accordingly the execution case was disposed of on 20-1-2010. Since the judgment debtor-petitioner failed to adjust his liability as per the terms and conditions of the Solenama, the decree holder Bank filed 2nd execution case on 20-1-2011 being Artha Execution Case No. 18 of 2011. During pendency of the 2nd execution prodeeding, the judgment debtor-petitioner and the decree-holder Bank again, executed a Solenama on 18-10-2011 and accordingly filed an application on 19-10-2011 for disposing of the execution case in terms of the Solenama. After hearing and examining the witnesses, the Adalat by order dated 19-10-2011 disposed of the execution case in terms of the Solenama and treated the Solenama as part of the order. Ultimately, the payment having not been made in terms of the Solenama, the Bank filed an application on 1-12-2013 for continuation of the execution case and the Adalat by order dated 8-1-2014 directed to put up the records on the next day. Subsequently, the Adalat allowed the application by order dated 27-5-2014 and thereby restarted the execution case and proceeded for selling the mortgaged property through auction. Thereafter, the property was put on auction and by order dated 11-3-2015 the highest offer of the auction bidder, namely, Sumon Ahmed was accepted by the Adalat. At this stage, the petitioner filed this writ petition challenging the revival of the execution case and continuation of same and obtained the present Rule Nisi.

3. The decree-holder Bank appearing in the Rule has filed an affidavit in opposition controverting the statements as made in the writ petition. Contentions of this respondent, inter alia, are that in condition No. 7(i) of the Solenama, it was stipulated that in case of failure to pay the installments, the decree holder bank would be entitled to file an application for continuation of proceedings of the Artha Rin Execution Case No. 18 of 2011. Accordingly, when the judgment debtor failed to adjust his liability as per terms of the Solenama, the decree holder Bank filed an application on 1-12-2013 for restarting the execution case and the Adalat allowed the prayer by its order dated 27-5-2014. By filing the Solenama the judgment debtor have accepted all the terms and conditions of the Solenama and therefore, he cannot take the plea that the application for restarting the execution case is illegal since he is the party in default.

4. Mr Md Asiful Huq, the learned Advocate with Mr Bhabesh Chandra Ghosh, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that by disposing of the execution case finally on the basis of a Solenama, the Adalat became functus-officio and so it has no authority to reopen the said execution proceeding. Therefore, the subsequent orders passed after disposing of the execution case, were nullity in the eye of law. He further submits that the decree holder Bank, had all the remedies by filing 3rd execution case for recovery of the decretal dues, but without doing so it filed the misconceived application and the Adalat by the impugned order allowed the same which warrants interference by this Court.

5. In reply, Mr Sikder Mahmudur Razi, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 2 (Bank) contends that the execution case was disposed of in terms of the Solenama treating the Solenama as part of the order. Clauses (f) and (i) of the said Solenama clearly provide that on failure to make the payment by the judgment-debtor (borrower), the execution will continue and therefore, there was no illegality in continuing the execution case by the Adalat. He further submits that according to Solenama the mode of payment was by 62 equal monthly installments, and thereby the payment period was for five years two months but the petitioner after paying 24 installments in two years, stopped the payment fraudulently in order to put the Bank in a limitation bar for filing the next execution case, and the Adalat on consideration of all aspects allowed the application and restarted execution proceeding. In support of submission, Mr Sikder refers to the case of Jahangir Kabir Chowdhury vs Bangladesh Government, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of law Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, reported in 22 BLC (AD) 139. He also contends that in disposing of the execution case on the basis of Solenama, the Adalat used the word “নিষ্পত্তি” instead of using the words “চূড়ান্ত নিষ্পত্তি” as provided in section 38 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (the Act, 2003) and so the execution case was not disposed of finally.

6. We have gone through the writ petition, the affidavit in opposition filed by the respondent-Bank and other materials on record.

7. It appears that the suit was decreed on contest for Taka 1,10,50,363.01. Subsequently, the Bank filed execution case No. 4 of 2010 on 3-1-2010. During pendency of the execution proceeding, the parties came to the settlement by a Solenama, and disposed of the said execution case No.04 of 2010 in accordance with the Solenama. But the terms for mode of payment having not been provided the Solenama could not be executed and so, the Bank again filed 2nd execution case on 20-1-2011 being No. 18 of 2011. During pendency of the said execution proceeding the Bank and the petitioner again executed a Solenama on 18-10-2011 pursuant to which the Adalat passed order on 19-10-2011 disposing of the execution case, in terms of Solenama treating the Solenama as part of order. In the said Solenama the parties incorporated the terms and conditions for making the payment within 62 equal monthly installments. After paying 24 monthly installments, the petitioner failed to continue payment and in the circumstances, the Bank filed an application on 1-12-2013 for continuing the execution case in terms of Solenama. The Adalat by order dated 27-5-2014 allowed the application and thereby restarted the execution case. Subsequently, the Adalat proceeded for disposing of the mortgaged property by auction and by order dated 11-3-2015 the highest bid was accepted.

8. At this juncture, question arises as to whether the Adalat can reopen the execution case after being disposed of by the order dated 19-10-2011. Therefore, to get the answer let us first see the Solenama dated 18-10-2011 relevant portions of which, in particular, clauses (f), (h) and (i) are as follows:

"(f) That after execution of the deed of compromise the decree-holder and judgment-debtors through their learned lawyers will also file a joint application before the learned court for stay or suspend the Artha Rin Execution Case No. 18 of 2011 for the period of repayment.

(h) All other terms and conditions of the earlier Deed of Compromise dated 20-1-2010 and Bank's Approval Letter No. BA-MCB-DII/CR-SGL/2009/ 5028 dated 27-12-2009 will remain unchanged and effective.

(i) That in case of failure to pay the installments as described in the earlier Deed of Compromise dated 20-1-2010 the Decree-Holder Bank will be entitled to file an application for initiating the proceedings of the Artha Rin Execution Case No. 18 of 2011 and the execution proceeding will be continued; that in case of any question of limitation if arises by the Second Party Judgment-Debtors will be deemed to be waived by the Second Party Judgment-Debtors."

9. Embodying the aforesaid Solenama dated 18-10-2011 both the parties filed a joint application before the Adalat and pursuant to same, the Adalat passed the order dated 19-10-2011 by which the execution case alleged to have been disposed of. Operating portions of the said order are as follows:

“শুনিলাম। উভয়পক্ষের যৌথভাবে দাখিলী সোলেনামার দরখাস্ত, পি,ডব্লিউ-১ মোঃ আব্দুল্লাহ আল মামুন ও ডি/ডব্লিউ=১ রেজওয়ান আহমেদ এর জবানবন্দি ও নথি পর্যালোচনা করলাম। পর্যালোচনায় সোলেনামার শর্তাবলী গ্রহণ যোগ্য এবং মোকদ্দমাটি সোলে সূত্রে নিস্পত্তি যোগ্য।

অতএব

আদেশ হইল যে,

অত্র ডিক্রীজারী মোকদ্দমাটি ১-২ ও ৩-৬ দায়িকের বিরুদ্ধে সোলেমূত্রে ও অন্যান্য দায়িকের বিরুদ্ধে একতরফা সূত্রে নিষ্পত্তি করা হলো। সোলেনামা আদেশের একাংশ বলিয়া গণ্য করা হলো।”

10. On a plain reading of the order dated 19-10-2011 and the relevant clauses of the Solenama, it appears that the very order of the Adalat was passed on the basis of Solenama and the said Solenama is also a part of the order. Therefore, although the word “নিস্পত্তি” has been used in the order dated 19-10-2011, but if we read the clause (i) of the Solenama and the order i.e “সোলেনামা আদেশের একাংশ বলিয়া গণ্য করা হলো” it is clear that the execution case No. 18 of 2011 would be continued on failure to pay the installment.

11. Furthermore, in section 38 of the Act, 2003, the words “চূড়ান্ত নিষ্পত্তি” have been used for finally disposing of the execution case on compromise, but here the word “নিষ্পত্তি” did not mean closure of the matter finally inasmuch as it referees to the contents of the Solenama which expressly provides for restarting the execution case on failure to follow the settlement terms. So much so, the word “নিষ্পত্তি” is subject to Solenama and so the case being reopened as per terms of the Solenama, there was no illegality in reopening the execution case. Moreover, the Solenama itself has provided time for making the payment by 62 months and so, unless the payment is paid completely within the time given in the Solenama the disposal order subject to Solenama, shall not get effect.

<u>12. We also find that section 28 of the Act, 2003 provides time frame for filing next execution case within one year from the date of disposal of earlier execution case. Knowing fully about said provision the petitioner took time of 62 months for making payment by equal monthly installments, but subsequently after expiry of one year i.e making some installments, he stopped the payment and thereby the Bank was not in a position to file next (3rd) execution case within the given time frame of one year as per section 28 of the Act, 2003. Thus, it is apparent that the petitioner entered into the Solenama with the Bank promising to pay within five years, two months (62 installments) and accordingly filed joint application before the Court to dispose of the execution case on the basis of said Solenama and on the other hand, after passing of one year (limitation period) he stopped the payment and thereby, practicing fraud the petitioner could able to create situation in disposing of the execution proceeding. In such circumstances, even after closing of execution case the Court is always open and empowered to exercise the authority under section 57 of the Act, 2003 to reopen the execution case. This view of ours finds support in the case of Jahangir Kabir Chowdhury vs Bangladesh Government represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, reported in 22 BLC (AD) 139 relevant portions of which run follows:</u>

<u>"There is no doubt that this power can be exercised sparingly it is a power to promote justice and prevent abuse of the process of the court, but if the Adalat finds that by practicing fraud or by false representation, a party has obtained a judgment or order, the Adalat can always interfere, and even the argument of functus officio cannot stand on its way to pass such orders which may advance justice to a party. Abdul Aziz vs Abani Mohan, 30 DLR (AD) 221, Bangladesh vs Khair Bhuiyan, 55 DLR (AD) 76. A court can set aside an execution case if it is found that a party by practicing fraud obtained an amendment of a decree to get over the bar of limitation and got possession. [M Majid vs Iqbal Bahar, 2000 BLD 285, affirmed in 5 BLC (AD) 7]"</u>

13. In view of above ratio, we are unable to accept the submission of Mr Asiful Huq that after disposing of the execution case the Adalat became functus officio.

<u>14. Although, in accepting Solenama the Adalat used the word “নিষ্পত্তি” subject to Solenama, but since the dispute between the parties was settled by the Solenama, and the terms for making the payment was about more than five years, the Adalat could pass the order adjourning execution case in terms of the Solenama instead of using the word “নিষ্পত্তি” which would be more applicable in order to avoid further dispute as arises in this case. However, by using the words “সোলেসূত্রে নিষ্পত্তি করা হলো” the Adalat is empowered to reopen the case inasmuch as basic order is on the basis of Solenama which provides for continuation of the execution proceeding on failure to make the payment and admittedly the petitioner has failed to pay as per the Solenama. Considering this aspect, for argument sake, if the use of word “নিষ্পত্তি” is considered as an error of the Court, it can be corrected in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 57 of the Act, 2003. This view of ours finds support in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs MA Khair Bhuiyan, reported in 55 DLR (AD) 76 relevant portions which run as follows:</u>

<u>"In the case of M Mazid vs Iqbal Bahar Chowdhury, reported in 5 BLC (AD) 7 the question arose as to whether the judgment-debtor-respondents could seek the remedy by 'ding an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, wherein he challenged the execution proceeding itself as illegal and without jurisdiction and prayed for restoration of possession as an ancillary relief after setting aside the entire execution proceeding. This Court held, inter alia, that "It is found that the modified decree was passed on 22-3-1960, and to avoid the question of limitation a modified decree was again drawn up by the trial Court on 9-8-1993 and what is so obvious that it was obtained from the Court by fraudulent means. Even if it is admitted that a mistake was committed by the executing Court itself even then there are innumerable authorities of this Court to hold that any error or wrong committed by the court itself can be corrected in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to secure the ends of justice and/or to prevent the abuse of process of Court."</u>

15. However, in order to avoid further dispute/confusion in disposing of the execution case on the basis of Solenama providing a time frame for making payment, the Adalat shall adjourn the proceeding in accordance with the Solenama instead of using the word “নিষ্পত্তি”.

16. In view of the above; we do not find any illegality in the impugned order, in particular, to restart the execution case and hence the Rule finds no merit.

17. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Communicate a copy of this judgment and order to the respondents at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Farah Mahbub J : In this Rule Nisi, issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the respondents have been called upon to show cause as to why Memo No. Reg/Academic-2/2014/ 18279-C dated 15-10-2014 (Annexure-A) passed by the respondent No. 1, refusing the respective students to re-appear in the Dhaka University Admission Tests for the second time, should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority, in violation of the principles of natural justice and in gross violation of the fundamental rights as guaranteed in the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and also as to why the respondents should not be directed to publish a new order cancelling earlier order and allowing the admission seekers a second chance to appear in the Honours Entry Level Admission Test in all Units of the University of Dhaka within a stipulated period of time. 2. Facts, in brief, are that all the petitioners are the respective parents of the admission seekers in the University of Dhaka (in short, the University) who had appeared in the Dhaka University Admission Tests for the first time in the year 2014 after passing the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) Examination in the same year. 3. It has been contended, inter-alia, that as per the rules and regulations of the respective academic institutions most of the public universities of the country follow a uniform system and curriculum concerning the entry level admission test for 1st year Honours Course. According to the general practice, however, any student who has passed his/her HSC Examination and has the required marks is eligible to sit and appear for the entry level examination tests for more than one occasion. In other words, those who have passed the HSC Examination either in the current academic session or the proceeding academic session used to get two chances to appear in the admission tests (Honours level) for entering the public universities. (Annexures-B, B-1, B-2, B-3 and B-4 respectively). 4. It has been stated that in the "Daily Prothom Alo" a report was published on 17-10-2014 informing, inter-alia, that around 3,01,138 students/applicants took part in the admission tests at different Units of the University of Dhaka at the Honours entry level in the academic session 2014-2015. The applicants who had passed their HSC Examination in the year 2013 and had appeared in the admission test of the said University in 2013-2014 academic session but failed to secure their admission were allowed to re-appear in the admission test for the second time in 2014. Ultimately, 45,053 candidates were selected in the academic session of 2014-2015, i.e. more than 47.71% students got chance in their second attempt in the Honours entry level admission test. Thus, it is apparent that a large number of students came out successful in the admission test of the said University having been allowed to re-appear for the second time in the Honours entry level admission test (Annexure-C). 5. In this regard it has also been contended that the "Daily New Age" on 16-10-2014 and 17-10-2014 respectively published articles regarding the statistical position of the students seeking admission in the public universities stating, inter alia, that in 2013-2014 academic session, out of 1,92,220 students 89,800 students were the applicants from 2012-2013 academic session who appeared in the admission tests of Dhaka University, and ultimately 3,680 (53.5%) students out of 6,890 students secured their admission in the said University. In 2012-2013 academic session, out of 2,35,700 students 96,750 students were the applicants from 2011-2012 academic session and out of 6,620 students 3,280 (49.5%) came out successful who were allowed to re-appear for the second time in the Dhaka University admission tests(Annexure-D and D-1 respectively). 6. Accordingly, it has been stated that in compliance with the prevalent rules and regulations regarding the admission procedure at the 1st year Honours entry level admission test being adopted by the public universities, most of the students who were unsuccessful in getting opportunity to secure their admission in the first attempt, were provided with opportunity for the second time to get admission in the respective public universities. In this connection, it has further been contended that Dhaka University authority vide its General Admission Notice dated 13-8-2014 invited applications from the aspirant applicants who passed HSC Examination either in the year 2013 or 2014 to sit for the 1st year Honours entry level admission test for 2014-2015 academic session. According to the said admission notice dated 13-8-2014 the applicants who had passed HSC Examination in 2013 and appeared in the admission test during the 2013-2014 academic session but became unsuccessful were also allowed to sit for the admission test for 2014-2015 academic session as a second attempt along with the students who had passed their HSC Examination in 2014. 7. However, the sons and daughters ("the admission seekers") of the petitioners after successfully passing their HSC examination in 2014 started to prepare themselves for the upcoming 1st year Honours entry level admission tests of Dhaka University (Annexure-E). To their utter shock and dismay, the respondent Nos. 1-3 in their meeting dated 15-10-2014 passed an order deciding not to allow any student to re-appear in the Dhaka University entry level admission tests (Annexure-A) who had passed HSC Examination prior to 2015-2016 academic session. Subsequent to the publication of the impugned order, the petitioners along with the admission seekers made representation to the respondents concern to re-consider their decision providing them an opportunity to re-appear in the admission test and to withdraw the impugned order dated 14-10--2014 issued by the University authority, but with no result (Annexure-G). Hence, the application. 8. Respondent Nos. 1-5 entered appearance by filing affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia, that University of Dhaka (in short, the University) is an autonomous body which reserves the right to make necessary rules and regulations to ensure quality education regarding the admission test of the students in the 1st year Honours course academic session 2014-2015. It has further been stated that 2(two) meetings were held on 13-10-2014 and 14-10-2014 respectively by the Deans' Committee and the General Admission Committee both chaired by the Vice Chancellor of the University. However, after elaborate discussion decision was taken, amongst others, that the students who appeared in the 2014-2015 academic session would not be allowed to re-appear in the University admission test for the second time i.e, in the 2015-2016 academic session. Such decision was taken following due process of law and in no way it violates the fundamental principles as embodied in the Constitution. Also, it has been stated that different universities follow different rules and procedure for the students who intend to have higher education. Each public universities are regulated by their own independent academic rules and there is no requirement in law to follow an uniform process in the academic affairs. However, the admission procedure of the University of Dhaka is not similar with other public universities and under no circumstances it can be termed as violation of the provisions of the Constitution, as alleged by the petitioners. 9. Mr Subrata Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the respondents concern did not provide any prior information with regard to refusal to re-appear in the Dhaka University admission tests for the second time and whimsically have issued the impugned order in an arbitrary mariner and, as such, the same is liable to be knocked down being violative of the principles of natural justice. He further submits that the respondents have failed to apply the test of reasonableness in not considering the fact that due to inadequate number of seats in the public universities it is not possible to get admission in a public university at the same academic session for huge number of admission seekers. He also submits that the respondents have issued the impugned order in gross violation of the State's obligation to ensure a uniform and universal system of education to meet the basic needs of the society and equal opportunity for education as per the fundamental principles of the state policy as guaranteed under Articles 15, 17 and 19 of the Constitution. He lastly submits that the arbitrary and discriminatory actions of the respondents in not allowing the admission seekers to re-appear in the upcoming admission test is in gross violation of the equitable principle of promissory estoppel that arose out of the long practice and procedure and their failure to provide any reasonable explanation for such prohibition of the age long system and departing from their own promise is unlawful inasmuch as it purports to malafide exercise of administrative power without any lawful explanation and, as such, the impugned order is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 10. Mr AFM Mesbahuddin, the learned Senior Advocate along with Ms Shimonti Ahmed, the learned Advocate on behalf of respondent Nos.1-5 submits that in Bangladesh primary education is free and compulsory and higher education depends on the competency of the students and, as such, there is no scope of violation of the principles of the state policy as enunciated in Articles 15, 17 and 19 of the Constitution. He further submits that the question of legitimate expectation only arises when the incumbent petitioner has legal right, in the instant case admittedly the petitioners have no legal right and, as such, question of legitimate expectation does not arise. He also submits that there are in total 35 public universities in the country and under those universities a large number of colleges are being in operation where both Honours and Pass Course system is prevailing. As such, Dhaka University cannot be termed as the last resort of higher education. He further goes to submit that the number of admission seekers at the entry level of the university is increasing day by day whereas the budget structure and other facilities allotted for the students remain almost the same; in this context allowing the students of 2(two) sessions in the admission test involves serious financial constrain for the University authorities. 11. He also goes to contend that by refraining the students from taking part in the admission test for second time would virtually put an end to the unequal competition in the admission test. In this regard, he goes to argue that from the statistics of 2010-2011 to 2014-2015, it appears that in the year 2010-2011 the number of applicant became double during the last 5(five) years and that those who were unsuccessful in the first attempt have appeared in the admission test examination for the second time getting one year additional time for preparation. Thus, curtail equal opportunity to the applicants who appeared for the first time. He further submits that it is a common practice amongst the students to re-appear in the 2nd time admission test to have a subject of his/her choice even though that student is already admitted in another subject in the same University. Consequently, when the existing student of Dhaka University wants to re-appear in the admission test for the 2nd time as per the earlier practice of the University after taking long one year preparation and gets admission in the subject of his/her own choice then his/her existing seat in the University against which he/she took admission in the proceeding year is blocked for 4 (four) years. Such practice is not only a loss for the University but for the whole nation. Keeping in view of the said aspects, he submits, the University authority is constrained to take the impugned decision, which cannot be knocked down in the given facts and circumstances. Lastly, he submits that the University authority is at liberty to put any reasonable restriction in case of admission test to be determined by the Academic Council of the University; as such, the alleged question of infringement of fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution does not arise at all. Accordingly, he submits that this Rule being devoid of any substance is liable to be discharged. 12. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney-General appearing for the respondent government adopts the submissions so have been advanced on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1-5 and submits that the impugned decision being based on policy decision of the University and having been taken by the respondents concern for betterment of education as well as to equalise the platform of competition amongst the respective students this Hon'ble Court should be reluctant to interfere in the matter in question. 13. University of Dhaka (in short, the University) is an autonomous body being governed by the Dhaka University Order, 1973, i.e., Presidents Order No.11 of 1973. The University authority is constituted with the Chancellor, the Vice Chancellor, members of the Senate, the Syndicate and the Academic Council [vide Article 3(1). However, Article 4 clause (n) provides power to the University, inter-alia, to do all such other acts and things, whether incidental to the powers as quoted in clauses (a)-(m) or not, as may be required in order to further the objects of the University as an affiliating, teaching and examining body. 14. The Academic Council, one of the authorities of the University [Article 19 clause (c)], is the academic body which has the control and general supervision over, and is responsible for maintenance of the standards of institution, education and examination within the University and exercise such other powers and perform such other duties as may be conferred upon it by the Statutes. It also has the right to advise the Syndicate, another authority of the University, on all academic matters (Article 25). University Ordinance, as provided under Article 40 clause (k), however, deals with the matters relating to the conduct of examination. 15. The main contention of the petitioners in support of the Rule Nisi is that as per the respective rules and regulations of the University of Dhaka including other public universities any student who has passed his/her HSC Examination and has the required marks is eligible to sit and appear for the entry level examination test for the second time. Further, it has been contended that even when the admission notice was published on behalf of the University on 13-8-2014 for admission in the academic session 2014-2015 the students who had passed HSC Examination in 2013 and could not secure admission in the academic session 2013-2014 were allowed to apply again and sit for the admission test of 2014-2015 academic session of the University along with the students who passed HSC Examination in 2014. However, in the meeting of the Deans Committee dated 13-10-2014 and the General Admission Committee dated 14-10-2014 chaired by the Vice Chancellor of the University the impugned decision has been taken disallowing the students to appear in the admission test of 2015-2016 academic session who earlier appeared for admission in the 1st year Honours course academic session 2014-2015. The said impugned decision of the University authority is violative of the principles of natural justice for having been taken without giving prior information and has also infringes their legitimate expectation to re-appear in the admission test for the second time as part of the long standing practice of the University, as alleged by the petitioners. 16. It is admitted that prior to academic session 2015-2016 as a general practice the University of Dhaka allowed the students having passed SSC and HSC Examinations with required grades to appear for admission in the 1st year Honours Course for more than one occasion. However, the said practice is not the product of the Ordinance or Regulations of the University, rather the same is the outcome of the administrative policy decision of the University authority; as such, question of legitimate expectation does not arise on the plea of long standing practice being not rooted in any statute. 17. The cardinal issue which drove the University to change its policy decision was that every year the number of applicants were increasing against limited number of seats; moreover, because of having the opportunity to re-appear in the admission test for the next academic session the students who had already been admitted in some other subjects in the earlier academic session had been re-appearing in the admission test for the next academic session upon getting one year additional time for preparation. Consequently, when they could get admission in the subject of their own choice the seat against which they got admitted earlier remained unnecessarily vacant for the next 4 (four) years. 18. A statistics to that effect conducted by the Dhaka University for the last 5(five) years (Annexure-X to the affidavit in opposition) is given below:

19. In addition, the earlier practice created unequal competition in the admission test amongst the applicants who were previously unsuccessful in getting admission in the University but was getting one year more time for preparation; whereas the new applicants who appeared for admission test immediate after passing the HSC Examination was getting comparatively less time to prepare themselves for the admission test. Such unequal competition has been put at hault vide the impugned decision dated 15-10-2014 (Annexure-A). 20. It is the established principles of law that the authority concern is entitled to make pragmatic adjustments and policy decision which may become necessary or called for under the prevalent circumstances. This Court cannot strike down a policy decision of the University merely because the petitioners feel that the earlier practice was proper. 21. Since the impugned decision of the University is not actuated with any malice and is not the outcome of an arbitrary act, rather in the given context taking such decision by the University is found justifiable; as such, question of offending the fundamental rights of the petitioners as guaranteed under the Constitution does not arise at all. Further, the earlier practice was creating scope of unequal competition treatment amongst the respective students and was leaving a large number of seats being blocked for the next 4 (four) years. Hence giving prior information to those applicants, who have already appeared for the entry level admission tests of 2014-2015 academic session, before the taking impugned decision is not at all required. Thus, the allegation of violation of the principles of natural justice is not attracted in the present facts and circumstances. 22. However, before we part it will not be out of place to observe that since the students, who have given '0' Level and 'A' Level Examination and obtained required grades, are permitted to sit for the admission tests for entry in the 1st year Honours Course in the University as such, the authority concern of the University may give active consideration to include English version of the question papers as well for convenience of those students. 23. Be that as it may, we find no substance for interference in the matter in question under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 24. In the result, this Rule is discharged. There will be no order as to costs. End.

full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J: The Rule issued calling upon the opposite parties No.01-145 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 24.04.2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Tangail in Other Class Appeal No.229 of 2000 reversing the judgment and decree dated 27.06.2000 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kalihati, Tangail in Other Class Suit No.26 of 1999 should not be set aside and/or such other order or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts giving rise to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present opposite parties No.01-145 as plaintiffs instituted the original Other Class Suit No.26 of 1999 in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kalihati, Tangail for declaration of their easement right to the suit pond described in the schedule of the plaint contending inter alia that the suit pond appertaining to settlement khatian No.39 comprising an area of 1.07 acres of land in plot No.181 under Mouza Nigoir of Kalihati police station of District-Tangail originally belonged to landlord Sreenath Bhattacharjee. One Biswanath Bhattacharjee under the landlord Sreenath Bhattacharjee being an authorized person prepared the suit pond useable for the inhabitants of the locality and thereafter surrendered in favour of the villagers of the concerned village which is commonly known as 'Bara Pukur'. The inhabitants of the locality since the regime of Ex-landlord, using the suit pond Tara Pukur' for their necessity and subsequently for the interest of the villagers, they prepared a Mosjid and Madrasha namely "Forkania Ebtedaye Madrasha" in the bank of the pond for their own use and accordingly the villagers use to possess the water of the pond and also using the holy Mosjid and Madrasha. The further case of the plaintiff No.01, Md. Tomijuddin and 149 persons, who on behalf of all the villagers of the concerned locality instituted the suit in representative character under the provisions laid down in Order I, rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that the predecessor of the present petitioners namely Abdul Rashid Miah out of ill-motive to grab the suit pond managed to create a false pattannama which is a: forged and anti-dated paper and in collusion with the concerned officials the predecessor of the present petitioners managed to create a collusive R.S. khatian being No.44 in his name. it is also the case of the plaintiffs that, despite; the predecessor of the defendants created the false papers showing his tenancy right, he never possessed the suit pond and after his demise the legal heirs of Abdul Rashid, who are the present defendant-petitioners also do not possess the suit pond. The matter of preparation of R.S. record in the name of Abdur Rashid was suppressed by the defendants all along and for the first time in the 1st part of Chaitra, 1405 B.S. they disclosing about the R.S. record in the name of their predecessor declared that they will possess the suit pond and on hearing that, the people of the locality being aggrieved instituted the original suit.

3. The contrary case of the defendant-petitioners in short is thus that Abdur Rashid, the predecessor of the present defendant-petitioners obtained the suit property by way of a pattan from the ex-Zamindar Biswanath Bhattacharjee in the year 1345 B.S. and after taking pattan, Abdur Rashid paid rents and obtained `Dakhilas'. Subsequently, during S.A. operation the property has been correctly recorded in the name of Abdur Rashid in Khatian No.44. The further case of the defendants is such that Abdur Rashid while owning and possessing the suit property, by a registered Heba dated 08.12.1990 gifted the suit property in favour of the defendant No.4, who is the contesting defendant to the original suit. Possession was delivered in favour of the defendant No.4 and the defendant after re-excavating the suit pond within the knowledge of all, using the property-in- dispute peacefully, but the plaintiffs out of ill-motive to grab the property on false allegations filed the suit which is vexatious and false.

4. The learned trial court during trial of the original suit after taking evidence from the sides of the respective parties, by its judgment and decree dated 27.06.2000 dismissed the suit on contest.

5. Being aggrieved the plaintiffs preferred an appeal being Other Appeal No.229 of 2000 in the Court of learned District Judge, Tangail, which was transmitted to the 1st Court of learned Joint District Judge, Tangail for hearing and disposal and the learned Appellate Court on hearing the appeal, allowed the same and reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 24.04.2003. The learned appellate court by the said judgment and order also decreed the suit on contest in favour of the plaintiffs, declaring their easement right to the suit pond.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree, the defendant-petitioners have preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule with an order of status quo.

7. During hearing of the Rule, Mr. Kamal Hossain, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioners while Mr. Md. Mizanur Rahman, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

8. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that, the learned Appellate Court during disposal of the appeal committed illegality and irregularity and without complying with the provisions laid down in Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure passed the impugned judgment and decree. The learned Advocate further submits that, the impugned judgment and decree is not a proper judgment of reversal inasmuch as the learned court of appeal below erred in law without adverting evidence and giving reasonings in support of its findings and decision. The learned Advocate also submits that in a suit for easement right the plaintiffs will have to file the suit against the servient owner, but in the instant case the plaintiffs did not institute the suit against the servient owner and as such, it is barred by law. The learned Advocate argued that, it has been contended by the plaintiffs in their plaint that the defendants threatened their possession, but without filing a suit for injunction, they have erroneously filed the suit for declaration of easement right and the learned trial court rightly dismissed the suit on contest. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the appellate court below without reversing the findings of the trial court adverting evidence on records illegally reversed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Kalihati, Tangail and as such the impugned judgment and decree deserve interference of this Court.

9. As against the aforesaid submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule controverted the argument advanced from the side of the petitioners and submits that the learned Appellate Court during disposal of the appeal committed no illegality, infirmity or irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned court of appeal below at the time of deciding the merit of the appeal, properly complied with the provisions laid down in Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and on due assessment of evidence in its true perspective arrived at a conclusive decision that the suit is maintainable as framed and the plaintiffs as representatives of the inhabitants of the localities concern, successfully discharged their onus of proof by adducing sufficient credible, tangible evidence. The learned Advocate submits that in fact, the plaintiffs instituted the original suit for easement right lawfully against the servient owners of the suit pond, inasmuch as; the legal heirs of the Ex-Chairman of the concerned Union Parishad, Abdur Rashid on the basis of their fictitious claim denied the easement right of the villagers to the suit pond, and since the S.A. record of right has been prepared in the name of Abdur Rashid, the original suit has been instituted against the legal heirs of Abdur Rashid Miah, and from the very facts of the suit it is clear that the defendants are the servient owners of the suit pond in absence of Abdur Rashid and the original owner Ex-Zamindar. Therefore, there exist no legal embargo in filing the suit for easement right as instituted. The learned Advocate also submits that the witnesses adduced from the side of the defendants, in their testimonies disproved their own case of acquisition of title and possession in the suit pond on the basis of pattan from Ex-Zamindar and on the contrary, they have proved the case of the plaintiffs in their testimonies and the matter has been properly addressed by the learned appellate court in the impugned judgment and decree. The learned Advocate lastly submits that, admittedly the defendants are the legal heirs of Abdur Rashid Mia, who is the S.A. recorded tenant and the S.A. khatian No.45 stands recorded in the name of Abdur Rasid Mia. From the testimony of the plaintiff's witnesses and from the pleading's case of the plaintiffs it is apparent that neither Abdur Rashid during his life time, nor after his death the heirs of Abdur Rashid ever tried to dispossess the plaintiffs and as such under section 33 and 35 of the Easement Act, there lies no scope to file any suit for injunction and as because the plaintiff's right to easement right has been denied from the side of the defendants, the plaintiffs lawfully instituted the original suit under the above provisions of law. In the concluding submission, the learned Advocate argued that in the impugned judgment and decree there is no misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with.

10. In order to appreciate the argument advanced from the sides of the learned counsels for the respective parties, having gone through the pleadings of the parties, the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court dated 27.06.2000 in Other Class Suit No.26 of 1999, the impugned judgment and decree dated 24.04.2003 passed by the learned appellate court, the evidence led from the sides of the respective parties along with the case records, it transpires that admittedly the suit property appertaining to Mouza Negoir under Kalihati police station of District-Tangail is a big pond which is commonly known as Tara Pukur', and that has been recorded in settlement khatian No.39 in the name of landlord Sreenath Bhattacharjee. Under the landlord the authorized person of the suit pond was one Biswanath Bhattacharjee, son of Loknath Bhattacharjee. It is the specific contention of the plaintiffs, who are the representatives of four neighboring villages namely `Negoir', `Manduria', `Vukta' and `Akua' that they have instituted the original suit for a declaration of their easement right after compliance of the provisions laid down in Order I rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure and on perusal of the original case record it is evident that the mandatory requirement of law with regard to publication of notice has been complied with by the plaintiffs. It has been asserted by the plaintiffs in their pleadings that the authorized person of the suit pond under the Zamindar Sreenath Bhattacharjee surrendered possession of the suit pond in favour of the villagers of village Negoir, Monduria, Vukta and Akua, which are adjacent to one another, to meet up their basic need of water. The suit pond under admitted settlement plot No.181 consists an area of 1.07 acres and it is the case of the plaintiffs that the villagers of the concerned locality from the regime of Ex. Zaminders, using the water of the suit pond and for their basic necessity they have erected a Mosque and a Madrasha in the bank of the pond Tara Pukur'. The holy mosque and the madrasha namely Torkania Ebtedaye Madras ha' are being managed by selling the fishes of the suit pond Tara pukur'. It is also the case of the plaintiffs in their pleadings that, beside the Madrasha there exist a graveyard of the villagers and the predecessor of the present defendant-petitioners Abdur Rashid Mia collusively to grab the suit pond in the name of pattan, created a forged pattannama and subsequently he also managed the settlement officials and during S.A. operation he has prepared the S.A. record in his name illegally using his power of Union Parishad Chairman showing his right, title, interest in the suit pond.

11. Vis-a-vis, I have come across from the pleadings of the defendant-petitioners and the written statement filed by the contesting defendant No.4, who claimed the suit pond in his name by a deed of gift in the year 1990 that the suit pond has been initially pattan settled and has become cultivable in which the defendants have got their right, title, interest and possession.

12. To substantiate the respective cases of the parties, the parties to the suit have adduced evidence and from the side of the plaintiffs they have examined as many as 08(eight) witnesses and on the other hand, the defendants have examined 05(five) witnesses. They also submitted some documentary evidence marked as Exhibit-`Ka', `Kha' series, `Ga' and their basic document pattannama in the name of Abdur Rashid Mia has been marked as Exhibit-`Gha'. The Hebanama deed dated 08.12.1990 in the name of defendant No.04 executed by Abdur Rashid is Exhibit-`Ga'. Exhibit-`Ka' is the relevant S.A. khatian of which stands recorded in the name of defendant-petitioner's predecessor, Abdur Rashid Mia. The other papers Exhibit-`Kha' series are the government rent receipts by which the defendants paid rents by virtue of their predecessor's record of right.

13. P.W.1 Md. Azim Uddin is the plaintiff No.1 to the suit. This witness in his testimony corroborated their plaint case and denied the case of the defendant-petitioners. In the examination-in-chief with regard to their cause of action to institute the suit, the plaintiff No.1 categorically testified that the record was not known to the villagers and for the first time in the 1st part of last `Chaitra', they came to know about the record of right and at that time the sons of Abdur Rashid disclosed before them that they have obtained pattan and the record lies in their names. They also told them (plaintiffs), not to catch fish, and hearing this, the villagers called a meeting and it was decided in the meeting that for establishment of the easement right of villagers, they will file a suit and in the resolution of that meeting, 300 people put their signatures. In a reply to a question from the side of the defendants, the plaintiff No.1 also testified that they had no talk with Rashid Mia and knowing about record in the name of Abdur Rashid, they requested the heirs of Abdur Rashid, not to claim the suit pond since it is being used by the people of the locality at large from the regime of landlord.

14. P.W.2 Abdur Rashid is a villager of village "Akua". This witness specifically testified in his testimony that he along with other villagers of the locality are using the suit pond from the very beginning. They also catching fish, and in using the pond water and catching fishes, nobody gave any resistance to them including the defendants. During cross-examination P.W.2 testified at a stage that, Abdur Rashid was a Union Parishad Chairman of the locality and in the bank of the suit pond to the northern side the mosque is situated.

15. P.W.3 Asgor Ali is a man of village Nigoir. This witness in his deposition corroborated the witness No.2 and in the cross-examination in a reply to a question from the side of the defendants, P.W.3 'testified that he has a Dingi boat' and that boat is under the water of this suit pond.

16. P.W.4 Rowshan Ali is another possession witness of the plaintiffs, who is an inhabitant of village `Akua'. This witness corroborated the other possession witnesses of the plaintiffs and categorically testified in his testimony that during the life time of Abdur Rashid Chairman, he did not raise any objection or obstruction in the possession of the plaintiffs in Tara Pukur'. P.W.4 also testified that from the time of his forefathers he and all the villagers are possessing the suit pond and they are also using the water of the pond in their household works. During cross-examination in a reply to a question, P.W.4 specifically testified at a stage that in the village `Vukta' there is no pond and the water of the suit pond is being used by the villagers of that village `Vukta'.

17. P.W.5 Md. Hazrat Ali in his deposition testified that he is a man of village `Nigoir West Para'. This witness is a man of 70/75 years of age and he has testified before the court that the suit pond is being possessed by the people of the locality at large from the very beginning and neither Abdur Rashid nor his sons possess the same.

18. P.W.6 Md. Mohor Ali Member, is the plaintiff No. 02, who is an elected Union Parishad Member of No.7 Sodebpur Union. This witness corroborated the plaint case in his examination-in-chief in toto and during cross-examination this witness categorically testified that the villagers jointly in the month of Chaitra of the year 1305 B.S. authorized them the authority to file the original suit in a meeting and in that meeting, there were 600/700 people.

19. P.W.7 Md. Zamir Uddin is the defendant No.21. This witness in his deposition testified that he knows the suit pond which is known as Tara Pukur' and this pond is being possessed by the people of the locality for the last 100 years and the heirs of Abdur Rashid Chairman do not possess the suit pond. This witness further testified that he has compromised with the plaintiffs and filer' a solenama. During cross-examination, P.W. denied that the plaintiffs have no title and possession in the suit pond and the defendants do possess the same.

20. The last witness of the plaintiffs, P.W. 8 Hasu Mia is the man of village `Negoir'. This witness testified in his testimony that the suit pond is known to him, which is being used by the people of the locality for the last 100 years and the heirs of Rashid Mia do not possess the suit pond. This witness also testified that, he himself also possess the suit pond and offer his prayer in the mosque situated in the bank of the suit pond.

21. On the contrary, the defendant's witness D.W.1 Golam Mostafa @ Tula Munshi, who is the defendant No.4 testified that the suit property was the 'Mash' land under Elenga Zamindar and previously it was a pond and subsequently it has been pattan settled and has become a cultivable land and his father Abdur Rashid in the year 1345 B.S. took pattan of the said land from the Zamindar and did Toro' cultivation there. D.W.1 further testified that his father Abdur Rashid in the year 1990 made a registered Heba deed in his (D.W.1) favour and after getting the land, this witness re-excavated the pond in the suit land and using the same. During cross-examination the defendant No.4 testified at a stage that he does not know as to whether the S.A. khatian was prepared by the concerned officials, sitting in their (defendants) homestead. With regard to pattan of his father in a reply to a question, D.W.1 testified that he cannot understand the writings of pattan, but in the pattan there is a recital 'Pukur' and in plot No.181 the area of land is 1.07 acres and the pattannama was not written in front of him (D.W. 1) and he does not know as to whether any registered ‘kabuliyate' is required for getting pattan, but he knows that for getting pattan, rent is to be paid at the time of granting pattan. During cross-examination D.W.1 further testified at a stage in a reply to a question from the side of the plaintiffs that, in the suit pond there are fishes. This witness (defendant No. 4) admitted in his cross-examination that in the bank of the suit pond there is a 'Mosque' and a `Madrasha'. This witness in his cross-examination categorically testified that the mosque is running at the expenditure of local people and he cannot say, who is the Secretary of that Mosque.

22. D.W.2 Md. Khorshed Alam in his deposition testified that, the suit pond is situated beside his homestead and the suit pond is being possessed by the defendants, not the people of the locality at large. In the cross-examination D.W.2 replied in a question from the side of the plaintiffs that the defendant No.4 happens to be his paternal brother and the defendants are the sons of Rashid Chairman. D.W.2 also testified in his cross-examination that the suit pond is possessed by them. He has admitted in his testimony that in the settlement record the suit property has been recorded as Tara Pukur'.

23. D.W.3 Sajahan in his testimony testified that, he knows the parties and the suit land and the suit pond was possessed by Rashid Chairman and at present the defendants are possessing the same and this is their personal pond. During cross-examination D.W.3 Sajahan expressed his inability to state the number of defendants. This witness admitted that he did not get any notice from the court to give evidence, and the defendant No.4 called him to depose. He cannot say the date on which Rashid Chairman went into possession of the suit pond. This witness in his testimony testified in a funny way that the suit pond is used as “হাল চাষ” and in the said pond at present (quote): “মানুষ পরিমাণ পানি আছে। চৈত্র মাসে এক কোমড় পানি ছিল। সত্য নয় তার মধ্যে নৌকা ডোবায়। মাছ ছেড়েছে। জনসাধারণ ঐ মাছ ধরে নিয়ে যায়।”

24. D.W.4 Abdul Gafur is a pattani witness of the defendants. This witness in his testimony testified that one Brojobashi Dey Sarker wrote the pattannama and he knows his handwriting, and Biswanath Bhattacharjee after putting his signature allowed it. In the cross-examination D.W.4 Abdur Gafur expressed his inability to state as to whether the pattannama was in printed form. This witness admitted in his testimony that the pattannama was not read over to him and he cannot say, what was the rent amount, which was fixed in that pattannama.

25. The last witness of the defendants, D.W.5 Thandu Khan in his testimony testified that he knows Rashid Chairman and Rashid Chairman told him to give some fish in the suit pond. This witness also testified in his examination-in-chief that, prior to liberation of Bangladesh he took fifty percent of fish. In the cross-examination this witness in a reply to a question states that he cannot recollect the month and year in which he was called by Rashid Chairman to give fish in the pond. This witness further testified in his testimony that after liberation no fish was taken by them from the suit pond. He has admitted that Golam Mostafa called him to depose before the Court.

<u>26. Scanning the documentary evidences as well as testimonies of the witnesses on records meticulously, it is obvious to note that the witnesses adduced from the side of the plaintiffs are more credible and trustworthy with that of the defendant's witnesses. Not only this; apparently it transpires from the depositions of the witnesses that the P.Ws. have successfully corroborated the pleadings case of the plaintiffs and they are assertive in their testimony. Except some minor discrepancy no material contradiction, omission or ambiguity is noticed in their depositions, by which they can be disbelieved.</u>

<u>27. Vis-a-vis; the witnesses from the side of the defendants by their own admission practically falsified the case of the defendant-petitioners and have established the pleading's case of the plaintiffs.</u>

28. In the instant nature of suit, the court is to rely upon the oral testimony of the witnesses of the concerned locality other than documentary evidences, when admittedly the documents produced from the side of the defendants are rebuttable and these documents have got no perspective value of correctness and already it has been rebutted by the plaintiff's sufficient tangible cogent evidence.

29. Having gone through the impugned judgment and decree along with the case records 1 find that the learned Joint District Judge, Court, Tangail in his observation and findings rightly addressed the pertinent matter of easement right as contended from the side of the plaintiffs and also apprised the evidence on records in its true perspective in deciding the matter of controversy between the parties to the suit. Under the ambit of Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure the appellate court reversed the findings and decision of the trial court, relying upon the evidences adduced from the side of the plaintiffs and I find no misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with.

30. Be that as it may, I am constrained to hold such a view that in the facts and circumstances of the case and having regard to the findings referred to above, the submission advanced from the side of the learned counsel Mr. Md. Mizanur Rahman, for the opposite parties are well founded and it is consistent with the case records.

31. In the foregoing narrative, the Rule having no merit is liable to be discharged.

32. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The impugned judgment and decree dated 24.04.2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Tangail in Other Class Appeal No.229 of 2000 reversing the judgment and decree dated 27.06.2000 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kalihati, Tangail in Other Class Suit No.26 of 1999 is hereby affirmed.

33. The order of status quo granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

34. However, there will be no order as to costs.

35. Communicate the judgment and order at once and send back to the Lower Court's Records immediately.

End.
