case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 18.04.2010, passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal Nos. 612 of 2000 and 310 of 2007)
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J. These two civil appeals, by leave, are directed against the judgment and decree dated 18.04.2010, passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 612 of 2000 heard and disposed of analogously with First Appeal No. 310 of 2007 allowing both the appeals upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated 17.10.1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (Now Joint District Judge), 3rd Court, Chittagong, dismissing Other Class Suit No. 233 of 1994 and decreeing Other Class Suit No. 234 of 1994.

<u>2. Short facts, leading to these two appeals, are that Sheikh Abdul Momin, present appellant of both the appeals, instituted Title Suit No. 44 of 1987 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (Now Joint District Judge), Chittagong, impleading present respondent Nos. 2 to 4, 10 and Md. Muzammel Huq Chowdhury (predecessor of present respondent Nos. 5 to 9) as principal defendants and present respondent Nos. 11 to 13 as proforma defendants for specific performance of contract wherein the present respondent No.1 got himself added as defendant No. 9.</u>

<u>3. It is stated in the plaint that Md. Enamul Huq Chowdhury (defendant No.1) was the owner of A(1) schedule land and Mvi. Abdul Huq Chowdhury (predecessor of defendant Nos. 1 to 5) was the owner of A(2) schedule land. On the death of Mvi. Abdul Hoque Chowdhury, defendant Nos. 1 to 5 inherited Schedule A(2) land as his heirs. On 12.11.1985, Md. Azizul Huq Chowdhury (defendant No.3), by dint of a power of attorney executed by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and upon taking the responsibility of defendant Nos. 4 and 5, entered into an agreement with the plaintiff for selling both A(1) and A(2) schedule lands at a consideration of Tk.18,40,000/- and executed a baina patra upon receiving Tk.2,50,000/- out of the entire consideration money from the plaintiff, stipulating that defendants would obtain the sale per-mission from the Co-operative Housing Society and they would give a letter of authority to the plaintiff who thereafter would pay Tk.12,50,000/= to the Pubali Bank Limited, C.D.A. Branch, Chittagong, within 15.02.1986, and get the suit property released from mortgage and would take delivery of the original documents from that bank. Thereafter, the plaintiff went to the bank and came to know from the bank that the outstanding dues were much higher than the amount he was asked to deposit and as such the mortgage could not be redeemed and the original documents relating to the suit property could not be taken back from the bank. The plaintiff informed the same to defendant Nos. 1 to 3, but they did not take any step either to release the suit property from the bank or to obtain sale permission from the Co-operative Housing Society Limited as per contract. In the meantime, the defendant Nos. 1 to 3 , on two occasions, received further amount of Tk. 1,50,000/- and Tk.40,000/- by endorsing on the agreement and as such the total sum received by the said defendants was Tk.4,40,000/- out of the total consideration money of Tk.18,40,000/- from the plaintiff. But the said defendants did not take any step for executing and registering the kabala in favour of the plaintiff as per bainapatra, though the plaintiff was always ready and willing to pay off the balance consideration money. Lastly, the plaintiff came to know that the said defendants are going to sell the suit property elsewhere which compelled the plaintiff to institute the present suit for specific performance of contract.</u>

4. Initially defendant Nos. 1 to 4 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the defendants were ready to take all steps as per contract for transferring the land to the plaintiff but since the plaintiff did not per-form his part of the contract in paying off the bank liabilities and get the original documents released within the stipulated time, the defendants were compelled to enter into an agreement with defendant No.9 (present respondent No.1 in both the appeals) for sale of the suit property who got the original documents released from the bank and kept those in his custody and as such he has been inducted into possession of the suit property. Accordingly, the defendants claimed that the suit of the plaintiff is liable to be dismissed.

5. Subsequently, defendant No.9 (present respondent No.1) added himself a party in the suit and contested the same by filing separate written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and supported the case of defendant Nos. 1 to 4. Thereafter, in 1990 he instituted Title Suit No. 91 of 1990 in the same Court for specific performance of contract dated 19.10.1986, executed by the present respondent Nos. 213, impleading the plaintiff and all the defendants of Title Suit No. 44 of 1987 making the same statement as has been made in his written statement filed in Title Suit No. 44 of 1987.

6. Both the suits were transferred to the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chittagong and renumbered as Other Class Suit Nos. 234 of 1994 and 233 of 1994 respectively and the same were heard analogously where-by Other Class Suit No. 234 of 1994, (filed by the present appellant) was decreed and Other Class Suit No. 233 of 1994 (filed by the present respondent No.1 who is defendant No.9 in Other Suit No. 234 of 1994) was dismissed by judgment and decree dated 10.10.1999. Against the same, the present respondent No.1 preferred First Appeal Nos. 612 of 2000 and 310 of 2007 before the High Court Division, which upon hearing were allowed by the impugned judgment and decree dated 18.4.2010 upon setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and thereby decreed Other Class Suit No. 233 of 1994 instituted by present respondent No.1 and dismissed Other Class Suit No. 234 of 1994 instituted by the present appellant.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, the plaintiff of Other Class Suit No. 234 of 1994, filed Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 662 and 663 both of 2011 before this Division which due to misunderstanding between the present appellant and the learned Advocate-On Record were dismissed by0 order dated 15.5.2014 for non-prosecution. Hence, the appellant filed Civil Review Petition Nos. 55 and 56 both of 2014. This Division by order dated 10.04.2016 set aside the orders dated 15.05.2014 passed in the aforesaid two civil petitions dismissing those for non-prosecution and thereby leave was granted in those two civil petitions giving rise to these two civil appeals.

8. Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that in the contract there were three reciprocal promises to be performed by both seller and the purchaser. But the sellers having not performed their part, the purchaser was not in a position to perform his part which was dependent on the performance of the sellers' part, and as such the contract cannot cease under sections 51, 52 and 54 of the Contract Act. He next submits that it is well settled that for specific performance of contract of sale of immovable property time is not the essence of the contract but the High Court Division was wrong in holding that time was the essence of contract in the present suit. Moreover when there is no stipulation in the contract that the same would stand cancelled for non-compliance of any of its terms or for non-compliance of any part thereof within' the time fixed in unmistakable language, time so fixed is not the essence of the contract.

9. Mr. Alam submits that when there is no intention of the parties to rescind the earlier contract altogether there is no substitution of the original contract by a subsequent one, and the original contract remains in force and still remains enforceable. And that being the position in the present case, the subsequent contract with present respondent No.1 is not enforceable in view of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act. He further submits that the plea of the subsequent purchaser that he entered into an agreement in respect of the suit property without notice of previous contract for sale having not been proved by him, the appellant's suit for specific performance of contract, which is of earlier date, will not be defeated. Thus the trial court rightly found that the subsequent agreement with Mostafa Kamal has been made to frustrate the earlier agreement with the appellant and also that the subsequent suit instituted by Mostafa Kamal(respondent No.1) is also barred by limitation. Moreover, on the face of admitted fact that none of the plaintiff's vendors(the sellers) having challenged the said decree of the trial court, even the brother and sister who did not sign the agreement as alleged, though appeared in the suit, also having not challenge the decree in appeal the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside.

10. In respect of the agreement with the appellant Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam submits that in clause-ii of the agreement the defendant Nos. 1-3 promised to give the plaintiff written authority for receiving the original documents from the bank upon depositing Tk. 12,50,000/, but they did not give any such authority letter to the plaintiff. Thus, payment of Tk. 12,50,000/- in the bank and receiving the original documents was condition precedent upon getting the letter of authority from the defendants, which the trial court rightly considered, but the High Court Division failed to consider that the defendants did not perform their reciprocal promise within the stipulated time of 15.02.1986, without which the plaintiff could not have received the original documents by depositing Tk. 12,50,000/- in the bank. The High Court Division did not reverse the said finding of the trial court which was based on evidence on record, rather it most erroneously observed that by the said clause the defendant Nos. 1-3 were not bound to give a letter of authority in favour of the plaintiff. He further submits that after being informed by the bank about huge liability of the defendants on the suit property the plaintiff contacted the defendants and requested to settle the matter, which he reiterated in his deposition as PW-1 and the same having not been specifically denied by the defendants in their pleadings or in their cross-examination, the claim of the plaintiff remained uncontroverted. But the High Court Division without considering all these aspects held that the plaintiff did not inform the defendants about such fact. Thus the decision of the High Court Division requires interference by this Division.

11. None appeared on behalf of defendant respondent Nos. 2 to 13.

12. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No.1 in both the appeals, submits that release of the suit land from mortgage by paying Tk. 12,50,000/- to the bank, was the major condition which the plaintiff-appellant was bound to perform under section 47 of the Contract Act, but he having failed to perform the same his right to claim specific performance has ceased on 15.2.1986 under section 54 of the Contract Act. He next submits that when the plaintiff-appellant found that the bank dues were much higher than Tk. 12,50,000/-, he could either pay the whole amount of dues and claim adjustment as well as specific performance of contract or could treat the contract voidable at his option. But he having not availed either of the two options, he cannot get any relief in this suit. He further submits that since the plaintiff-appellant did not pay the contractual money within the stipulated period of 15.2.1986, he cannot claim specific performance of contract. He next submits that time being the essence of contract by lapse of the stipulated time the contract stood frustrated and as such the plaintiff cannot seek any relief. He also submits that pursuant to the contract of the present respondent No.1 dated 19.10.1986 the bank duly delivered the title deeds to him as he paid off the bank dues and was authorised to take delivery thereof; so no separate letter of authority was necessary. Lastly, he submits that the cause of action of the present respondent No. l's suit (Title Suit No. 233 of 1994) accrued on 1.5.1990 so, his suit was not barred by limitation; hence, the High Court Division rightly decreed his suit which is liable to be upheld by this Division.

13. From the materials on record, it appears that admittedly, defendant Nos.1 to 5 being the owners of schedule A(1) and A(2) properties authorized defendant No.3 to execute and register the sale deed, in favour of the plaintiff-appellant and accordingly he entered into an agreement on 12.11.1985 with him to sell the suit property as described in schedule A(1) and A(2) on his behalf and also on behalf of defendant Nos. 1, 2, 4.and 5, at a consideration of Tk. 18,40,000/- and upon receiving TK.2,50,000/- as earnest money executed the Bainapatra on 12.11.1985. Subsequently he also received further amount which brought the total earnest money to TK.4,40,000/-. On the other hand the defendants claimed that the plaintiff-appellant did not pay the contractual amount to the bank within the stipulated time and as such the contract failed. From the evidence on record, it appears that as per agreement, when the plaintiff- appellant went to deposit Tk. 12,50,000/- to the bank, the bank authority informed him that the total amount due to the bank was more than thirty lacs, which was much higher than Tk. 12,50,000/-. Thus the plaintiff could not deposit the same which he informed to defendant No.3 but he did, not take any step in this regard for releasing the suit property from the bank nor obtained sale permission from the Co-operative Housing Society Ltd as per contract. This appears to have been admitted by defendant No. 3 in his cross-examination deposing as D.W.3 stating "১২.১১.৮৫ তে বায়না হয়।..সেই বায়না বলে দফে দফে আমি ৪৪০,০০০/- টাকা নিয়েছি। প্রত্যেক বারে সই করে নিয়েছি .... মাহমুদের সাথে ২ মাসের মধ্যে কবলা নেবার কথা ছিল । ব্যাংকে তখন ২০/৩০ লক্ষ টাকা দেনা ছিল আমাদের ৷ এ কথা বায়নায় উল্লেখ করা হয়নি । ...১২,৫০,০০০/- (বার লক্ষ পঞ্চাশ হাজার) টাকা ব্যাংকে  জমা দেবার ও দলিল গ্রহণ করার জন্য কোন Letter of authority প্রদান করিনি । ব্যাংকে কোন চিঠি প্রদান করিনি ।” The Principal Officer, Pubali Bank, CDA branch, having received summons from the court deposed as PW-4 who stated “মেসার্স নূরী অয়েল মিলস নামীয় সিসি হিসাব নং ১৬৩ এর হিসাবের স্টেটমন্টে চাওয়া হয় সেমতে সত্যায়িত বিবরণী আনয়ন করেছি। ১৬৩ হিসাবে ইং ১৫.২.১৯৮৬ তারিখে ৭,৮২,৮৬৪.৭০/- টাকা; আর ৩৫০৬ হিসাবে ইং ১৫.২.১৯৮৬ তে ২৩,৬২,২৮৩.৬২/- টাকা. এই মোট হিসাব ঘরের বিবরণী (প্রদ-৩ সিরিজ) । ব্যাংকের সকল টাকা পরিশোধের পূর্বে দলিল ফেরত দেবার কোন বিধান নাই।”It further appears that in the meantime, the said defendants, entered into an agreement with defendant No.9 to sell the suit property and the same is also admitted by defendant No.3 in his deposition as DW-2 stating: "৮৬ এর শেষের দিনে ২৩৩/৯৪ মামলার বাদী মোস্তফা কামাল পাশার সাথে নালিশী সম্পত্তি বিক্রয়ের চুক্তি করি। ১৯.১০.৮৬ তারিখে লিখিত চুক্তি হয়। সেই চুক্তি পত্রে সকল বিবাদীর পক্ষে আমি সই করি। চুক্তিতে সম্পত্তির মূল্য ১৯১,০০,০০০/- (িনিশ লক্ষ) টাকা ধার্য হয়। তন্মোধ্যে আমাকে ২ লক্ষ টাকা নগদ দেয় । ১০ লক্ষ টাকা আমাকে দেয় আমি ব্যাংকে তা প্রদর্শন করি খণ পরিশোধের জন্য। ব্যাংক আমাকে বন্ধকী দলিলাদি ফেরত প্রদান করে।” [In his cross-examination he further stated that “আমরা ব্যাংকের বন্ধকের সংশ্লিষ্টতার জন্য ওখানে ৩০/৪০টি দলিল দিয়েছিলাম । ব্যাংকে আমাকে ফেরত দলিল দিয়েছে।”

14. The aforesaid oral testimony clearly proves that when the plaintiff appellant informed defendant No. 3 about the huge bank liabilities which is admittedly much higher than the amount he was supposed to deposit for releasing the property, they did not take any step to release the suit property from the bank, rather on the contrary they entered into an agreement with defendant No.9 without disclosing about the agreement with the plaintiff-appellant and took every step to handover the documents in favour of defendant No.9. All these steps clearly prove that the defendants(sellers) entered into a contract with defendant No.9 only to frustrate the contract the plaintiff-appellant. Moreover, the defendants (sellers) though claimed that they were ready to execute and register the sale deed in favour of plaintiff-appellant but they failed to prove the same by producing any oral or documentary evidence. From the above evidence, it is also clear that the plaintiff-appellant could not get the documents returned from the bank because of the non-cooperation of the defendants specially defendant No.3 who neither gave the letter of authority as per terms of the contract, nor took any step to mitigate the bank liabilities amounting to Tk. 31,45,148.32/- which is almost double of the total consideration money of TK.18,50,000/- and nearly three times more than Tk. 12,50,000/-, the amount which the plaintiff appellant was asked to deposit in the bank and clear all the bank liabilities and receive the original documents.

<u>15. On perusal of clause-ii of the agreement in question it appears that the defendant-transferers agreed to give a letter of authority in favour of the plaintiff to receive the original documents from the bank by paying Tk. 12,50,000/-. So, paying Tk. 12,50,000/- to the bank by the plaintiff and taking back the original documents from the bank was condition precedent on receiving a letter of authority from the defendant-transferors which was a reciprocal promise.</u>

16. Reciprocal promise is dealt with in sections 51 to 54 of the Contract Act. Section 51 of the Act provides that when a contract consists of reciprocal promises to be simultaneously performed, the promisor need not perform his promise unless the promisee is ready and willing to perform his part of the reciprocal promise'. Section 52 of the Act provides that 'where the order in which reciprocal promises are to be performed is expressly fixed by the contract, they shall be per-formed in that order'. In the present case, the plaintiff was ready to perform his part of the promise and went to the bank to pay TK. 12,50,000/- as per agreement and get the suit property released from mort-gage and get the original documents back but the defendant-transferers having not performed their part by providing a letter of authority to him this part of the contract could not be materialized. Moreover, it is clear from the evidence of bank official and admitted by D.W.3 that at that time bank dues on the suit property was more than thirty lacs and as such the bank in its evidence clearly stated that there is no scope to return the original documents unless the entire liability is paid off. Hence the plaintiff was unable to perform his part of depositing TK. 12,50000/- to the bank. Moreover due to non-handing over of the letter of authority it was not possible on his part to receive the original documents upon releasing the suit property from mortgage. Thus nonperformance of the promise of defendant Nos. 1 to 5 prevented the plaintiff from performing his part of the reciprocal promise. Again section 53 of the Contract Act provides that if a contract contains reciprocal promises and one party to the contract prevents the other from performing his promise, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party so prevented and he is entitled to compensation from the other party if he sustains any loss due to such prevention'. Section 54 of the said Act provides that 'when a contract consists of reciprocal promises, and that one of such promise cannot be performed, or that its performance cannot be, claimed till the other has been performed, and the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it, such promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise, and must make compensation to the other party to the contract for any loss which such other party may sustain by the non-performance of the contract'. In the present case on perusal of evidence on record, the trial court found that since the defendant-transferers did not perform their part of the contract, the plaintiff was not bound to perform his part which was dependent on the condition to be fulfilled by the defendant-transferors. But the High Court Division by the impugned judgment reversed that finding without considering that the terms of the contract was based on reciprocal promises of both the parties.

17. On perusal of the materials on record, it appears that the time difference between the first contract with the appellant dated 12.11.1985 and that of the subsequent contract with respondent No.1 dated 19.10.1986 is of more than 11 months and there is no material on record to show that the earlier contract was ever canceled or terminated by either of the parties to that contract at their option. Nor in the body of the said contract there was any specific term for termination of the same for non-performance of anyone's part. In the case of Renuza Begum and others Vs. Md. Waziullah Mia and others reported in 18 BLC(AD)201 this Division held that "After execution of a new contract, substituted contract gives new cause of action and obligates the earlier ones. If there is no intention to rescind the prior contract altogether, there is no substitution and the original contract is still enforceable." Again in the case of Mahua Khair vs. Amena Begum Ali Ispahani, (X ADC 11) this Division settled that 'in a contract for the sale of immovable property, time is not the essence, unless such is the unmistakable intention of the parties to make the time essence of the contract'. In the present case there being no such clause in the agreement the same remains valid which the trial court rightly observed but the High Court Division set aside the same without considering the evidence and materials on record and the law. Moreover, when the contract is dependent on the performance of both the parties' reciprocal promises and for non-performance of either party's part has been caused due to the nonperformance of the other party's part, it cannot be said that the contract stood terminated. In the present case when the appellant's part was to pay Tk. 12,50,000/- to the bank, and receive the original documents upon releasing the property from mortgage on producing the letter of authority was fully dependent on issuance of such letter of authority by the sellers (defendant Nos. 1-5) for the purpose of paying off the entire bank liabilities the performance on the part of the plaintiff appellant stood dependent on the performance of the sellers' part. But the defendant transferers having failed to issue the letter of authority the appellant is not guilty of non-performance of his part. Moreover, when the bank informed the plaintiff appellant that the bank liability was more than Tk. 31 lacs, which was much higher than the plaintiff's liability to pay Tk. 12,50,000/- paying the said amount would not, under any circumstances, redeem the suit property and as such there was no question of returning the original documents to the plaintiff-appellant upon releasing the suit property from mortgage as admitted by P.W.4, the bank official. In this regard the role of the defendant sellers in not taking any step on receiving such information from the plain-tiff appellant is also not bona fide. On the contrary defendant No. 3 having received further amount of balance consideration money, there arises no question of termination of the earlier contract. Thus during the subsistence of the earlier contract with the appellant, the subsequent contract with respondent No.1 (defendant No.9) is hit by section 53B of the Transfer of Property Act which provides:-

"No immovable property under a con-tract for sale shall be transferred except to the vendee so long the contract subsists unless the contract is lawfully rescinded, and any transfer made otherwise shall be void."

18. Defendant Nos. 5 though claimed that the contract ceased to exist on plaintiff's failure to pay the contractual amount within the stipulated time i.e. 15.2.1986, but from the discussion made above it is clear that the plaintiff was always ready to deposit the contractual amount but due to the huge bank liability which is much higher than what he was contractually liable to pay and the defendants' indolent and indifferent attitude to release the suit property from the bank made the plaintiff unable to perform his part of depositing the said amount. So, the contract of the plaintiff-appellant shall prevail over that of defendant No.9 respondent No. l. On the other hand pursuant to section 53B of the Transfer of Property Act during the existence of the agreement for sale of the suit property with plaintiff-appellant of earlier date the subsequent agreement with defendant No.9 (respondent No.1) is void as the same has no legal effect. Moreover, the defendant No.9 in his pleadings claimed that the cause of action of his suit arose on 20.12.1986 but he instituted his suit on 12.7.1990 which is more than three and half years after he got himself added as defendant No.9 in the plaintiff's suit No. 44 of 1987 (Other Class Suit No. 234 of 1994) which is beyond the three years period of limitation as prescribed in Article 113 of the Limitation Act. Thus the trial court rightly found the said suit barred by limitation. But the High Court Division without taking this aspect into consideration decreed the present respondent Nod's suit reversing the judgment and decree of the trial court which cannot be sustained in the eye of law.

<u>19. The plaintiff appellant though filed his suit claiming the whole of schedule A(1) and A(2) land but on perusal of the agreement dated 12.11.1985 (Exhibit-1) it appears that only defendant No.1-3 entered into the contract in question by putting their signatures therein but defendant Nos. 4 and 5 neither put their signature in the said contract nor they appointed defendant No.3 as their attorney or authorized him to enter into the agreement on their behalf. Rather, defendant No.3 took the responsibility and promised to get the kabala executed and registered by them in favor of the plaintiff'. It further appears that the trial court without considering this aspect decreed the plaintiff appellant's suit in full. Hence, we are of the view that defendant No.4 and 5 being not parties to the contract, enforcement of which is sought for, the plaintiff is not entitled to get a decree to that extent. Thus the plaintiff is entitled to get a full decree in respect of schedule A(1) land belonging to defendant No.1 and part of schedule A(2) land to the extent to which defendant Nos.1-3 have title. Defendant No. 4 and 5 being not parties to the contract, their property in schedule A(2) is beyond the ambit of this decree.</u>

20. Thus the findings and decision arrived at by the High Court Division being not based on proper appreciation of fact and law the same calls for interference by this Division.

<u>21. Accordingly, we find merit in the sub-missions of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant and hence Civil Appeal No.320 of 2016 is allowed and Other Suit No. 44 of 1987 (renumbered as Other Suit No. 234 of 1994) instituted by the plaintiff appellant is decreed in part. Title Suit No. 91 of 1990 (renumbered as Other Suit No. 233 of 1994) filed by the Mostafa Kamal (present respondent No.1) is dismissed and Civil Appeal No. 321 of 2016 is allowed in part.</u>

22. However, there will be no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 5th of June, 2007 passed by the High Court Division in Admiralty Suit No.6 of 2002)
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 05.06.2007 passed by the Admiralty Court of the High Court Division in Admiralty Suit No.6 of 2002 dismissing the suit.

<u>2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the appellant herein as plaintiff filed the aforesaid admiralty suit claiming damages and compensation for a sum of Tk.6,02,37,692/- contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff had imported a consignment of machinery, accessories and spare parts from CMI Trading (U.K.) which consisted of re-conditioned secondhand tractors, vans chassis with cabins, reefer vans and trailers, semi-trailers, a portable compressor, a sand blasting machine and certain used and new spare parts. The owner of defendant No.1 vessel is the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation, defendant No.3 which is a statutory body engaged in shipping business. The plaintiffs consignment was inspected by Inspectorate Griffith (UK) Ltd. before shipment from the UK and certified to be in good Pinning condition in the Clean Report of Findings (CRF) dated 21.10.1999. The consignment was shipped On board M.V. Banglar Kakoli-defendant No.1 vessel for carriage from Hull, UK to Mongla, Bangladesh. The loading of the plaintiffs cargo commenced on 22.09.1999, when the vessel arrived at the load port Hull, 10 days after her advised Estimated Time of Arrival (ETA) and the Estimated Time of Departure (ETD) was revised to 24.09.1999 with the ETA at the discharge port Mongla on 25A 0.1999. The vessel was arrested at Hull by third parties and eventually left Hull for Mongla on 20.10.1999. Three bills of lading dated 20.10.1999 were issued in London in respect of the plaintiffs cargo. The bills of lading described the cargo as "Shipped in apparent good order and condition." Sometime after the vessel had Sailed from Hull, it was towed to Southampton for repairs. Eventually the vessel arrived at Chattogram in Bangladesh and had to undergo repairs at the Chattogram dry dock jetty. The vessel finally arrived at Mongla and discharge of the cargo commenced on 22.02.2000 and was completed on 24.02.2000. A joint survey of the plaintiffs cargo was conducted on board the vessel during discharge of the same from 22.02.2000 to 24.02.2000. It was found that the cargo had suffered loss and damage as set out in the Survey Report dated 05.03.2000. According to the plaintiff, the cargo was eventually received in completely unserviceable and nonoperational condition rendering them useless and beyond economic repair. The plaintiff had to employ mechanics for making them tow-worthy and had to hire prime movers and special drivers to tow the units all the way from Mongla to Dhaka via Khulna/Aricha at a considerable cost. As a consequence of the defendants' delivering the cargo short and damaged, the plaintiff not only had to pay duties and taxes on the items lost and missing but also had to order the replacement of parts and spares from UK for which additional duty and sales taxes had to be paid. The plaintiff sent a letter of demand dated 08.08.2000 claiming a sum of Tk. 5,94,28,890/- for the losses suffered, but failed to recover the amount.</u>

<u>3. The plaintiff filed a suit being Admiralty in Rem No.600196 of 2001 in the High Court of Singapore on 05.05.2001 which date is within time to file the case against an international liner vessel operator like BSC in a Court of competent jurisdiction and another vessel M.V. Banglar Shikha owned by defendant No. 3 which was arrested by the Court in Singapore on 06.05.2001 as security for the plaintiffs claim. The vessel was subsequently released by order of the Court on 210542001 after security was furnished by the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (BSC) in the form of an undertaking issued by the Protection and Indemnity Club (P&I Club). The Court in Singapore passed an order on 10.09.2001 upon a sworn application made by BSC that all further proceedings in the Singapore High Court would be stayed, inter alia, on the condition that BSC would not rely on the time bar in the suit to be commenced in Bangladesh by the plaintiff. The suit was ultimately filed in Bangladesh on 12.01.2002 and was dismissed by the impugned judgment.</u>

<u>4. The plaintiff sought a decree for an amount of Tk.6,02,37,692/- with interest and cost at the rate of 20% per annum against defendant Nos.1-6 jointly and severally.</u>

5. The cause of action as stated in the plaint arose on 20.10.1999 when the Bills of Lading were issued; on 20.10.1999 when Inspectorate Griffith Ltd. (UK) gave the Clean Report of Findings; on 05.03.2000 when the Joint Survey Report was prepared by James Finally PLC with Lloyds sub-agents along with the Chief Officer of the defendant vessel; on 08.08.2000 when the plaintiff lodged a claim with the defendants for compensation; on 06.05.2001 when the vessel was arrested in Singapore; on 23.05.2001 when the US$ 1 million was furnished and finally on 10.10.2001 when the order dated 10.09.2001 was served upon the plaintiffs lawyers in Singapore.

6. Defendant Nos.1-4 entered appearance in the suit and filed a written statement denying the averments made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the suit was barred by limitation. It was further stated that the agent of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation had refused to load 10 trailers on board due to shortage of space, but the shipper's agent/freight forwarder compelled the agent of Bangladesh Shipping Corporation to load the same on the deck. The vehicles were found very old, broken and damaged in a tally made by the steve-dores and the same was recorded by the Chief Officer of the vessel in the Daily Working Report. Although the commercial invoice, packing list and Clean Report of Findings by Inspectorate Griffith Limited state that all the 27 vehicles had been manufactured in the year 1995-96, evidence obtained from M/s. Leyland Exports, M/s. HASA (Export) Limited and British Car Numbers registration system covering motor vehicles prove that the vehicles imported by the plaintiff had been manufactured in the 1980s and that the plaintiff has imported banned vehicles into Bangladesh in violation of the Import Policy Order,1997-2000. The defendants further contended that after loading of the goods on board the vessel, it sailed from Hull on 20.10.1999. The vessel encountered severe, cyclonic storm in the Bay of Biscay on 23.10.1999 and called at Southampton on 26.10.1999 for emergency repairs, re-stowage and relashing of cargo for safe prosecution of the rest of the voyage. The vessel resumed her voyage on 06.11.1999. The defendants claimed that due to unforeseen weather conditions which were an act of God, the vessel had lost 14 days. After discharging Jeddah-bound cargo the vessel proceeded to her next port of call at Male. Due to the ongoing holy month of Ramadan the daily working hours at Male were reduced to almost half of the normal working hours because of which the vessel suffered a delay of 12 days at Male. When the vessel arrived at Chattogram it had to stay at the outer anchorage for 13 days for getting a discharge berth due to severe port congestion prevailing at Chattogram port at that time. Further delay was encountered by the vessel due to the expiry of the vessel's cargo gear Jumbo Derrick fitness certificate. As a result, the vessel could not sail from Chattogram for her next destined port at Mongla without renewal of the said certificate by the classification society, the Lloyds Register of Shipping. The vessel arrived at Mongla on 21.02.2000 for dis-charging the Mongla-bound cargo. The defendants contended that in the Joint Survey Report, the surveyors had not stated any significant structural damage to the secondhand vehicles. It was further contended that in view of clause 4 of the Bill of Lading, the carrier and the ship shall be discharged from all liability in respect of loss or damage unless suit is brought with-in one year after delivery of the goods or the date when the goods should have been delivered. The defendants also contended that the deadline for commencing the proceedings in Bangladesh in accordance with the order dated 10.09.2001 passed by the Court in Singapore expired on 10.01.2002, but the suit was filed on 12.01.2002 and hence the suit is barred by limitation and liable to be dismissed. It was argued that since the suit was not filed within the time stipulated by the court in Singapore, the undertaking given by the defendants not to rely on time bar, not to adopt package limitation under the Hague Rules were no longer applicable. Also the condition to apply the HaqueVisby Rules is applied in Singapore, are no longer applicable. The defendants claimed that, recognising the fact that the suit in Bangladesh was not filed within the period of limitation, the court in Singapore dismissed the suit and accordingly the suit in Bangladesh is also to be dismissed as barred by limitation.

7. Upon hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record, the High Court Division dismissed the admiralty suit on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation. Hence, the plain-tiff filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.719 of 2009 and leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner: "I. That the goods in question having been carried from a point outside Bangladesh to Mongla Port of Bangladesh and section 2 of Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 limiting the application of the Act and the Rules to have effect in relation to and in connection with carriage of goods by sea in ship carrying goods from any port of Bangladesh, the High Court Division erred in applying the limitation mentioned in Article III Rule 6 of the Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 to the present case and as such the impugned judgment and order dismissing the suit is liable to be set aside."

<u>8. Mr. Kamal ul Alam, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He also submitted that the High Court Division hopelessly failed to appreciate the undertaking dated 10.09.2001 given by BSC in the High Court of the Republic of Singapore "not to adopt in the Bangladesh proceedings the package limitation under the Hague Rules as applied by Bangladesh law but on condition that the defendants may rely on the limitation provisions applicable under the Hague-Visby Rules as applied in Singapore and/or the tonnage limitation under the Singapore Merchant Shipping Act (Cap. 179)" waiving the legal requirement to file the suit within one year as per Hague Rules, from the date of discharge of the cargo, the petitioner was well within time to file the suit both in Singapore Court and in Bangladesh as per the Hague-Visby Rules which the parties freely agreed to be the law applicable in settling the dispute and as such the High Court Division was wrong in relying only upon Article III Rule 6 of Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 and as such, the impugned judgment and order calls for interference. He further submitted that the High Court Division before passing the impugned judgment and order did not at all apply its judicial mind in considering the fact that in Admiralty in Rem No.600196 of 2001 in the High Court of Singapore upon a sworn application made by Bangladesh Shipping Corporation in which Bangladesh Shipping Corporation undertook, inter alia, that it would not rely on the time bar in the suit to be commenced in Bangladesh, the Court in Singapore passed an order on 10.09.2001 giving 3 (three) months' time to commence proceedings in Bangladesh and, accordingly, the plaintiff commenced the instant Admiralty Suit in Bangladesh within the stipulated time as 10th and 11th of January being Court holidays, it was filed on 12.01.2002, which was within time as per section 4 of Limitation 1908 and as such the impugned judgment and order dismissing the suit could not be sustained. He submitted that the High Court Division wrongly dismissed the suit without considering the undertaking provided by BSC in Singapore read with the provision of law incorporated in section 4 of the Limitation Act 1908 and as such, the impugned judgment and order dismissing the suit is liable to be set aside as the Court of Singapore cannot arbitrarily determine the time of filing the case in Bangladesh Court disregarding the provision of the Bangladesh Law as per the Limitation Act. He submitted that the High Court Division erred in not holding that the plaintiff is entitled to the benefit of the time lost in filing the suit in Singapore High Court; the guarantee given in Singapore High Court shows the relevance of filing the suit there. He submitted that the defendants gave an undertaking in Singapore High Court not to press the point of limitation in the High Court in Bangladesh the period of one year to file the suit will be deemed to have been automatically extended until the suit is tiled; the defendants should have been estopped from pleading limitation after leading the plain-tiff to believe that limitation will not he pressed and causing the plaintiff to act on that representation by not proceeding with the suit in Singapore; the three-months period to file the suit in Bangladesh Court applied only to the question of security given in Singapore High Court but is not related to the compensation and damages claimed in the Admiralty Suit filed in Bangladesh. He further submitted that the High Court Division before passing the impugned judgment and order did not at all consider the evidence produced by the plaintiff which are sufficient to prove that the plaintiff is entitled to get the damages and compensation as prayed for and therefore, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside.</u>

9. Mr. Fida M Kamal, learned Senior Advocate appearing for respondent Nos.1- 4 made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He also submitted that as regards the issue of damages and compensation and losses suffered by the plaintiff, it appears that the plaintiff has miserably failed to substantiate its heads of claim in the plaint with documentary evidence and, on the other hand, D. W.1 has denied all the heads of claims made by the plaintiff including the plaintiffs total claim and DW 1 has exhibited all the documentary evidence in its favour disproving the claims of the plaintiff and prayed for dismissal of the plaintiffs suit and hence the High Court Division rightly dismissed the suit. He submitted that P.W.1 has adduced oral evidence and produced photocopies of documents and the same have been marked as exhibits with objection and no explanation has been given as to the whereabouts of the originals thereof. So, these documents cannot be taken into consideration as they are all photocopy. He submitted that the goods in question, although have been carried from a port outside Bangladesh to Mongla Port Bangladesh, the High Court Division committed no error of law in applying the limitation period prescribed in Article III Rule 6 of the Schedule/Rules relating to Bills of Lading of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 since in the present case the Bill of Lading contains an express statement in the Clause Paramount to the effect that it is to have effect subject to the provisions of the said Rules as applied by this Act. He submitted that the High Court Division therefore relying upon Article III Rule 6 of the Schedule/Rules relating to periods of limitation, rightly dismissed the suit and accordingly the instant Appeal is also liable to be dismissed. He submitted that from clause No.4, the jurisdiction clause, in the Bills of Lading, and it is clear that the contract would be governed by the law of the place where the carrier has its principal place of business. Hence, the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 would be the law applicable to the instant voyage and accordingly the Courts in Bangladesh would also have exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute arising out of carriage of goods and thus the 1 year limitation period as contained in Article III Rule 6 of the Schedule/Rules relating to periods of limitation, to file the instant suit shall be fully applicable in the instant proceedings. Since the suit was filed after the expiry of 1 year after the delivery of the goods, the High Court Division rightly dismissed the suit and the respondents/defendants have been discharged from all liabilities under the terms of the Bills of Lading which incorporate Article III Rule 6 of the Schedule/Rules relating to periods of limitation. He submitted that the rights of the holder of the Bills of Lading thus has been completely extinguished in respect of the claim made in this case and, therefore, the plaintiff has no right to enforce his time-barred claim and hence the High Court Division rightly relying upon Article III Rule 6 of the Schedule/Rules relating to periods of limitation, dismissed the suit. He submitted that the High Court of Singapore passed a conditional order on 10.09.2001 stating that in the event proceedings are not commenced in Bangladesh by the plaintiff in respect of the claim being the subject matter of the action in Singapore within 3 months from the date the said security provided by the defendants to the plaintiff shall become null and void and the same shall be returned by the plaintiff to the defendants forthwith on demand for cancellation and the action herein, i.e. the suit filed in Singapore shall stand dismissed with costs to the defendants without further order.

10. However, the plaintiff did not commence action in Bangladesh during the three-month period which expired on 10.01.2001 and, accordingly, the court in Singapore by order dated 25.01.2002 dis-missed the plaintiffs action with costs and ordered the plaintiff to return the security provided by the defendants to the plaintiff and hence the instant appeal is liable to be dismissed with costs and the plaintiff should immediately pay to these defendants the costs of S$ 1,39,773.20 as ordered by the court in Singapore. The learned Advocate further submitted that the vessel M.V. BANGLAR KAKOLI carried and discharged the plaintiffs consignment with all due care and diligence at the port of Mongla and in the same condition as was loaded at the port of loading at Hull, United Kingdom and these defendants are not liable if the plaintiff has imported very old, damaged and broken second-hand vehicles and spare parts and the plaintiff is also liable to pay the costs of S$1,39,773.20 immediately to these defendants as ordered by the Court in Singapore for wrongful arrest of their vessel. It was submitted that goods in question although have been carried from a port outside Bangladesh to Mongla Port Bangladesh the limitation period prescribed in Article III Rule 6 of the Hague Rules relating to Bills of Lading as appended in the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 would apply since in the present case the Bill of Lading contains an express statement that it is to have effect subject to the provisions of the said Rules as applied by this Act/Clause.

11. Mr. Fida M Kamal also submitted that in view of the settled principle of law regarding incorporation of the Hague Rules relating to bills of, lading as appended to the Schedule of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 clearly providing for a limitation period of 1 year for a suit to be instituted against the ship/carrier, the suit filed by the plaintiff beyond the period of 1 year, the instant Appeal is liable to be dismissed. It was argued that it is clear from clause No.4, the jurisdiction clause of the Bill of Lading, that the con-tract would be governed by the law of the place where the carrier has its principal place .of business, and the laws of Bangladesh provide that the period of limitation is one year, and hence the impugned judgment is correct and does not call for interference by this Division.

12. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

13. We find from the impugned judgment that the Admiralty Court noted that the consignment of goods carried on board the defendant vessel had apparently suffered loss and damage whilst it was under the custody, care and control of the ship owners. The Clean Report of Findings (CRF) issued on 21.10.1999 certified the goods to be in good running condition with 10 years of economic life. The joint survey report dated 05.03.2000 shows that at the time of delivery at the port of Mongla certain loss and damage to the goods was incurred. Hence, in view of the provisions of section 3(2) of the Admiralty Court Ain, 2000, there was no doubt that the Admiralty Court had jurisdiction to hear the matter. However, although there was an observation that the plaintiff appears to have a claim for damage to the cargo suffered as a result of the vandalism and theft on board the defendant vessel, ultimately the decision of the court was based upon finding that the plaintiffs claim was barred by limitation. It was thus not necessary to deal with the plaintiffs itemised claim since the suit was dismissed on a point of law.

Jurisdiction

14. An Admiralty suit in rem is an action that is instituted against the vessel carrying goods from one port to another, which may be brought at any place where the vessel might be located at the time of filing the suit, in order to realise the claim for loss/damages. This was elaborately discussed in the case of M.V. Elisabeth and Ors. Vs. Harwan Investment and Trading Pvt. Ltd. and Ors. AIR 1993 SC 1014, where it was observed as follows:

44. "The law of admiralty, or maritime law,.... (is the) corpus of rules, concepts, and legal practices governing... the business of carrying goods and passengers by water." (Gilmore and Black, The law of Admiralty, page 1). The vital significance and the distinguishing feature of an admiralty action in rem is that this jurisdiction can be assumed by the coastal authorities in respect of any maritime claim by arrest of the ship, irrespective of the nationality of the ship or that of its owners, or the place of business or domicile or residence of its owners or the place where the cause of action arose wholly or in part."

15. Section 6 of the of the Admiralty Court Ain, 2000 (the Ain, 2000) permits the filing of a suit in the Admiralty Court of the High Court Division for, inter alia, loss of or damage to goods carried in a vessel, as provided by section 3(2)(chha) and (ja). The latter provisions are reproduced below:

“৩। (১) হাইকোর্ট বিভাগ এডমিরালটি কোর্ট হইবে।

(২) এডমিরালটি কোর্টের নিম্নবর্ণিত যে কোন প্রশ্ন বা দাবী সম্পর্কে শুনানী এবং সিদ্ধান্ত গ্রহণ করিবার এখতিয়ার থাকিবে যথা:

(ছ) জাহাজে পরিবহনকৃত পণ্য হারাইয়া যাওয়া বা তির দাবী

(জ) কোন জাহাজে পণ্য পরিবহন বা কোন জাহাজের ব্যবহার বা ভাড়া সংক্রান্ত চুক্তি উদ্ভুত কোন দাবী;”

16. With regard to jurisdiction, in the facts of the instant case, we find that the Bill of Lading, which is the contract of carriage, stipulates that the jurisdiction for any action arising out of the contract will be Bangladesh and the applicable laws will be the laws of Bangladesh. The jurisdiction of any other court is specifically excluded by clause 4 of the Bill of Lading. Clause 4 provides as follows:

"4. Jurisdiction: The contract evidenced by this Bill of Lading shall be governed by the law of the place where the Carrier has his principal place of business and disputes determined at that place (or at the option of the Carrier, at the port of destination) according to that law to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the courts of any other country."

17. The Bill of Lading appears to be a valid contract entered into between the parties at arm's length and of their own volition. The terms of the contract, being lawful in nature, are binding on the parties. Hence, any suit arising out of the said Bill of Lading would have to be filed in Bangladesh. Of course, any ancillary action by way of arrest of the vessel in any port outside Bangladesh would be competent for realisation of the claim. It is our view that the suit initiated in Singapore would not have been within the jurisdiction specified in the Bill of Lading, although the arrest of the vessel in Singapore would have been perfectly valid and legal. Nevertheless, it transpires that the defendant acceded to the jurisdiction of the court in Singapore and did not challenge the jurisdiction of that court, and in fact filed an application with various prayers, thereby waving the right to challenge the jurisdiction of the court in Singapore. We note, however, that the suit was filed in Singapore on 05.05.2001. Whether that was within the period of limitation allowed by law will be discussed below.

Limitation

18. Leave was granted in the instant case on the sole ground of limitation. No additional ground has been taken by the plaintiff-appellant in the concise statement, although in the written submissions the learned Advocate for the appellant added a point relating to the merit of his claim for loss/damages. Since the merit of the claim was not a ground for granting leave and since the concise statement does not contain any further ground relating to the merit of the plaintiffs claim, we do not propose to go into the merit of the plaintiffs claim with regard to loss/damages, but will-confine ourselves to the question of limitation.

19. In the case of New Zealand Insurance Co. Ltd., Chittagong.tvs. M.A. Rouf & ors., 13 DLR 186, the point of limitation was elaborately discussed. The facts of that case were similar to those of the instant case. In that case the plaintiff had imported goods from Belgium, which were shipped from Antwerp to the port of Chattogram in Bangladesh and were discharged before the vessel left Chattogram on 10.6.52. The suit was filed on 10.8.53 claiming that it was filed within the period of limitation since the certificate showing short landing was issued on 07.03.1953. The question of applicability of the Hague Visby Rules were discussed at length. The High Court Division observed that the rules relating to bills of lading contained in the International Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules of Law relating to Bills of Lading ("Hague Rules") were included in a schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 (the Act, 1925). It was further observed that the Act, as in force in Pakistan, applies to the carriage of goods by sea from any port in Pakistan to any other port whether in or outside Pakistan, but does not apply to the carriage of goods by sea from a foreign port to a port in Pakistan as provided in section 2 of that Act, 1925.

Section 2 provides as follows: "2. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the rules set out in the Schedule (hereinafter referred to as "the Rules") shall have effect in relation to and in connection with the carriage of goods by sea in ships carrying goods from any port in Bangladesh to any other port whether in or outside Bangladesh."

20. There are conflicting decisions of our courts as well as those of India as to whether or not the rules contained in the Schedule to the Act apply to cases where the goods are shipped from a foreign port. We are of the opinion that, in view of the wording of section 2 of the Act, 1925 the rules contained in the Schedule to the Act, 1925, which provide periods of limitation, do not apply in the instant case since the goods concerned were not shipped from any port in Bangladesh. The submission of the learned advocate for the appellant that the rules mentioned in section 2 do not apply in the facts of the instant case and hence, the period of limitation mentioned in the rules detailed in the Schedule to the Act, 1925 have no manner of application in the instant case, is a correct proposition of law. He submitted that, therefore, the High Court Division fell into error in dismissing the suit on the ground of limitation. We are of the view that the decision of the Admiralty Court to the effect that the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 was applicable, cannot be sustained. He went further to argue that since the Admiralty Court Ain, 2000 does not pro-vide for any period of limitation for filing any suit, the instant suit was most erroneously dismissed on the grounds of limitation basing its decision on the limitation stipulated in the Schedule to the Act, 1925.

21. The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 is a special law and the limitation provided in the Schedule to the Act is a special limitation and would thus exclude the provisions relating to limitation as pro-vided in the Limitation Act, 1908. However, where the special law by its own provision (section 2) excludes the special limitation in certain specified circumstances, namely when the goods are not shipped from a port in Bangladesh, then the general law of limitation' would apply. We are unable to accept the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that there would not be any limitation applicable to file the suit.

22. We note that in the above cited case of New Zealand Insurance Co. Ltd., it was further observed that the shipment of goods from a foreign port to Pakistan is governed by the conditions of the relevant contract of carriage, the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 not being applicable thereto. It was noted that a bill of lading embodies the conditions of such a contract and usually contains a clause exactly in the words of Article III, clause 6 of the Schedule to the Act, 1925. The said clause 6 provides, inter alia, that the carrier and the ship shall in any event be discharged from all liability whatsoever in respect of the goods, unless suit is brought within one year of their delivery or of the date when they should have been delivered. Hence, it was held that in the case of shipment of goods by sea from a foreign port to a port in Pakistan, such shipment is governed by the conditions of the relevant contract of carriage. If the connected bill of lading contains a clause corresponding to clause 6 of Article III of the rules relating to bills of lading referred to herein before, no rule of limitation shall apply, but the claim against the carrier and the ship in respect of loss or damage shall be extinguished at the expiry of one year from the date of delivery of the goods or the date when the goods should have been delivered.

23. At this juncture, it would be pertinent to note that although there is no period of limitation mentioned in the Ain, 2000, nor in the Admiralty Rules, 1912 (which are the applicable rules in accordance with section 11 of the Act), rule 51 of the said Rules, 1912 provides as follows:

"51. Where other provision not made rules and practice of ordinary original civil jurisdiction to apply. Where no other provision is made by these rules proceedings in suits brought in the Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction under the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890, shall be regulated by the rules and practice of the Court in suits brought in it in the exercise of its Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction."

24. Hence, it cannot be said that no rules of limitation are applicable in this case. We find that the facts of the instant case, since the claim is for loss and damage to goods in the course of carriage by sea, in the absence of any other special rules of limitation, the appropriate rules of limitation would be those in article 30 of the schedule to the Limitation Act, which provides that in an action against a carrier for compensation for losing or injuring goods, the period within which to bring the action is one year from the time when the loss or injury occurs.

25. The learned Advocate for the appellant cited the case of Union of India v. M/s Probhat Marketing Company Ltd., AIR 1963 190 and submitted that the provision of the Limitation Act relevant in the facts of the instant case is article 115 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act which provides for limitation of three years within which to file the suit for breach of contract.

26. The facts of the cited case in brief are that a consignment of sugar was carried by rail from one place to another within India. Out of 110 bags, 11 were found cut and the weight was found less at the time of delivery. The claim of the plaintiff was for short landing. A claim was made to the Railway authorities just after two months of delivery and there were several exchanges of correspondence. But the suit was filed about sixteen months after the date of delivery. The learned judge of the High Court of Assam observed that articles 30 and 31 in the Schedule to the Limitation Act relate to suits based on tort or tortious acts and are not applicable to any claim arising out of breach of contract.

27. Upon perusal of that decision, we find that the learned judge observed that the decisions cited on behalf of the appellant in the case related to article 31 and not article 30, and hence he did not consider those decisions. Thereafter, observing that the suit could not be regarded as one in tort for compensation against a carrier either for losing or for injuring the goods, article 30 was not applicable.

28. It appears to us that in the cited case no reference was made to the earlier decision in the case of Union of India vs. Amar Singh, AIR 1960 SC 223, where the claim against the Railways was for loss and damage to goods incurred in transit. The Supreme Court of India held that article 30 applies to a suit by a person claiming compensation against the carrier for its losing or injuring his goods.

29. It is our view that the facts of Amar Singh case are more applicable in the facts and circumstances of the case before us, where the claim is for damage to goods which took place during transit when the goods were in the custody of the carrier. Hence, the period of limitation is one year from the date of delivery of the goods in question.

30. Moreover, we find from the Bill of Lading that in any event the Hague Rules are applicable in view of the Paramount Clause, namely clause 1 of the Bill of Lading, clause 1 (a) of which provides as follows: "(a) Where the port of loading or failing the port of loading the port of discharge is in territory where legislation giving compulsory effect to the Hague Rules contained in the International Convention concerning Bills of Lading of 25th August, 1924 is in force subject to such legislation and (b) in any other case as if the said Hague Rules other than Article IX thereof applied and the carrier shall be entitled to the benefit of all the privileges, rights and immunities conferred by the said legislation and Rules as if the same were herein specifically set out."

31. Both the United Kingdom and Bangladesh have clause incorporating the Hague Rules in their legislation and hence the terms and conditions of the Bill of Lading will have effect, subject to the legislation of the two countries. According to sub-clause (b), if the laws of the two countries mentioned do not apply, then the Hague Rules, other than Article IX, shall apply. It thus appears that since the parties agreed to be bound by the laws of Bangladesh, which are made non-applicable by section 2 of the Act, 1925, the Hague Rules per se would be applicable. The period of limitation for bringing an action for loss or damage is specified in the International Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules of Law relating to Bills of Lading ("Hague Rules"), and Protocol of Signature, Article 1, clause 6, the relevant portion of which provides as follows: .... In any event the carrier and the ship shall be discharged from all liability in respect of the loss or damage unless suit is brought within one year after delivery of the goods or the date when the goods should have been delivered."

32. Hence, there can be no doubt that in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the period of limitation for filing any suit for loss or damage to goods that occurred in the course of carriage, will be one year from the date of delivery of the goods, i.e. within 12 months from 24.02.2000. In any event, it is apparent from the records that the plaintiff was aware of the extent of loss/damage to his goods on 05.03.2000 when the joint survey report was issued. Thus, the suit filed in Singapore on 05.05.2001 was beyond the period of limitation prescribed in the Hague Rules.

33. The application in suit in Singapore filed on behalf of the defendants for staying further proceedings of the suit cannot be taken as a waiver by the defendants of their right to challenge the filing of the suit as barred by limitation. In this context we may refer to the provisions of section 3 of the Limitation Act, which provides as follows:

3. Subject to the provisions contained in sections 4 to 25 (inclusive), every suit instituted, appeal preferred, and application made, after the period of limitation prescribed therefor by the first schedule shall be dismissed, although limitation has not been set up as a defence.

34. The well-established principle of law based on this section is that the defendant's failure to plead the bar of limitation as a defence will not save the suit from being barred by limitation unless any of the provisions mentioned in sections 4 to 25 are applicable.

35. In the facts of the instant case, the pro-vision which may be argued in aid of the plaintiffs case is found in section 19 of the Limitation Act, which provides as follows: 19. (1) Where, before the expiration of the period prescribed for a suit or application in respect of any property or right, an acknowledgement of liability in respect of such property or right has been made in writing signed by the party against whom such property or right is claimed, or by some person through whom he derives title or liability, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the acknowledgement was so signed.

36. The plaintiff, by reference to a letter written by the defendants dated 14.02.2001 sought to overcome this hurdle of limitation by claiming that the defendants had agreed to extend the period by three months from 21.02.2001. The said letter of the defendants' states as follows: "With reference to your letter No .1B SC/KAKOLI/3/2001 dated 12th February 2001. We are pleased to grant you 3 (three) months' Time Extension with effect from 21.02.2001 in respect of your alleged claim.

This is without prejudice and without accepting any liability/claim whatsoever."

37. The plaintiff did not produce its own letter dated 12.02.2001'by which time was sought. So, we do not know the exact purpose for which time was sought and granted. But we find from the language of paragraph 18 of the written statement that the plaintiff might have sought extension of time for examining its claim. This is borne out by paragraph 10 of the plaint, although the wording of the paragraph appears confusing since we find from exhibit 7 that the letter dated 14.02.2001 was in fact written by the defendants granting extension of time to the plaintiff, but the purpose was not stated. Be that as it may, for the limitation period for filing the suit to be saved, the situation would have to be covered by section 19 of the Limitation Act, quoted above, i.e. there must be acknowledgement of liability.

38. In this regard reference may be made to the decision in Khan Bahadur Shapoor Freedom Mazda Vs. Durga Prosad Chamaria and ors., AIR 1961 SC 1236: "8. The question as to what is an acknowledgment has been answered by Fry, L.J., as early as 1884 A. D. in Green v. Humphreys (1884) 26 Ch. D. 474. This answer is often quoted with approval. "What is an acknowledgment", asked Fry, L.J., and he proceeded, "in my view an acknowledgment is an admission by the writer that there is a debt owing by him, either to the receiver of the letter or to some other person on whose behalf the letter is received but it is not enough that he refers to a debt as being due from somebody. In order to take the case out of the statute there must upon the fair construction of the letter, read by the light of the surrounding circumstances, be an admission that the writer owes the debt". With respect, it may be added, that this statement succinctly and tersely gives the substance of the provisions contained in s. 19 of the Limitation Act."

39. It was stated in the case of Lakshmirattan Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. and Ors. Va. The Aluminium Corporation of India Ltd., AIR 1971 SC 1482 as follows: "In this connection the decision in Maniram v. Rupchand L.R. 33 Ind App 165, was relied on and in particular the famous dictum of Mellish, L.J., in more River Steamer Company v. Mitchell L.R. 6 Ch. App. 822, approvingly cited therein. The dictum was that an acknowledgement to take the case out of the statute of limitation must be either one from which an absolute promise to pay can be inferred, or secondly, an unconditional promise to pay the specific debt, or thirdly, that there must be a condition-al promise to pay the debt and evidence that the condition has been performed."

40. We find from the letter of the defendants dated 14.02.2001 that there was no acknowledgement of liability and hence that letter, although it purportedly extends the period for three months as requested by the plaintiff for examining its claim, it would not have the effect of extending the period of limitation for filing the suit. Hence, we find that the filing of the suit in Singapore on 05.05.2001 beyond the period of one year from the date when the goods were delivered, or at the latest from 05.03.2000 when the joint survey report was published, was barred by limitation. Of course, this matter was not adjudicated upon by the court in Singapore since the suit did not reach the trial stage and we are not aware whether the defendants filed any written statement in Singapore alleging that the suit was barred by limitation. However, as stated earlier, even if the defendants do not plead the bar of limitation, the court cannot ignore the provisions of section 3 of the Limitation Act in the absence of the provisions of sections 4 to 25 of the said Act.

41. It transpires that the defendants gave an undertaking that they will not raise the issue of limitation if and when the suit is filed in Bangladesh. That could only relate to any delay in filing the suit in Bangladesh after the order passed by the Court in Singapore. The High Court of Singapore allowed the plaintiff three months’ time within which it was to file a suit in Bangladesh. That order was dated 10.09.2001 and was communicated by fax to the defendants' lawyers on 10.10.2001. This is evident by the facsimile letter dated 10.10.2001 from the defendant's lawyers, namely Allen & Gledhill (Ext.K) addressed to Haridass Ho & Partners (lawyers for the plaintiff). Haridass Ho & Partners by their facsimile letter dated 10 October 2001 (Ext.K(1)) wrote as follows: "We thank you for your letter dated 10 October 2001. For the avoidance of doubt please confirm that the time to commence suit in Bangladesh expires on 10 January 2002."

42. In the letter (Ext. K) the defendant's lawyers replied as follows: "Thank you for your fax dated 10 October 2001 and we confirm that the time for your clients to commence suit in Bangladesh expires on 10 January 2002"

43. Thus, there was no doubt that the last day for filing the suit in Bangladesh was 10 January 2002. It is not denied that in fact the plaintiff filed, the suit in Bangladesh on 12 January 2002. The learned advocate for the appellant argued before the Admiralty Court that 10 January 2002 was a court holiday and 11 January 2002 being a Friday, the suit was filed on the next opening-day, i.e. Saturday, 12 January 2002. The same argument was placed before us. Before the Admiralty Court the learned advocate for the defendants produced the notification dated 13.11.2001 issued by the Registrar which showed that the offices of the Court were open on Thursday from 09:45 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. we have also enquired from the relevant Section of the Supreme Court and found that the offices of the Supreme Court were indeed open on Thursday, 10 January 2002.

44. The High Court of Singapore by order dated 25 January 2002 dismissed the suit which the plaintiff had filed there on the basis of an application filed by the defendants that the suit in Bangladesh was not filed within time specified in the order of the court in Singapore. A subsequent application by the plaintiff before the court in Singapore to set aside its earlier judgment was dismissed by order dated 29 April 2002.

<u>45. With regard to the submission of the learned Advocate for the defendants that this court should order the plaintiff to pay the costs awarded by the court in Singapore, we are of the view that such a prayer is untenable in view of the fact that the Admiralty Court of the High Court Division in the impugned judgment did not order such payments and the defendants chose not to appeal against that decision.</u>

<u>46. In the facts and circumstances discussed above, we do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment and order of dismissal of the suit, save and except as mentioned in the body of this judgment. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed, without any order as to costs.</u>

End.
