full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique J. These two appeals are directed against the judgment and decrees dated 16.08.2011 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal Nos.5 and 6 of 2007 reversing those dated 08.08.2006 passed by the learned District Judge, Narayangonj in Title Suit Nos.1 and 2 of 2006.

2. The relevant facts, for the disposal of these appeals, are that the respondent No.1 Ayub Ali as plaintiff instituted Title Suit Nos.72 and 73 of 2003 which were subsequently renumbered as Title Suit Nos.01 of 2006 and 02 of 2006 respectively, for specific performance of contract. The case of the plaintiff in Title Suit No.02 of 2006, in short, was that the land as described in the schedule to the plaint originally belonged to the defendants. The defendants No.1-6 jointly executed 3(three) "bainanamas" and the defendant No.6 executed one "bainanama" in favour of the plaintiff on 31.05.1999 to sell the suit land at a consideration of taka 54,63,750.00 and upon receiving taka 12,50,000/- they executed those bainanamas. The defendant No.1 and his wife Kamrunnahar also came to an agreement with the plaintiff to sell 2.26 acres of land appertaining to plot Nos.165, 166, 167, 168, 169 and 163 of Ratandi Mouza at a consideration of taka 56,50,000/- and upon receiving taka 15,00,000/-, they executed the said agreement. Similarly, the defendant No.1 to 6, upon receiving taka 2,00,000/- out of total consideration of taka 6,66,666/- from the plaintiff, executed another "bainanama" in respect of land measuring an area of .801/2 acre of plot No.94 and 96 of Mouja Chhoto Sadipur and Ratandi. The defendant No.6, upon receiving taka 50,000/-out of total consideration taka 1,20,000/-to sell .06 acre of land of plot No. 155, executed "bainanama" in favour of plaintiff. The plaintiff paid taka 30,00,000/- to the defendant No.1 to 6 by issuing different cheques. The defendant No.1 received those cheques on behalf of defendant Nos.2 to 6. The defendants also received taka 5,00,000/- vide cheque No.157784 dated 21.02.2000. The defendants received taka 17,50,000/- through cheque. The defendants executed a sale deed in respect of .20½ acre of land from plot No.17, 18 and 19 out of the suit land in favour of the wife of the plaintiff upon receiving consideration of taka 5,25,483/-. The plaintiff also paid taka 7,55,000/- to the defendant No.6 in cash. By this way, the defendants received a sum of taka 30,30,483/- from the plamtat. On 01.01.2000, the plaintiff also paid tk.31,50,000/- vide cheque No.157800/-. Thereafter, on 06.05.2000, the plaintiff again paid tk.10,00„000/- vide cheque No.157783 to the defendants. The plaintiff again paid taka 5,25,483/- to the defendants. On behalf of the defendants, the defendant No.6 received the said amount by executing an acknowledgement slip. The defendants No.1 to 6 executed a sale deed in favour of the plaintiff on 07.09.2000 in respect of 2.26 acres of land of aforesaid 6(six) plots of Ratandi and Chhoto Sadipur Mouja. The defendants also executed another sale deed in respect of .203/4 acre of land to the plaintiff. On 31.05.2006, the defendants received a sum of taka 2,00,000/- out of total consideration of taka 6,66,666/- to sell .80'/2 acre of land of Ratandi and Chhota Sadipur Mouja. Thereafter, the defendants, receiving rest amount of taka 4,66,666/- from the plaintiff on 7.9.2000, executed and registered a sale deed. The defendants, in order to sell .06 acre of land of plot No.155 appertaining to khatian No.70 of Ratandi Mouja, received taka 50,000/- out of total consideration of taka 12,00,000/-and executed a "bainanama" in favour of the plaintiff. The defendant No.6 also received taka 20,000/- from the plaintiff out of rest consideration. Though, the plaintiff performed his part of agreement but defendants did not execute and register sale deed in respect of land as described to the schedule to the plaint. The plaintiff issued a notice through his learned Advocate to get sale deed executed and registered but the defendants did not respond. Thus, the plaintiff instituted the suit.

3. The defendant Nos.1 to 6 contested the suit by filing 2(two) separate sets of writ-ten statements contending, inter alia, that suit was barred by limitation and the same was not maintainable in view or me provisions 01 section 28 of the Specific Relief Act. It was further contended that in the "bainanama" dated 31.05.1999, there was stipulation that the plaintiff would get the sale deed executed and registered within 3(three) months and the plaintiff instituted the suit on 23.04.2003 so the same was barred by limitation. The defendants further contended that since the plaintiff failed to pay the rest consideration, the defendants, taking loan from House Building Finance Corporation and from the Bank, met up the necessity of money by this time. The defendants paid tk. 26,00,000/- as interest to those financial institutions. The plaintiff was liable to pay the said amount as compensation. It was further contended that the plaintiff man-aged to get "binanamas" by practising fraud, as such, the suit should be dismissed.

4. The respondent Ayub Ali filed T.S. No.73 of 2004 (renumbered as Title Suit No.1 of 2016) against defendant appellant Hafeez Meer Mobarak Hossain and another for specifc performance of contract in respect of the land measuring .06 acre of plot No.155 appertaining to S.A. khatian No.70 of Ratandi Mouza. The defendnat No.1 executed a "bainanama" upon receiving consideration of taka 50,000/-out of total consideration of taka 1,20,000/- on 31.05.1999. He again received taka 20,000/- but he started to make pretext to execute and register the sale deed. Hence, was the suit.

5. The defendant No.1 also contested this suit making similar statements as they had made in Title Suit No.2 of 2006.

6. The trial Court, considering the pleadings and evidence on record, dismissed both the suits but directed the defendants to repay tk.12,50,000/- to the plaintiff within 45 days, failing which, the plaintiff would realize the said amount with 10% interest. Against the said judgment and decree, the plaintiff preferred First Appeals No.05 of 2007 and 6 of 2007 in the High Court Division and the High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and decree, allowed both the appeals and decreed the suits directing the defendants to execute and register sale deed upon receiving the rest consideration.

7. Thus the defendant No.1 has preferred these two appeals upon getting leave.

8. Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant submits that having regard to the established principle of law that the plaintiff, in order to get a decree in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract, must prove that he was always ready and willing to perform his part, that is, he must prove that he offered the rest consideration for getting the sale deed registered. In this case, the plaintiff failed to prove that he offered the rest consideration within the stipulated time as provided in the agreement for sale, the High Court Division erred in law in decreeing the suit. He further submits that the High Court Division misdirected itself in decreeing the suits without reversing the finding of the trial Court. He, lastly, submits that the High Court Division erred in law in decreeing the suits for Specific Performance of Contract inasmuch as the suit lands were enlisted as vested and non-resident property.

9. Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent No.1, submits that the High Court Division upon proper appreciation of the evidence on record decreed the suits and there is no illegality in the judgment and decrees of the High Court Division. He submits that the bainanamas are admitted and the defendants took money in different times and dates and the plaintiff has proved the story or payment of those amounts and, lastly, he offered the rest consideration to get sale the sale deeds registered, the High Court Division rightly decreed the suit.

10. The plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.72 of 2003 for specific performance of contract on 23.04.2003 stating that in order to purchase the suit land at a consideration of tk.54,63,750/-, he came to an agreement dated 31.05.1999 with the defendants who upon receiving a sum of tk.12,50,000/- executed the "bainanama". It is further case of the plaintiff that on 21.05.2000 the plaintiff paid a sum of tk.5,00,000/-, that is, in total, he paid tk.17,50,000/-. By way of amendment of the pleading the plaintiff further stated that, thereafter, he had paid tk.7,55,000/- and then tk.6,0,5000/- in different dates. According to the plaintiff, he had paid a sum of tk.36,35,483/- for the suit land and only tk.18,28,267/- was remained as unpaid.

11. To prove the payments, allegedly made after execution of "bainanama", the plaintiff produced exhibit-2 (acknowledgement receipt). He deposed that he had paid tk.3,55,000/- on 20.11.2000, tk.5,25,483/- on 09.09.2000, tk.1,00,000/- on 21.11.2000, tk.1,00,000/- 23.01.2001, tk.1,00,000/- on 04.02.2001 and tk.20,000/- on 25.02.2001. He paid those amounts through exhibit-2 (acknowledgement receipt) which was admitted in evidence with objection. From exhibit-2 it appears that the plaintiff allegedly paid a sum of tk.5,25,483/- on 09.09.2000, tk.3,55,000 on 20.11.2000, tk.2,00,000/- on 22.11.2000, tk.1,00,000/- on 23.01.2001, tk.1.00,000/- on 04.02.2001 and tk.20,000 on 25.02.2001. The defendants challenged the authenticity of the exhibit 2 seriously stating that the same was a torged document. Accordingly, ext.2 was sent for examination seeking opinion of hand writing expert upon comparing the signatures of the plaintiff appeared in the ext.2 those, with the admitted or proved signature of the plaintiff and the handwriting expert, holding examination of the signatures appeared in Ext.2 those with the specimen signature of the plain-tiff; opined that, “ আলোচ্য খ, খ-১ হইতে খ-১৮ চিহ্নিত স্বাক্ষরগুলি সাথে প্রাপ্তি ১০ টাকার পাত্রে থাকা মীর মোবারক হোসেন নামীয় ক, ক-১ হইতে ক-৫ চিহ্নিত স্বাক্ষরগুলি পরীক্ষা করিলে আপাতঃ দৃষ্টিতে- কিছুটা সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ মনে হইলেও উহাদের সাথে পূংখানুপূংখ রুপে পরীক্ষা করিলে দেখা যায় যে, উহারা একই হাতের সম্পাদিত নহে।” Handwriting expert was examined as P.W.6 who proved the report (ext.1). The trial Court on consideration of the report of hand writing expert, oral evidence and after comparing the signatures of plaintiff as appeared in exhibit-2 those with the admitted signature of the plaintiff, came to the conclusion that exhibit-2 was forged document and the plaintiff has failed to prove the story of payment of the amount as mentioned in exhibit-2 to the defendants. Accordingly, the trial court dismissed the suit directing the defendant-appellants to pay sum of tk.12,50,000/-, that is, the earnest money mentioned in the "bainanama". The trial Court disbelieved the story of all other alleged transactions of the plaintiff with the defendants in respect of the suit land. The High Court Division, being the last Court of facts, without reversing the aforesaid finding of the trial Court, erroneously reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and decreed the suit.

12. It was the legal duty of the High Court Division as the last Court of facts to state in its judgment the reasons for its decision. It must set forth the evidence relied upon and must come to its own independent conclusion upon consideration of the evidence while reversing the findings of the trial Court. The object of the provisions of Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure in making it incumbent on the appellate Court to raise points for determination, is to consider the pleadings, evidence adduced by the parties and rival contentions of the parties which are absent in the appellate judgment of this case.

13. We have gone through the evidence and other materials on record. It appears to us that the discussion and conclusion as arrived at by the trial Court, so far the same relates to exhibit-2 is concerned that the same is forged one, has got basis. Except the story of payment of tk.12,50,000/- at the time of execution of the "bainanama", the plaintiff failed to prove the subsequent payments so far the same relates to transfer of the suit land. Production of forged document for getting relief of specific performance of contract, which is equitable and discretionary relief, was an uncleaned attempt of the plaintiff The High Court Division has committed error of law in reversing the well reasoned judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit without reversing the finding in respect of Ext.2, acknowledgment receipt of the alleged payment.

14. In respect of C.A. No.350 of 2016 arising out of Title Suit No.1 of 2006 it appeals that the land measuring an area of .06 acre of Plot No.158 as described in the schedule to the plaint of this suit was enlisted as vested and non-resident property and the same has not yet been released. Accordingly, the trial Court held that the instant suit in respect of vested property was not maintainable. The High Court in First Appeal decreed the said suit without reversing the aforesaid finding as to its maintainability, thereby, committed an error of law.

<u>15. However, since the plaintiff had paid a sum of tk.12,50,000/- to the defendants in 1999 as earnest money and that amount is still lying with the defendant-appellants, we are of the view that the ends of justice would best be met if we allow solatium of tk.12,50,000/- to the plaintiff-respondent.</u>

<u>16. Thus, both the appeals are allowed. Impugned judgment and decrees of the High Court Division are set aside. However, the defendant-appellants are directed to pay sum of tk.25,00,000/- (12,50,000 as earnest money+ 12,50,000 as solatium) to the plaintiff respondent within three months from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Surendra Kumar Sinha CJ. Since the subject matter of these appeals are identical they are disposed of by this judgment. The dispute relates to a house on Plot No.33 (New), Road Nc.45, 90, Gulshan Commercial Area (Dhaka).

2. Short facts are that the above plot in question was put on auction for sale by Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakka (RAJUK) on 13.2.1990. Appellant Dr. Md. Habibullah's bid was highest, but RAJUK did not accept his offer for various reasons. Again the property was advertised for auction sale. Dr. Md. Habibullah filed Writ Petition No.585 of 1990 challenging the said publication of notice. The matter ultimately came up before this court in Civil Petition No.125 of 1999, in which, there was an observation that RAJUK shall hold fresh auction and that Dr. Md. Habibullah should be given an option to purchase at the highest bid amount if he did not become the highest bidder. Thereafter, RAJUK again invited tender for auction sale and in terms of the direction given by this court Dr. Habibullah requested RAJUK to inform the highest bid price so that he could match with the price. RAJUK did not communicate him anything in pursuance of his letter. He then filed Writ Petition No.1670 of 2003 seeking a direction upon RAJUK for communicating the highest bid. The rule was made absolute but RAJUK did not comply with the direction. He then filed Writ Petition No.4445 of 2008 for execution of the lease deed and to hand over possession upon receiving the highest bid money. In the said writ petition Anwar Alam, respondent was added as writ-respondent by order dated 5.3.2014. Civil Appeal No.201 of 2015 arose out of the said order.

3. Respondent Anwar Alam filed a writ of mandamus (Writ Petition No.1779 of 2004) against RAJUK to mutate his name in respect of the disputed plot. Rule was made absolute by the High Court Division on 21.4.2004. Against the said judgment RAJUK filed Civil Petition No.287 of 2005 in this court. This petition was dis-missed for non-prosecution by order dated 12.6.2005. Pursuant thereto the disputed plot was mutated in the name of Anwarul Alam with RAJUK on 17.11.2005. Subsequently, on the basis of an inquiry report as per direction of the concerned Ministry RAJUK cancelled the mutation of the plot. Anwar Alam filed Title Suit No.113 of 2006 for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in respect of the said plot. The suit was dismissed on 11.11.2009. Anwar Alam then filed First Appeal No.349 of 2009. The suit was ultimately decreed on compromise in the High Court Division. In the suit Dr. Md. Habibullah prayed for addition of party. His prayer was rejected and the High Court Division affirmed the said order. This has given rise to Civil Appeal No.202 of 2015.

4. Other appeal being Civil Appeal No.203 of 2015 arose out of Civil Petition No.970 of 2015 which arose from a judgment passed by the High Court Division in refusing to condone the delay in filing review petition by Dr. Md. Habibullah against the compromise decree passed in First Appeal No.349 of 2009.

5. Mr. Moudud Ahmed has taken us to the concise statements and other documents.

In support of the appeals he has submitted a written argument and a chart showing different events basing upon which various litigations had cropped up over the plot in question. The substance of the argument of Mr. Moudud Ahmed is as under:-

(i) the compromise petition filed in the High Court Division was by suppressing material facts such as injunction order passed in Writ Petition No.4445 of 2008, judgments passed in Writ Petition Nos.7530 of 2008, 1670 of 2003, and Civil Revision No.611 of 2007, and had this fact been placed before the High Court Division, it would not have passed the decree for compromise.

(ii) The compromise decree was unlawful, inasmuch as, it was filed in violation of Order 23 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

(iii) There was misconduct on the part of RAJUK's lawyer, inasmuch as, he did not press Civil Petition No.287 of, 2005 preferred against judgment passed in Writ Petition No.1779 of 2000. More so, he had not obtained written authority from RAJUK for not pressing the writ petition. (iv) There was misconduct on the part of the government's lawyer, inasmuch as, without filing power the Deputy Attorney General submitted the High Court Division that the government had no objection in effecting compromise in the first appeal.

(v) The lawyer appearing for the RAJUK in connivance with the other side consented the compromise petition.

(vi) Since gigantic fraud has been perpetrated in obtaining the decree this court has inherent, power to look into the matter.

6. In support of his contention h4 has referred to some decisions.

7. There is little scope to address the points raised by Mr. Moudud Ahmed because of the fact that Civil Appeal No.201 of 2015 has been preferred against an order allowing the respondent Anwar Alam to be added as writ respondent No.11. In the application the respondent stated that though he has right, title and interest in respect of the plot in question, he has not been impleaded in the writ petition. In support of his claim he has enclosed documents. Admittedly various litigations are pending between the appellant and the respondent over the plot and that he has obtained a decree on the basis of compromise in First Appeal No.349 of 2009 arising out of Title Suit No.113 of 2006 and in fact the appellant has filed a review petition against the compromise decree. Writ petition No.4445 of 2008 has been filed by the appellant for a direction upon RAJUK to lease out the disputed plot in his favour on receipt of the highest bid money. From the very relief claimed in the writ petition, it is apparent that the respondent is a necessary party in the writ petition and the High Court Division has rightly added him as writ respondent No.11. This appeal is thus liable to be dismissed on this ground.

8. Civil Appeal No.202 of 2015 has arisen by leave from a judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.7530 of 2008 in which the High Court Division made the rule absolute and directed the writ respondent No.3 RAJUK to revoke the order of cancellation of the mutation made in favour of the respondent Anwar Alarm. The High Court Division noticed that in pursuance of the judgment passed by the High Court Division on 21.8.2004 in Writ Petition No.1779 of 2004, Anwar Alam's name was mutated on 17.11.2005. More so, the respondent's right, title and interest has been declared in F.A.No.349 of 2009 by compromise. The RAJUK cancelled the mutation order pursuant to an inquiry report at the behest of the Ministry. Since mutation was made in pursuance of a judgment of the High Court Division, neither RAJUK nor concerned Ministry has/had right or authority to sit over the judgment of the High Court Division.

9. In this connection Mr. Moudud Ahmed has stressed upon the inquiry report from which he submits that a gigantic fraud has been perpetrated in obtaining the compromise decree in appeal. This inquiry was held pursuant to an application made by Momtaz Hasan Chowdhury, the defendant No.1 in Title Suit No.420 of 2006 and the respondent No.3 in Civil Appeal No.203 of 2015 addressing the Secretary, Ministry of Works. This inquiry report cannot be taken as evidence particularly when the matter in dispute has been adjudicated upon by the civil court, the High Court Division and this court. We fail to understand how the observations made by the inquiry committee have been given precedence over the judgment of the High Court Division. If this, process is allowed there will be no need on the part of the litigants to take shelter to the court of law. This is none of the functions of the executive and RAJUK has undermined the authority of the High Court Division in cancelling the mutation order.

<u>10. The High Court Division, in the premises, acted no illegality in making the rule absolute. Whether or not fraud has been perpetrated by the respondent in obtaining decree is a disputed question of fact and this issue cannot be decided in a summary proceeding. The decisions referred to by Mr. Moudud Ahmed in National Engineers Limited V. Jubak Housing and Real Estate Development Limited, 67 DLR(AD)176; Master Abdul, Aziz V. Abani Mohan Mukherjee, 30 DLR(SC)221; MIS Hajee Mohammad Ali & Sons V. Burma Eastern Ltd.; 38 DLR(AD) 41, Jahanara Begum V. Md. Aminul Islam Chowdhury; 2 MLR(AD)216, Deputy Commissioner V. Md. Aswab Ali; 53 DLR(AD)186, Md. Nurul Huq @ M.N.Huq V. Nirmal Chandra Dutta; 7ADC 87, S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu V. Jagannath(dead), 1994(1SCC)1 have no manner of application in the facts of the given case. We do not dispute the statements of law expressed in those cases but the applicability of the opinions expressed therein depends upon the facts in a given case. So we are not inclined to examine the decisions in support of the cases.</u>

11. Mr. Moudud Ahmed has given emphasis in Civil Appeal No.203 of 2015 and vigorously argued that in the interest of justice, this appeal should be allowed ignoring the technicalities. Before addressing question raised by Moudud Ahmed, it is pertinent to examine the impugned order out of which this appeal has arisen. Pursuant to a review petition filed under Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by Dr. Md. Habibullah, the High Court Division issued a rule on the question of delay of 868 days in filing the review of the compromise decree passed in F.A.No.349 of 2009. The High Court Division disbelieved the explanation for delay on the reasoning that the appellant impliedly challenged the compromise decree by filling Title Suit No.890 of 2014 in the First of Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka, and that it is stated in the pleadings that he came to know about the existence of compromise decree on 05.0.3.2014, but the appellant was conspicuously silent about the delay from 05.03.2014 to 10.06.2014. It further observed that since the compromise decree is the subject matter in Title Suit No.890 of 2014, the explanation for delay does not inspire confidence; that the appellant can agitate this point in the suit and that if the appellant could not get remedy in Title Suit No.890 of 2014, his remedy lies in the appellate forum.

12. Respondent Anwar Alam instituted the suit in question against Momtaz Hasan Chowdhury and others seeking different declarations including a declaration of title in respect of the disputed plot. The trial court dismissed the suit and on appeal from the said judgment, a Division Bench of the High Court Division decreed the suit on compromise between the plaintiffs and the defendant Nos.1-6. In the suit RAJUK and its officials have been made as defendant Nos.7-9. The High Court Division allowed the compromise observing that the terms of compromise are not contrary to law; that though there was appearance on behalf RAJUK through Mr. Waliul Islam, he did not oppose the prayer for compromise and that the Deputy Attorney General also did not oppose the petition. We find no error in the decision of the High Court Division.

<u>13. On the question of fraud argued by Mr. Ahmed we find no substance at all, inasmuch as, the defendant No. 9, the Secretary Ministry of Works and Housing did not contest the suit, and the defendant Nos.7 and 8 RAJUK though appeared did not contest the suit. Under the amended provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, the plaintiff is not required to substitute the heirs of the uncontested defendant, and the appellate court may pass a decree in the absence of substitution of the heirs of deceased defendant. The same principle is applicable in respect of allowing a petition for compromise because the non-contesting defendants have waived their right to contest the suit. His remedy, if any, is by filing an appeal in the higher forum, if he is at all aggrieved by the compromise decree, on limited point of law only. More so, the High Court Division's order shows that it was made in presence of RAJUK and the Government and that they did not oppose the compromise.</u>

14. Now the question is whether the court can look into the alleged fraud in obtaining the compromise decree where the lessor RAJUK did not dispute and/or challenge the compromise decree as yet. Despite its full knowledge about the decree, it did not file any appeal. The government is not a necessary party rather it may be a proper party, but RAJUK is a necessary party in the suit. If the lessor relinquishes its right, title and interest whatever might have, how a third party who has no semblance of interest can challenge the compromise decree? The respondent does not seek any relief against the appellant in the suit. He seeks relief against some private individuals and RAJUK.

15. Appellant has not .gotten any lease hold right in respect of the disputed property. His basis of claiming interest in the property is the observations made by this court that in the event of selling the plot in auction, the appellant may be given an opportunity to match the highest price to be bided. This Court made the above observation overlooking the other litigations as those facts were not placed before it. This observation does not confer any right or interest upon, the appellant to review the compromise decree because-it relates to an opportunity in the event of selling the land in auction by RAJUK and not otherwise.

<u>16. What's more, the real owner RAJUK does not dispute the compromise decree and therefore, the question of selling the land in auction does not arise. After a decree passed by a court of law, how RAJUK would put the plot in auction is not clear to us. This observation is an obiter dictum, inasmuch as, it is not an issue in the matter before this court. If the appellant is given an opportunity to match with the highest bidder's offer, the auction sale would become a mockery. Nobody would participate in the auction sale if he knows that whatever might be the price to be quoted, his .offer would not be accepted and in that case, why such party would participate in the auction sale by making deposit of certain percentage of the price. Secondly, the appellant in such circumstances, would have the opportunity of arranging a collusive sale at a low price by setting up 3/4 bidders of his choice and claimed to deposit the highest price. This auction process would render an arbitrary transaction. If the appellant has no right or interest in the disputed plot, he has no right to seek review of the judgment passed in F. A. No.349 of 2009.</u>

17. A review is available under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure if there is discovery of new and important matter or evidence which after exercise of due diligence was not within the applicant's knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when decree was passed or order was made or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record or for any other sufficient reason. The question of discovery of evidence does not arise since the appellant was not a party to the suit. Now the question is whether he can file a review 'for any other sufficient reason'. The words have been interpreted by seven member Bench in Chhajju Ram V. Neki, 49 Indian Appeal(I.A.) 144 AIR 1922 PC 112. In that case it was observed that the words 'any other sufficient reasons', if it were all, 'would naturally be read asmeanina sufficiency of a kind analogous to the two already specified, that is to say, to excusable failure to bring to the notice of the court new and important matters, or error on the face of the record. But before adopting this restricted construction of the expression 'sufficient' it is necessary to have in mind, in the first place, that the provision as to review was not introduced into the code for the first time in 1908 as meaning a reason sufficient on grounds at least analogous to those specified immediately previously. This view has been approved by the Privy Council in a latter case in Bisheshwar Pratap Sabi V. Parath Nath, AIR 1934 P.C. 213, the Federal Court in Hari Shankar Paul V. Anath Nath Mitter, AIR 1949 F.C. 106 and the Supreme Court of India in M.B.B. Catholicos V. M. P. Athana Sius, AIR 1954 S.C. 526. That a decision is erroneous in law is certainly no ground for ordering review. If the court has decided a point and decided it erroneously, the error could not be one apparent on the face of the record.

<u>18. The words 'error apparent on the face of the record' means if applicant fails to satisfy the court that he could not collect the evidence as he had no knowledge about the case. In that case also he must have a right in the property and he must be a party to the litigation. Every error will not attract - the error must be one which is apparent on the face of the record. No error can be said to be an error apparent on the face of the record if it is not self-evident and requires elaborate examination (Tangabhadra Industries V. A:P., AIR, 1964 S.C. 1372). In that case it has been held that where without any elaborate argument one could point to the error and say, here is a substantial point of law which stares one in the face, and there could reasonably be no two opinions entertained about it, a clear case of error apparent on the face of the record would be made out.</u>

<u>19. An error which is not self evident and has to be detected by process of reasoning can hardly be said to be an error apparent on the face of the record. If any patent glaring mistake is detected or there being an element of indefiniteness inherent in its very nature, the court has power to reopen the matter. It must be a patent error which can be seen by a mere perusal of the record without reference to any other matter or an omission on the part of the Court overlooking a proposition of law well settled by the apex court (CST V. Pine Chemicals (1995) 1 SCC 58).</u>

<u>20. Second point is the question of limitation. The court must be strict on the question of limitation so far as it relates to review is concerned. In the Limitation Act a very short period of time is provided it the schedule for review of a judgment, and the object and purpose for such limitation is obvious. There should be an end of litigation and the court is strict to the period of limitation unless there are compelling reasons on the part of the applicant in no making the petition in time, which was beyond his control. The court in exceptional case can condone the delay Secondly, if there is alternative remedy available to the applicant, there is no scope to review the judgment by condoning the delay. The High Court Division has rightly observed that the appellant if at all is aggrieved can raise this point in his suit. Therefore, we find that the High Court Division is perfectly justified in no condoning the delay.</u>

21. The appeals are accordingly dismissed.

End.
